fell.objection: The edge as posed asked two things — institutional continuity Rowbotham → UZS → Shenton, and whether Blount's UZS is the documented intermediary — and the reviewer's own text answers NO to both, at both hops, with counter-evidence. "partly_documented" is earned only by silently changing edge_type to "textual_descent" and grading a relation that was not asked about. That surviving positive half rests on exactly one source (Garwood 2007, pp. 220-222) that nobody on this project has opened; it reaches the report through a Wikipedia footnote. I independently re-tried and confirm the block (archive.org full-text search returns 502/connection-reset through this proxy, the Google Books API returns quota 0, and the books.google.com search page returns no snippet), so the finding stands as "a wiki carrying a load-bearing claim about what a book says". Meanwhile the project's own principal scholarly source, Schadewald ch. 9 — written from the Shenton correspondence — says nothing about Shenton discovering Rowbotham's book, and both Schadewald and Moore say Shenton's system differed from the earlier flat-earthers'. The honest label for E04 as posed is not_documented, with the textual-descent anecdote recorded as a separate, thin, second-hand edge at low confidence. As labelled, E04 sits on the positive side of the "12 of 12 hold, zero not_documented" ledger that its own reasoning refutes.

Dubay's Airy paragraph agrees with MALCOLM BOWDEN against Galileo Was Wrong at four diagnostic points, and every word Dubay shares with GWW is also present in Bowden. Bowden's version of the argument is attested in print in 2002 — four years before GWW — in a source already sitting in this project's own genealogy doc, cited to the very page (Journal of Creation 16(2), p.80) whose next section is headed "(iv) 'Airy's failure'". Dubay credits Bowden by name for this material on his own forum. So GWW is excluded as Dubay's proximate exemplar, and Sungenis/Bennett cannot be shown to be the origin of the sentences either.

The verdict label does not describe the edge that was claimed. E11's claim (review/_edge_candidates.json) is "Esoteric iconography from Manly P. Hall reaching the flat-earth/firmament lane," PER-HALL to PER-SKIBA. Every element of that claim is negated by evidence the reviewer gathered and I reproduced independently: Hall and the iconography vocabulary are absent from both searchable Skiba flat-earth corpora; the one Hall citation sits in a 2011 Great Seal page containing zero occurrences of "flat earth"; and the iconography that did reach Skiba's firmament lane arrives inside a credited Robert Schadewald block quote. "partly_documented" is earned only by substituting a narrower, unclaimed edge - "Skiba cited Hall once, off-topic and off-lane" - for the one on the board. The reviewer says as much in plain words ("it must not be drawn into the flat-earth/firmament cluster", "our own record does not claim this edge", "E11 looks like a diagram hypothesis"), then files a positive-family label anyway. Compare the batch's other split verdicts: in E07 the documented half is inside the claim (succession documented, corpus inheritance not); in E12 a Blavatsky text is documented reaching the movement's own organ. E11 has no half inside the claim. Correct label: not_documented, with the 2011 Hall citation recorded as an off-lane note. This is the specific case that produces the "12 of 12, none negative" aggregate the parent suspected - E11 is the candidate that came back negative and was scored positive.

source_problems.problem: Both sources tagged kind:'scholarly' — Schadewald's The Plane Truth and Forrest's More Things in Heaven and Earth — are self-published personal-website texts. The cantab.net e-books index lists both under 'First published on this site' (c.2015; Schadewald died in 2000), i.e. never print-published, not peer-reviewed, posted by Michael Behrend. The site's description of Schadewald as 'an acknowledged authority' is a publisher's blurb, not a credential. They are the best available sources and I found nothing in them that is wrong, but under the house rule 'say what it is' they should be labelled unpublished/self-published secondary, not flatly 'scholarly'.

The scholarly tier of this edge consists entirely of two websites. Christine Garwood, Flat Earth: The History of an Infamous Idea (Macmillan 2007) — the one properly published monograph covering exactly Rowbotham, Carpenter, Hampden and the Bedford Level — is cited in the very Wikipedia article the record audited, and was not consulted. That is the gap to close before this edge is called settled scholarship rather than settled primary evidence.

Source 1 is described as 'Carpenter, One Hundred Proofs (Baltimore 1885), full text'. The Gutenberg #55387 text reprints press notices dated 22 May 1886 and 5 June 1886, so the scanned copy is a later issue than its 1885 title page. Given the README's note that edition dates have caught this project out twice, the citation should read '1885 title page; text includes 1886 additions'. Direction is unaffected — still 20 years after 1865.

The record's 'says' field for Schadewald renders the key sentence as 'Theoretical Astronomy is entirely derivative... Carpenter had obviously absorbed'. The elided clause is 'even though the early chapters were published before Rowbotham's Earth Not a Globe' — i.e. the ellipsis swallows the chronology qualifier. The record does carry that point separately in its own caveat, so this is a presentation flaw rather than a misreading, but the ellipsis hides exactly what a skeptic needs to see.

Forrest's More Things in Heaven and Earth is co-credited on the source site to Patrick Moore and Bob Forrest ('a belated sequel to Patrick Moore's Can You Speak Venusian?'). The record cites it to Forrest alone.

Schadewald's load-bearing verbs on the descent claim are inferential — 'obviously absorbed', 'evidently had'. The record passed those through as though documentary. They are now redundant: Carpenter's own 1864-66 statement that he copied the passages from a Parallax publication supersedes the inference, and the record should cite that primary line rather than lean on Schadewald's adverbs.

Wikipedia is correctly flagged and correctly refused. I re-checked the wikitext: the 'with Carpenter's assistance' and 'mostly printed by Carpenter' sentences carry a single ref, Parallax, Zetetic Astronomy 3rd ed. 1881 (sacred-texts za32.htm), which does not support either. The record's handling of this is exemplary and should be the template for the other eleven edges.

Schadewald, The Plane Truth — labelled 'scholarly' in the sources block with no statement of what it is. Its own index page: the book 'was incomplete at the time of his death, and has been lightly edited for publication here', first published on Michael Behrend's personal site in 2015, copyright Wendy S. Schadewald. An unfinished posthumous typescript edited by a third party, by a genuine authority, with a full reference apparatus — but not a peer-reviewed monograph, and it should be labelled as the former. Not load-bearing here because the artefact and the MARC record attest the same object independently.

MIS-CITED LOCATION. The sources block attributes to Chapter 5 that it 'documents Carpenter's own later editions (12th, 13th) with author's notes running to 1892-97'. I fetched Chapter 5 and grepped it: the strings 12th and 13th do not occur there. The substance is correct but lives on the References page — [4.6] notes to the 12th ed. dated 12 Oct 1892; [4.33] and [4.35] notes to the 13th ed., p. 78; [4.34] a notice dated 29 March 1897; [5.3], [5.12], [5.19] notes to the 12th ed. This is precisely the failure mode the report itself invokes against source-genealogy.md: a citation verified as existing rather than as saying what was attributed to it.

NAME ERROR, twice, in new_person_needed and reasoning: 'M. C. Morse'. Schadewald's Bostonian is CHARLES W. MORSE, a 64-year-old Brookline 'practical watch and clock repairer' who published the 78-page Unpopular Truth in 1913. If he ever reaches the page, distinguish him from the identically named financier.

UNSCOPED ABSENCE inside a corroborating sentence: 'a publisher-field query of Open Library for Wilbur Glenn Voliva returns exactly one book IN THE WORLD'. It returns one book in Open Library (numFound 1, which I re-ran and confirmed). Open Library publisher-field indexing is patchy and derived from contributed MARC, so on its own this is weak corroboration; the Schadewald sentence carries the point. The scope_note is meticulous, which makes the slip in the reasoning field more likely to be repeated downstream.

Open Library and WorldCat are one OCLC record exposed twice, not two witnesses. The report says so explicitly and does not double-count it — noted here only so a downstream reader counting 'three ways' does not read it as three independent attestations. The genuinely independent pair is (i) the photographed physical object Schadewald handled and (ii) the San Francisco Public Library MARC record.

CONFLICT TO REPORT, NOT TO SETTLE: E03 says no full-text 1881 scan was located on archive.org; E06, in the same report file, says it pulled 'Rowbotham 3rd ed. 1881 (archive.org, the enlarged 430pp text)' and used it as a rival ancestor. Both cannot be right. My own check favours E03 on the substance and finds E06's description inaccurate: the item (archive.org/metadata/zeteticastronomy-earthnotaglobe) is a user upload whose metadata title is 'Zetetic Astronomy - Earth Not a Globe 1865', which also bundles Dubay's 200 Proofs, and whose 3e text file stops at page 254 — before ch.15 (p.255) and ch.16 (p.289) listed in its own contents. It is not a 430pp text and it is not a library scan. E06's use of it as a discriminating rival ancestor should be audited.

My own new evidence carries the same caveat: /tmp/za3e.txt and /tmp/za3e_fresh.txt are that unprovenanced re-typeset, with no imprint page in the extraction. My page-37 identification rests on its internal consistency with its own table of contents, not on an examined copy of the 1881 printing. It also cannot discriminate the 1873 second edition from the 1881 third.

The LoC guide is a library research guide reproducing a catalogue record — encyclopaedic, correctly labelled as such in the report, but it is now proposed as the authority for recording a 1897 first edition. It rests on the LC catalogue alone, with no examined copy, and diverges from Winship's own 'unpretentious pamphlet of 48 pages' (46 vs 48). The report flags this; keep the flag when the record changes.

Guimont 2026 (Springer) is cited but unread behind a paywall. The report claims nothing from it beyond the citation pattern, which is the right handling — but it must not later be upgraded into scholarly support for this edge by anyone reading the source list alone.
TFES wiki is movement-internal and is used only as negative evidence (the movement does not itself assert this lineage). Correctly labelled; do not let it migrate into the positive column.

Garwood 2007, pp. 220-222 is the ONLY support for the one thing E04 grades positively, and it is read at second hand via the Wikipedia Samuel Shenton article. I confirmed the wikitext: the 'instant convert' paragraph is footnoted {{harvnb|Garwood|2007|pp=220-222}}, and I confirmed independently that the book cannot be reached from here (archive.org item flatearthhistory0000garw exists, but its search-inside endpoints return 502 / connection reset through the proxy; books.googleapis.com returns quota_limit_value 0; the books.google.com in-volume search page returns no snippet). A verdict of confidence 'medium' rests on a Wikipedia sentence reporting a book.

Schadewald, The Plane Truth, is tagged kind='scholarly' on three of the ten sources and carries the decisive negative plus most of the report's dating corrections. Its own Preface, by Lois Schadewald, says the book 'has been a work in progress since at least 1984', is 'unfinished in places', and 'remained unfinished because Bob felt that it never met his standards closely enough to be published' (https://www.cantab.net/users/michael.behrend/ebooks/PlaneTruth/pages/Preface.html). It is an author-unpublished, non-peer-reviewed, posthumously web-posted manuscript by a science writer, hosted on a private site. It is the best available history and I found it accurate everywhere I checked it, but the house rule is to say what a source is.

The report asserts of the movement's own wiki: 'Even the movement does not assert an institutional handover from the UZS to Shenton.' That is an unscoped absence and it is false. The sibling page on the same wiki, https://wiki.tfes.org/Universal_Zetetic_Society (raw text retrieved), opens 'The Universal Zetetic Society (UZS) was the precursor to the Flat Earth Society' and states 'In 1971, the UZS was revived as The Flat Earth Society when Samuel Shenton became its leader.' The reviewer sampled only wiki.tfes.org/Flat_Earth_Society and generalised. This does not make the handover documented — the page is movement-internal and its date is wrong — but the rhetorical point built on it collapses.

Patrick Moore is used selectively: the circular, the 23 November meeting, the 'It will die' quotation and 'not the same as those of the Flat Earthers of the early twentieth century' are all taken as authoritative (I verified each verbatim in the PDF), while the same author's adjacent sentence, 'Following a period of comparative inactivity, the British branch of the I.F.E.S. was revived in 1956', is discounted as 'a memoirist's loose phrase'. Same page, same eyewitness. Moore also writes that the November meeting 'put the Society back on a really firm footing', and Schadewald independently says Shenton was 'trying to revive the British flat-earth movement'. Two independent sources use revival language; the report should record that conflict rather than dissolve it.

The 1906 back-cover notice is dismissed as retrospective self-description that 'Schadewald contradicts'. Schadewald in fact corroborates both of its dates: ch. 7 has de Lacy Evans as 'vice president of the original Zetetic Society when it formed in December 1883', and ch. 4 refers to 'the original Zetetic some twenty years earlier' than 1892, i.e. c. 1872-73, matching the notice's 'New York in Sept., 1873'. The sources agree on dates and disagree only about continuity of the body. Reported as a flat contradiction, it picks a side.

record_problems[0] says Blount was 'one of twenty-four committee members' of the founding body, cited to Schadewald ch. 4. 'twenty-four' does not appear in ch. 4; it is ch. 7's count of the 1906 reorganised committee. Ch. 4 names a nine-member founding Committee (Williams, Albert Smith, Perry, Isaac and John Smith, Adams, Naylor, Skellam, Lady Blount).

new_person_needed calls John Williams 'the founder of record'. Schadewald never says that: he calls him 'the founding Secretary' and writes that the founding meeting 'was apparently held' at his home — a hedge, carrying ref. 4.2. The same chapter elsewhere writes 'the UZS (as reorganized under Lady Blount)', and ch. 7 has her 'now president', bankrolling it, over 'the new Universal Zetetic Society'. So the repo's shorthand 'Lady Elizabeth Blount's Universal Zetetic Society' needs its date fixed (1892, not 1893), not the flat correction the report demands. This inverts the project's own hedge rule: the report beats the repo's compressed phrasing using a hardened version of the source's hedge.

Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch. 9, labelled 'scholarly' in the sources array: per its own preface it is an UNFINISHED manuscript the author 'felt... never met his standards closely enough to be published', assembled posthumously by his sister and widow and web-hosted privately in 2015. Primary research, yes; peer-reviewed scholarship, no. Relabel as unpublished primary-research manuscript.

Schadewald is not independent of the beneficiary. The preface records Johnson 'once nominated me to Outstanding Young Men of America'; ch. 9's handover passage names no transferor, cites no document, and is narrated from what 'Johnson believed'. E05's reasoning treats personal acquaintance as corroboration when it is a dependency.

Garwood 2007 p. 320 is reached only through Wikipedia and was NOT verified first-hand by the original pass or by me (archive.org scrape endpoints empty; Google Books API 429 over daily quota; no independent secondary repetition located — HandWiki and markfoster.net are Wikipedia mirrors). That single unverified page supplies BOTH the 'from Lillian' transferor correction AND the SFF-archive finding that kills the 'its archive' claim. One unverified relay carrying two loads in opposite directions.

NCSE/Cole is labelled 'scholarly'. It is an obituary in Reports of the NCSE, an advocacy organisation's newsletter — better than press, not scholarship. Re-fetched: it gives no succession year and no fire date, so it corroborates the succession only, not '1972'.

Smithsonian is a popular magazine blog post containing a demonstrable error ('Johnson's good friend Samuel Shenton', contradicted by Schadewald's account of Johnson learning of Shenton from a press article). It is obituary-cycle derivative, not an independent witness to 1972.

The record's 'independent confirmation' framing overstates the NCSE / Irish Times / Smithsonian trio: two are 2001 obituaries from the same news cycle and one is a 2016 popular retelling. What they jointly establish is that Johnson's leadership from 1972 went unchallenged for 29 years — consistent with, but not proof of, a conferred transfer.

MISSING SOURCE, new conflict: the NY Press obituary (2001) says Shenton 'requested that Johnson succeed him' before dying in 1971, contradicting Schadewald and Garwood/Wikipedia, which both name Ellis Hillman as Shenton's designated successor. Same piece also miscredits the 1956 founding to Samuel and Lillian Shenton where Schadewald says Shenton and William Mills. Not in the record; should be reported as a conflict, not silently dropped.

No contemporaneous 1971-72 document of conferral was located by either pass — no Flat Earth News masthead, no Lillian Shenton correspondence, and the California Secretary of State business search for the incorporation filing was blocked by an Incapsula WAF on my attempt, so the one genuinely contemporaneous record on this edge remains unchecked.

Rival-ancestor panel incomplete: Scott, Terra Firma (1901) was not tested despite the report itself calling him a documented Victorian source feeding 200 Proofs directly. Consequence: the Dubay 5 / Carpenter 4 Nile pair should move from 'CONFIRMED, CARPENTER-DISTINCTIVE' to the 'would not let through' bucket, with Scott named as the textual ancestor of Dubay 4 and 5 (Terra Firma pp. 126-27). Dubay 42's Challenger 69,000/'indirect' pair does survive the expanded test, including against Scott's 70,000.

Overclaim in the reasoning: 'Dubay had Carpenter's text in hand.' What is documented is descent from Carpenter's text, not access to the 1885 Baltimore printing. The project's own doc records Voliva reprinting 100 Proofs at Zion in 1929 and Skiba reprinting the Victorians; the list is also widely reproduced online. An intermediary that reproduces Carpenter verbatim would leave identical evidence, and the 98+80 splice could itself have been inherited. This does not affect the edge type (textual_descent), only the 'in hand' phrasing.

Edition detail the record does not carry: the Gutenberg base text states on its title page '5th Edition: 6th Thousand', Baltimore 1885. So 'Carpenter 1885' is the fifth edition of a text already in circulation, and the proof numbering used throughout (36, 98, 80, 78, 4, 40, 5) is that edition's numbering. Earlier editions were not compared. This is directly relevant to the project's own known limit about Carpenter 1885 being the earliest identified rather than the first numbered list.

Pannofino 2024 (Genealogy 8(2):32) could not be re-verified in this pass: mdpi.com and doi.org both returned HTTP 403 through the agent proxy for the landing page and the PDF. I confirmed via the OpenAlex record that the article, year, journal and genealogical scope are as stated, but not the two quoted sentences. The report's 'I fetched it and the quoted sentence is genuinely there' is not reproducible from here. Not load-bearing, since the report already labels it as asserting structure rather than documenting transmission.

Absence claims rest on single OCR files ('Hatteras' 0 in the Dubay djvu; 'nile' 0 in the Rowbotham 1881 djvu). I reproduced both, but from the same files, which is corroboration of the parse rather than independent confirmation against print. State these as 'not located in <named OCR>' rather than as absences from the works. I did check OCR variants of 'Nile' in the Rowbotham scans and found none, so that particular absence is reasonably robust.

The Dubay edition is unspecified. The record does not say whether the archive.org OCR corresponds to the 2015 free PDF or the 2018 print edition, and every proof number cited is edition-dependent. The text is authentically Dubay's (it closes with his own site promos, not the 'SlightlyEdited' variant bundled in the movement-internal archive item), but the edition should be named. My parse also recovered 199 of 200 markers, missing only 111, where the report reports losing 102 and 111 - a small parse discrepancy worth noting.

FALSE NEGATIVE, load-bearing and directionally convenient. Source #11 (geocentricity.com/bibastron/ts_history/de_labore.pdf, filed as 'primary (queried, negative result)') claims 'no mention of Gerardus Bouw anywhere'. Checked: file downloaded 2026-08-10, md5 1132e04145f9d9cc960ad53a0b3556fc, pdftotext = 44,004 words; two hits for 'Bouw' — endnote 21 ('Quoted in Gerardus D. Bouw, With Every Wind of Doctrine. privately published, 1984, p.187'), endnote 22 ('Ibid. p.188'), plus 'Editor: Gerardus D. Bouw' in the back matter. The conclusion drawn from the false negative is reversed by the document.

UNCONSULTED TEXT IS THE DECIDING TEXT. Bouw, With Every Wind of Doctrine (1984) — the record notes it was not consulted but treats that as a footnote-level gap. It is not: it is now known to be quoted inside van der Kamp's 1988 Airy chapter, so it is the single text that would settle the direction of the 'Airy's failure' frame. Schadewald's Appendix D bibliography gives it as 'Cleveland: Tychonian Society, 1984'; van der Kamp's note 21 says 'privately published, 1984' — a minor imprint conflict worth recording, not resolving.

EULOGY READ AS DOCUMENTATION. The sole positive argument-credit ('Walter's pioneering work in pointing out the geocentric nature of Airy's failure ... the father of modern geocentricity') is from Bouw's editorial in the Spring 1998 memorial issue of Biblical Astronomer No. 84, printed with Elmendorf's Don Quixote tribute and Byl's obituary. Movement-internal, posthumous, running WITH the lineage story — outside the against-interest justification the record uses to license its internal sources. Evidence of what the movement says about its descent; not evidence of textual transmission.

INFERENCE ATTRIBUTED TO A SOURCE THAT DOES NOT MAKE IT. The record says Biblical Astronomer No. 67 shows 'the LABEL descends from van der Kamp'. No. 67 uses the phrase impersonally — Airy's failure to detect the added aberration 'is called “Airy’s Failure”' — credits the experiment's design to Boscovich, and names van der Kamp nowhere in that section. Bouw there explains the null by Fresnel drag and says Airy 'saw what he expected so it was a success and not a failure', which is the mainstream reading, not the geocentric one the eulogy credits to van der Kamp.

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION / CONFLATION in new_person_needed. It states Bouw learned of van der Kamp 'from Armstrong's 1976 remark in that newsletter, and from van der Kamp's Jan 1976 article “I Make Its Pillars Firm” in it.' Checked against no084 obits.pdf: the Jan 1976 Bible-Science Newsletter reading is R. G. Elmendorf's, in a signed tribute (Glenshaw PA, 17 March 1998), not Bouw's — as the record's OWN record_problems item 1 correctly states. Bouw's editorial names only Armstrong and gives no venue for his 1976 remark. The recommendation that the Bible-Science Newsletter is 'the channel' by which the lane recruited therefore rests on a venue no source states; Armstrong was first editor of the Creation Research Society Quarterly (Schadewald, App. D), so CRSQ is at least as likely.

INDEPENDENCE OVERSTATED. 'Documented, and from four independent directions' is soft. Van der Kamp and Bouw are the two parties, publishing in the same organisation's serial; the ABA history page is that organisation's own record (a third item from the same house); Faulkner (AiG, 2020) and Wikipedia are tertiary and neither shows independent sourcing. Schadewald is the only outside line, and his Appendix D selected bibliography lists no Society bulletins — so whether he is an independent witness or a careful reader of the same internal record is not shown. CONFLICT REPORTED, NOT RESOLVED: the repo's own scripts/_b8_D02.py asserts Schadewald 'wrote the movement's history from its own bulletins'; if that is right he is not an independent direction at all. I did not locate a statement of sourcing in Appendix D either way.

UNREPORTED CONFLICT WITH THE ONE TEXTUAL-INFLUENCE SOURCE. Bouw's own editorial has him arriving with the equivalence argument from undergraduate relativity coursework, finding van der Kamp's scriptural answer 'rather weak', and printing his own study in Bulletin No. 13 (1976). That flatly contradicts Wikipedia's 'reading the works of Walter van der Kamp ... became convinced'. The record downgrades Wikipedia but does not report the contradiction, which is the strongest available common-ancestor/parallel-derivation evidence against the corpus half.

SCOPE. My own negatives are bounded: I searched the de_labore.pdf and no084 obits.pdf text layers named above, the four geocentricity.com HTML pages, Schadewald Appendix D and the ABA history page. I did NOT locate With Every Wind of Doctrine (1984) or Geocentricity (1992) in any form, and did not read the Bulletin run 1-53. Nothing here should be read as 'no earlier use of “Airy’s failure” exists'.

Faulkner, Answers in Genesis, 4 Sept 2020 is the report's only non-movement source for the causal/biographical narrative, and it is presented as 'independent (non-movement) confirmation of the causal direction'. I fetched it: the sentence 'Around 2002, Sungenis read Bouw's book Geocentricity: The Biblical Cosmology and became an advocate for geocentrism a few years later' carries no citation, no source, no documentation. In the same breath it mis-titles Bouw's book (every citation inside GWW, including Bouw's own endorsement line, gives the plain title Geocentricity) and dates GWW to 2007. It is an uncorroborated secondary narrative from a partisan in an intra-creationist dispute, not confirmation. It should be labelled as such. This costs the verdict nothing only because direction is independently established by Sungenis's own page citations — but the word 'confirmation' should go.

Bouw's endorsement blurb and his book report in The Biblical Astronomer no. 117 are movement-internal mutual endorsement, contemporaneous with a consultancy Sungenis thanks him for. The report labels them correctly and explicitly declines to rest descent on them, which is the right discipline — flagged here only so the labelling is not lost downstream.

The Biblical Astronomer citation is given as 'vol. 16 no. 117, Summer 2006'. The fetched page states neither journal name, issue number, nor date; only the URL path (/ba1/no117/) supports 'no. 117'. The volume and season are inferred from elsewhere and should be marked as such.

PER-BOUW's dataset sources are Wikipedia plus creation.com/geocentric-gobbledegook — a page the corrections log in claude/source-genealogy.md forbids citing for Bouw, since it is Faulkner reviewing Marshall Hall. WRK-BOUW-1992 carries the same URL as its only link. The report flags this; it remains true that Bouw's node currently rests on a wiki and a mis-cited review.

Minor: the report puts 'geo-lock' in quotation marks as the name of the Selbrede frame-dragging argument. The string does not occur in either OCR file. The Selbrede citation itself checks out verbatim in both editions ('Geocentricity's Critics Refuse to Do Their Homework,' The Chalcedon Report, 1994, p. 11), so only the coined term is unverified.

review/edge-evidence-report.json, TFES wiki source note (movement-internal): the note says the wiki 'cites Airy's Proc. Roy. Soc. paper, a Malcolm Bowden video, Neville Thomas Jones and van der Kamp' and concludes the flat-earth side 'does not record the route the text actually took'. The raw wiki source (wiki.tfes.org/index.php?title=Airy%27s_Failure&action=raw) in fact reproduces the traveling sentences AS the Bowden video description, under a section header '==Malcolm Bowden==' — including the GWW-identical clause about the fast orbiting earth and the comparatively stationary stars. The one source in the file that names the rival carrier was read as confirming the verdict while it disconfirms it.

Malcolm Bowden, Journal of Creation (TJ) 16(2), 2002, pp. 79-82 — a dated, peer-of-record creationist periodical, already logged in the project doc claude/source-genealogy.md with a verbatim quote from p.80 — was never consulted for this edge, although the record's own problem list flags Bowden twice (as the video Dubay credits, and as the better match for the 2% figure).

'A Wyatt route would still run through the Sungenis project' rests on GWW's copyright page crediting Mark J. Wyatt for illustrations 'used by permission' plus an acknowledgement thanking him for 'insight and advice'. An image-permission credit is not evidence of authorship of prose; this inference is doing load-bearing work to close off an alternative the record admits it could not check.

Dating of Dubay's text leans on iamtymaximus.wordpress.com (11 May 2012), an uncredited movement-internal reblog. It happens not to matter — GWW 2006 precedes The Atlantean Conspiracy 2013 regardless — but it is the only anchor offered and it is a single anonymous blog.

Faulkner (Answers in Genesis, 2020) is labelled 'movement-internal' and correctly described as naming nobody, yet is listed under CORROBORATION; it supports only the movement-level direction of flow, which was never in dispute.

claude/source-genealogy.md already asserts Sungenis & Bennett are the 'Direct source of the Michelson-Gale, Sagnac, Miller, Foucault, Airy and CMB material in modern lists'. E09 was researched against a prior the doc already held, and returned it strengthened. Bowden is filed there as 'Peripheral'.

geocentricity.com/geocentricity/ (movement-internal, one landing page) carries an unscoped impossibility claim: Bouw 'is not the carrier either, and structurally cannot be'. That is an inference from model type (Tychonic abolishes nested Ptolemaic spheres), not a search of Bouw's corpus. Bouw's Geocentricity Primer (1999/2004) indeed does not mention Ptolemy — but geocentricity.com hosts 'Will the Real Number of Epicycles Stand Up?' (3rd International Conference on Absolutes, Houston, 2007), which walks through the Almagest's thirteen books and reduces Ptolemy's model to 'just nine circles' via Gingerich and Fitzpatrick. Ptolemaic material does circulate through Bouw's organisation, at exactly the same secondhand-via-historians grade as Sungenis. The scope_note's wording ('no route ... was located') is honest; the reasoning body's 'structurally cannot be' is not, and it is the reasoning body a downstream editor will read.

"Smith's 'Rise and Progress of Astronomy'" is nominated in new_person_needed as a missing intermediary WORK to be added to the record — 'the actual conduit between Ptolemy and the zetetic canon' and 'a nineteenth-century popular history'. Neither attribute is sourced. The work is known only from Rowbotham's own unfootnoted in-text citation; I did not locate a work of that title by an author named Smith in four web searches (title+author, title+quote, title+archive.org, the quoted sentence verbatim). Its century, genre and even existence as cited are being inferred from the flat-earth text that quotes it. Rowbotham's same paragraph also quotes Partington, Sir Richard Phillips and Somerville with page numbers; nominating Smith alone as 'the conduit' is a choice the evidence does not force.
flatearth.ws is filed as kind='press'. It is an anonymous debunking blog. It carries no load in this verdict (the record correctly says it supplies no carrier), but the class label overstates it.

refutations.reasoning:
Verdict stands at "documented". I tried to break it four ways and it got stronger, not weaker — but three sub-claims inside the reasoning need repair.

WHAT I VERIFIED AGAINST THE ACTUAL TEXTS (not the summary)

Edition attack — FAILED, which is the point. My first move was the one the README warns about: I suspected Gutenberg #69892 was the 1881 third edition, which would have made "Rowbotham first" edition-dependent. It is not. The title page in the file reads "London: SIMPKIN, MARSHALL, AND CO. / Bath: S. HAYWARD, GREEN STREET. 1865." It is genuinely the 1865 second edition. Both files also match the record's byte counts exactly (143,011 and 299,419), so the fetches were really run.

Quotation evidence — VERIFIED, including cut points. My first grep found no Wesley in Rowbotham; that was my error (line-wrapping plus curly quotes), and on re-check both passages are there (Rowbotham lines 466-481 Elliott, 4017-4024 Wesley). The cut points really are identical: Carpenter ends the Wesley extract at "ninety millions of miles", exactly where Rowbotham's first extract ends, omitting the vol.3 and vol.13 extracts Rowbotham goes on to give. Elliott is taken whole. Carpenter's Introduction quotes all verify verbatim at lines 183-237 and 424.

Schadewald quotes — VERIFIED verbatim, all seven probes, in Chapter_01.html.

NEW EVIDENCE THE RECORD DID NOT HAVE (settles direction outright)

I pulled Carpenter's own Theoretical Astronomy Examined and Exposed, which the record's scope_note admits was not read directly (archive.org identifier TheoreticalAstronomyExaminedAndExpos, Google scan, djvu.txt). In it Carpenter writes, in his own voice: "We quote the following passages — for which we are indebted to 'Parallax:' as we copy them from a paper, which he has published, on Zetetic Astronomy" — and there follows the balloon block (Wise, Mayhew, Elliott, London Journal) carrying Rowbotham's own framing sentence verbatim: "Mr. Elliott, an American aeronaut, in a letter giving an account of his ascension from Baltimore..."

This is the author, contemporaneously, in 1864-66, naming Rowbotham as the text he is copying from. Direction is settled by acknowledgment, not by plausibility, and it upgrades Schadewald's inference ("he evidently had a late and possibly expanded edition of Rowbotham's old Zetetic Astronomy pamphlet") from inference to documented. It also confirms and sharpens the record's own directionality caveat: the ancestor for the early Carpenter works is a pre-1865 Rowbotham paper, not the 1865 book. The volume is also dedicated "To 'PARALLAX,' The Founder of Modern Zetetic Philosophy" exactly as Schadewald reports, and its imprint reads "PRINTED BY WILLIAM CARPENTER, GREENWICH" — corroborating Forrest's "London printer" from a primary source.

WHAT I DID BREAK (repairs, not a refutation)

1. The "28 shared runs of 8+ words" does not reproduce. I re-ran the comparison on the identical files. Maximal contiguous runs of 8+ shared words: 11 with Gutenberg boilerplate stripped, 14 unstripped (4 of the 14 are licence text). Non-overlapping shingles 51/419; distinct 8-grams 361/3205. I swept N=5..14 with and without stripping; no configuration gives 28 maximal runs at N=8 (the only 28 anywhere in the sweep is non-overlapping shingles at N=13, a coincidence). The README's sourcing standard demands "a reproducible calculation"; this figure is not one. Note the qualitative claim survives and is in fact sharpened: after boilerplate there are ~7 substantive runs, and they are overwhelmingly the two quotation blocks (Wesley 65 words; Elliott 99+23+11 words) plus short generic phrases. Carpenter genuinely does not copy prose and genuinely does reproduce the quotation apparatus.

2. "Rowbotham's book is the intermediary" is wrong for the Elliott passage. Carpenter had already reprinted Elliott, with Rowbotham's framing sentence, in 1864-66. So the 1885 Elliott text may descend from Carpenter's own earlier reprint rather than from Earth Not a Globe (1865). I ran a stemmatic test on the three witnesses and it came back mixed: 1885 agrees with Rowbotham 1865 on "sink away--while" (dashes) and "As we ascend,", but agrees with his own earlier book on "Thus, upon a clear day". Since the 1864-66 witness is Google OCR of 19th-century print, punctuation variants cannot bear weight. Proximate exemplar: undetermined. Ultimate ancestor: Rowbotham on every path. Soften the named text, keep the edge.

3. The Wesley cut-point argument is weaker than presented, taken alone. Wesley does not appear in Theoretical Astronomy (searched that djvu.txt case-insensitively for "wesley" and "systems of astronomy": zero hits — OCR could in principle mangle the name), so Wesley is new in 1885 and does come from a Rowbotham book. But Rowbotham's cut point is the natural end of the Journal sentence, where any quoter would stop, and Carpenter's own 1885 press notices show him circulating in Baltimore Methodist papers (Methodist, Oct 28 1885; Western Christian Advocate, Oct 21 1885), a plausible independent channel for a Wesley quotation. It is the obscure Elliott passage carrying Rowbotham's framing sentence, not Wesley, that is the real fingerprint.

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS TESTED AND REJECTED
Common source, parallel invention and shared third text all fail against Carpenter's explicit "indebted to 'Parallax'". The one live variant is Hampden, who per Schadewald ch.2 published extracts from Earth Not a Globe with Rowbotham's permission and bought Carpenter's stock and copyright — so a Hampden intermediary is possible for some 1885 material. That changes the route, not the origin, and the record already declines to run the edge through him. Correctly.

ONE PLACE THE RECORD UNDER-REPORTS ITSELF
On the "associate" limb the record recommends downgrading to "disciple and populariser". I agree, but note it overlooked Carpenter's own phrase: the duty falls to "those, especially, who knew him personally and who labored with him in the cause of Truth against Error". That is a self-attested "laboured with him" — but it is a movement partisan's generic collective eulogy for a dead founder, not evidence of joint work. The conservative call is right; the phrase should be recorded so a future editor does not "discover" it and upgrade "disciple" back to "associate".

SCOPED ABSENCES
Not located, in: Carpenter 1885 (Gutenberg #55387), Rowbotham 1865 (#69892), Carpenter's Theoretical Astronomy (archive.org djvu.txt), Schadewald ch.1/2/5, Forrest ch.2 — any evidence of collaboration, employment or agency, or of Carpenter co-producing the 1849 pamphlet. I did not consult Rowbotham's 1849 pamphlet, the 1881 third edition, or Garwood.
refutations.strongest_objection: The "28 shared runs of 8+ words" is presented as a machine-checked result and does not reproduce: re-running the identical files gives 11 maximal runs boilerplate-stripped, 14 unstripped, and no configuration across N=5..14 yields 28. In a repo whose sourcing standard is "a public source or a reproducible calculation", a precise-sounding number that no method regenerates is exactly the kind of figure that should never have been load-bearing. Compounding it, the strand it supports is narrower than stated: the Elliott passage was already in Carpenter's own 1864-66 book, so it cannot by itself demonstrate 1885 copying from the 1865 book, and the substantive overlap after boilerplate is ~7 runs, not 28. None of this touches the verdict, because the descent limb rests on Carpenter's own explicit attribution — which I independently strengthened — rather than on the n-gram count.
source_problems: Both sources tagged kind:'scholarly' — Schadewald's The Plane Truth and Forrest's More Things in Heaven and Earth — are self-published personal-website texts. The cantab.net e-books index lists both under 'First published on this site' (c.2015; Schadewald died in 2000), i.e. never print-published, not peer-reviewed, posted by Michael Behrend. The site's description of Schadewald as 'an acknowledged authority' is a publisher's blurb, not a credential. They are the best available sources and I found nothing in them that is wrong, but under the house rule 'say what it is' they should be labelled unpublished/self-published secondary, not flatly 'scholarly'.

The scholarly tier of this edge consists entirely of two websites. Christine Garwood, Flat Earth: The History of an Infamous Idea (Macmillan 2007) — the one properly published monograph covering exactly Rowbotham, Carpenter, Hampden and the Bedford Level — is cited in the very Wikipedia article the record audited, and was not consulted. That is the gap to close before this edge is called settled scholarship rather than settled primary evidence.

Source 1 is described as 'Carpenter, One Hundred Proofs (Baltimore 1885), full text'. The Gutenberg #55387 text reprints press notices dated 22 May 1886 and 5 June 1886, so the scanned copy is a later issue than its 1885 title page. Given the README's note that edition dates have caught this project out twice, the citation should read '1885 title page; text includes 1886 additions'. Direction is unaffected — still 20 years after 1865.

The record's 'says' field for Schadewald renders the key sentence as 'Theoretical Astronomy is entirely derivative... Carpenter had obviously absorbed'. The elided clause is 'even though the early chapters were published before Rowbotham's Earth Not a Globe' — i.e. the ellipsis swallows the chronology qualifier. The record does carry that point separately in its own caveat, so this is a presentation flaw rather than a misreading, but the ellipsis hides exactly what a skeptic needs to see.

Forrest's More Things in Heaven and Earth is co-credited on the source site to Patrick Moore and Bob Forrest ('a belated sequel to Patrick Moore's Can You Speak Venusian?'). The record cites it to Forrest alone.

Schadewald's load-bearing verbs on the descent claim are inferential — 'obviously absorbed', 'evidently had'. The record passed those through as though documentary. They are now redundant: Carpenter's own 1864-66 statement that he copied the passages from a Parallax publication supersedes the inference, and the record should cite that primary line rather than lean on Schadewald's adverbs.

Wikipedia is correctly flagged and correctly refused. I re-checked the wikitext: the 'with Carpenter's assistance' and 'mostly printed by Carpenter' sentences carry a single ref, Parallax, Zetetic Astronomy 3rd ed. 1881 (sacred-texts za32.htm), which does not support either. The record's handling of this is exemplary and should be the template for the other eleven edges.

I tried to break this and could not. I re-fetched every load-bearing source rather than reading the summary, and the summary is accurate where it matters.

WHAT I VERIFIED FIRST-HAND (not from the report's paraphrase)
1. The photograph. Downloaded https://www.cantab.net/users/michael.behrend/ebooks/PlaneTruth/images/Carpenter_pamphlet_100_Proofs.jpg (1125x829 JPEG, HTTP 200) and looked at it. The left cover is legible and matches the report's transcription: "ONE HUNDRED PROOFS THAT THE EARTH IS NOT A GLOBE / Dedicated to Richard A. Proctor, Esq. 'The Greatest Astronomer of the Age' / By WM. CARPENTER / Referee for John Hampden, Esq., in the Celebrated Scientific Wager, in 1870; Author of 'Common Sense' on Astronomy (London, 1866)... / 'Upright, Downright, Straightforward' / SPECIAL EDITION / Published by WILBUR GLENN VOLIVA / Zion, Illinois, U. S. A. / 1929 / TWENTY-FIVE CENTS. Five Copies, Postage Paid, for One Dollar." The right-hand cover independently carries Carpenter's name over a flat-earth polar map, i.e. the second (1955) reprint is real too.
2. The catalogue record. openlibrary.org/books/OL22936307M.json, HTTP 200: edition_name "Special ed.", publishers ["Wilbur Glenn Voliva"], publish_places ["Zion, IL"], publish_date "1929", pagination "47 p. ;", oclc_numbers ["39522200"], by_statement "by Wm. Carpenter.", notes "Originally published: Baltimore : The author, 1885.", source_records ["marc:SanFranPL08..."]. Every field the report quotes is there, unaltered.
3. Schadewald ch. 5 caption, verbatim: "Reprints of Carpenter's pamphlet One Hundred Proofs that the Earth is Not a Globe. Left: Zion, Illinois, 1929; right: St. Petersburg, Florida, 1955."
4. Schadewald ch. 8, verbatim, and the limiting sentence is the one immediately preceding, exactly as reported: "...neither Voliva nor any of his disciples ever produced a flat-earth book, or even a pamphlet, to defend zetetic astronomy. The Christian Catholic Apostolic Church reprinted Carpenter's One Hundred Proofs that the Earth Is Not a Globe in 1929..." Also confirmed verbatim in ch. 8: the "exchanged information, documents, and (presumably) copies" network sentence; Morse's flat-earth reading list including "Carpenter's One Hundred Proofs"; Goudey's acknowledged debt to "Dr. Samuel B. Rowbotham, Prof. Wm. Carpenter, Prof. Alex. Gleason..."; and "Voliva put every title in his own name", which is the report's explanation for the split imprint attribution.
5. Re-ran the publisher query: openlibrary.org/search.json?q=publisher:"Wilbur Glenn Voliva" returns numFound 1, that one title being Carpenter's.

1. DIRECTION — unbreakable, and this is the least assumption-dependent edge of the twelve. Nothing here rests on plausibility. Carpenter died 1 September 1896 (Schadewald ch. 5, sourced to the Baltimore Sun obituary of 2 Sept 1896); Schadewald opens ch. 8 with Voliva a 26-year-old student at Hiram College at that date. The two men were never contemporary authors, so "who copied whom" cannot arise. The 1929 object carries Carpenter's name, his 1866 and 1870 credentials and his dedication; Voliva's name appears only in the "Published by" slot. Edition dates caught this project out twice before; they cannot here, because the later artefact self-identifies as a reprint of the earlier author and the catalogue note says so independently.

2. SOURCE CLASS — five real problems, none load-bearing. Listed in source_problems. The most substantive: The Plane Truth is labelled "scholarly" in the sources block without saying what it is. Its own index page states it plainly: "Bob Schadewald (1943-2000) was an authority on the history of the flat-earth movement. This book on the subject was incomplete at the time of his death, and has been lightly edited for publication here. First published on this website, 2015. Copyright (c) 2015 Wendy S. Schadewald." That is an unfinished posthumous typescript, lightly edited by a third party and hosted on a private site — not a peer-reviewed monograph. The house rule that a dealer catalogue is not scholarship cuts the same way here. It does not move the verdict, because on this edge Schadewald is not carrying the weight alone: an artefact photograph and a MARC record from an unrelated library both attest the same object. But the label should say what it is.

3. ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATION — none available, structurally. This is not an inference from shared material, where a common ancestor or shared intermediary could explain the overlap. The evidence is a republication bearing the earlier author's name, dedication, motto and credentials on its cover. There is no third text both parties could have drawn on: the object IS the transmission. The only alternative worth testing was "the Zion printing is not really Carpenter's text", and the cover, the by-statement, the cataloguer's note and Schadewald's prose independently foreclose it.

4. VERDICT STRENGTH — I pushed hardest here and it holds. See strongest_objection. Compare the calibration: E04 earned partly_documented because the best sources ran AGAINST half its claim (Schadewald has Rowbotham's society fading into oblivion and the UZS "dominated by flat-earthers having little connection to the previous organizations"). Nothing on E02 is contradicted by anything; the weak clause is merely unextended, and the report refuses to extend it in terms ("Do not extend this arrow past 1929 without new evidence"). "Documented" is not doing work "partly_documented" earned.

TWO THINGS I CAN ADD THAT THE REPORT DOES NOT HAVE
(a) The 47 pp. vs 39 pp. inference should be dropped in both directions. Carpenter's own pagination is unstable across his editions: the Library of Congress's own scanned Baltimore 1886 copy (archive.org/details/onehundredproofs00carp, metadata "32 p. 24 cm") is 32 pages; the LoC guide's 1885 6th ed. is 39; and Carpenter's 13th edition had author's notes running to at least p. 78 (Schadewald refs 4.33, 4.35), with a notice dated 29 March 1897 in them. So 47 pp. is unremarkable and is NOT evidence of added Zion matter. The real consequence runs the other way: the exemplar behind the Zion printing is unidentified and may be one of Carpenter's 1890s editions rather than the 1885 text. Open Library's "Originally published: Baltimore : The author, 1885" is a cataloguer's statement about the WORK, not evidence about which edition was set from. Nothing on the page should say Zion carried "the 1885 text"; say "Carpenter's pamphlet".
(b) One of the report's unreachable negatives is now resolvable. HathiTrust is reachable from here by a different endpoint — catalog.hathitrust.org/api/volumes/brief/oclc/39522200.json returns HTTP 200 with {"records":{}, "items":[]}, i.e. no HathiTrust record or digitisation for that OCLC. That converts an "unreachable, silence is not evidence" into a scoped negative. loc.gov item pages still 403 (I confirmed on /item/52055019/), and the Google Books API returned HTTP 429 quota-exceeded to this environment, so Google Books is untested rather than negative.

Scope of my own searches: Schadewald's The Plane Truth chapters 5 and 8, plus the site index, Notes and References pages, fetched raw and grepped; the Open Library edition JSON and publisher-field query; the archive.org metadata API for onehundredproofs00carp; the HathiTrust brief-volumes API by OCLC; loc.gov item 52055019; the Google Books volumes API; and one web search. Not located in those: any scan or page images of the 1929 Zion printing, any holding of it outside the single SFPL/OCLC record, and any source connecting it onward to Shenton, Johnson or the IFERS.
refutations.strongest_objection:
The candidate claim in review/_edge_candidates.json is two clauses — "Voliva's Zion organisation reprinted Carpenter's numbered proofs c.1929, FORMING A DOCUMENTARY BRIDGE INTO THE 20TH CENTURY" — and only the first is documented at artefact level. A bridge is defined by its far bank, and the report found nothing on it: no source links the Zion printing onward to Shenton, Johnson or anyone else, and the two onward carriers Schadewald does document bypass Zion entirely (Morse read Carpenter in 1913, sixteen years before Zion printed him; Goudey in 1930 acknowledged Carpenter directly). Johnson naming Voliva as a predecessor is acknowledgement, not receipt. So a reader taking "verdict: documented" against that claim string inherits a transmission-onward implication the evidence does not carry, and the report's own record_problems ask for the repo's definite article to be downgraded — which is an argument that the claim as recorded is partly documented and the verdict field should say so.

WHY IT FAILS ANYWAY. The clause is satisfied without the onward step: a 1929 American printing of the Victorian list, priced at twenty-five cents with five for a dollar (i.e. produced for bulk distribution), IS the Victorian text present and in circulation in the 20th century. That much is proven by the object itself. The stronger reading — that later flat-earthers received Carpenter THROUGH Zion — is a different claim, and the report neither asserts it nor smuggles it: it states in the reasoning that Zion is "one documented carrier among at least three", puts the missing link in scope_note, and instructs "Do not extend this arrow past 1929 without new evidence." The right repair is to rewrite the claim string in _edge_candidates.json to drop the article and the bridge metaphor before the verdict travels attached to it — not to downgrade a verdict that a photograph of the object supports.
source_problems: Schadewald, The Plane Truth — labelled 'scholarly' in the sources block with no statement of what it is. Its own index page: the book 'was incomplete at the time of his death, and has been lightly edited for publication here', first published on Michael Behrend's personal site in 2015, copyright Wendy S. Schadewald. An unfinished posthumous typescript edited by a third party, by a genuine authority, with a full reference apparatus — but not a peer-reviewed monograph, and it should be labelled as the former. Not load-bearing here because the artefact and the MARC record attest the same object independently.

MIS-CITED LOCATION. The sources block attributes to Chapter 5 that it 'documents Carpenter's own later editions (12th, 13th) with author's notes running to 1892-97'. I fetched Chapter 5 and grepped it: the strings 12th and 13th do not occur there. The substance is correct but lives on the References page — [4.6] notes to the 12th ed. dated 12 Oct 1892; [4.33] and [4.35] notes to the 13th ed., p. 78; [4.34] a notice dated 29 March 1897; [5.3], [5.12], [5.19] notes to the 12th ed. This is precisely the failure mode the report itself invokes against source-genealogy.md: a citation verified as existing rather than as saying what was attributed to it.

NAME ERROR, twice, in new_person_needed and reasoning: 'M. C. Morse'. Schadewald's Bostonian is CHARLES W. MORSE, a 64-year-old Brookline 'practical watch and clock repairer' who published the 78-page Unpopular Truth in 1913. If he ever reaches the page, distinguish him from the identically named financier.

UNSCOPED ABSENCE inside a corroborating sentence: 'a publisher-field query of Open Library for Wilbur Glenn Voliva returns exactly one book IN THE WORLD'. It returns one book in Open Library (numFound 1, which I re-ran and confirmed). Open Library publisher-field indexing is patchy and derived from contributed MARC, so on its own this is weak corroboration; the Schadewald sentence carries the point. The scope_note is meticulous, which makes the slip in the reasoning field more likely to be repeated downstream.

Open Library and WorldCat are one OCLC record exposed twice, not two witnesses. The report says so explicitly and does not double-count it — noted here only so a downstream reader counting 'three ways' does not read it as three independent attestations. The genuinely independent pair is (i) the photographed physical object Schadewald handled and (ii) the San Francisco Public Library MARC record.

refutations.reasoning:
I tried to break this one and could not. Every load-bearing quotation checks out against the primary texts, and the two things the report left as inferences I was able to close in the verdict's favour.

WHAT I CHECKED MYSELF (files on this machine; fresh downloads where noted)
1. Winship 1899, two independent scans: /tmp/winship.txt (Google scan, 86,132 words) and /tmp/win.txt (Boston Public Library copy, 84,860 words). Both are the same "SECOND EDITION—Enlarged ... By RECTANGLE ... T. L. CULLINGWORTH ... 1899" printing. Verified verbatim: the attributed block "'Parallax,' in his invaluable work 'Zetetic Astronomy,' says" (page markers put it at p.148/149 — the report's "p.148" is right); the balloon dossier closing "—Zetetic Astronomy. Page 37."; the polar extract "taken from 'Zetetic Astronomy' by 'Parallax'"; the lunar-eclipse doctrine credited to "the celebrated Zetetic Astronomer known as 'Parallax'"; the index entry "Zetetic Astronomy, by Parallax"; J. Williams, Hon. Secretary, Universal Zetetic Society, 32 Bankside; the Bedford Canal material sourced to "the Field for 26th March" 1870; and the capitalised "THE SUN IS THEREFORE 2,700 MILES DISTANT FROM THE EARTH" from a 45-degree plane triangulation. The preface and introduction name no forerunner — the report's "not named as a forerunner anywhere in the front matter" holds.
2. DIRECTION is not an inference here, which is what defeats the usual attack. Rowbotham died 1884; Winship's book is 1899 and names Rowbotham's pseudonym, his title, and a page number. No reversal, no parallel-invention and no common-ancestor reading survives for the four attributed passages. The common-source alternative only bites on the UNattributed shared blocks (the Foucault pendulum via "Iconoclast" in Earth Review; the Britannica "Levelling" refraction extract) — and the report already assigns those away from the direct edge itself rather than counting them as descent.
3. I reproduced the machine measurement independently with my own normaliser: 110 shared 8-word runs, 1,987 words, 2.32% of Winship against Gutenberg #69892 (report: 103 runs, 1,741 words, 2.1%). Same order; the gap is normalisation, not invention. The largest shared runs are exactly where the report says they are (the Scripture/"hodge-podge"/plurality-of-worlds block, the London Journal balloon item, the refraction-and-levelling passage).
4. I CLOSED THE OPEN QUESTION THE REPORT LEFT. It says the "Page 37" citation cannot match 1865 (pp.18–19) and is "consistent with" a later enlarged edition, but that it could not machine-compare the third edition. Using a third-edition text (/tmp/za3e.txt, and my fresh re-download /tmp/za3e_fresh.txt from the archive.org item E06 used), whose page markers are footers and self-consistently reproduce its own TOC (ch.14 TOC p.159 begins after marker 158; ch.5 TOC p.83 begins between 81 and 84), the section heading "THE APPARENT CONCAVITY OF THE EARTH AS SEEN FROM A BALLOON" falls on page 37 and the Elliott/Baltimore quotation runs onto p.38. Winship's "—Zetetic Astronomy. Page 37." lands on it. And I separately confirmed the 1865 printed pagination from the Google scan (/tmp/rowb1865.txt): Elliott and the London Journal 18 July 1857 item are on pp.18–19, exactly as the report states. So Winship had a later edition of the BOOK in hand and page-cited it correctly — which is the single best answer to the "he only ever saw extracts in a periodical" alternative. It strengthens the edge. (Caveat I am flagging, not hiding: 1873 cannot be excluded from 1881 on pagination, and my 1881 text is an unprovenanced user upload — see source_problems.)
5. Corroboration checks. SOURCE CLASS. This is the cleanest-handled edge I have seen in this file. refutations.strongest_objection: The verdict token is attached to a candidate claim worded "descends textually from Rowbotham's SYSTEM", and the system half is not what the evidence shows. Documented: attributed reuse of Rowbotham's prose and of his quotation apparatus, four explicit credits, a correct page citation. Not documented: that Winship's cosmology descends from Rowbotham's. Overlap is 2.3% (3.3% pooled with the third edition, both floors); Winship's Bedford Level material comes from the 1870 Hampden/Wallace trial via The Field, not Rowbotham's own experiment; the book is his own alphabetically arranged compendium of mainstream astronomy, navigation manuals, newspapers and shipboard observation; and on the headline quantity he contradicts his source outright, computing the sun at 2,700 nautical miles by his own triangulation against Rowbotham's figure. The report's reasoning says all of this in capitals ("WHY THE LINE MUST BE THIN, NOT THICK"), so the record is not deceptive — but a reader who sees only "E03: documented" against that claim string will publish more than was proven. Recommend the claim be restated to what was actually established: Winship quotes and reuses Rowbotham with attribution (partial borrowing, not a digest), alongside an equally documented Earth Review route carrying at least as much of the material. That is a labelling fix, not a defeat: the edge itself is real and citable.

That surviving positive half rests on exactly one source (Garwood 2007, pp. 220-222) that nobody on this project has opened; it reaches the report through a Wikipedia footnote.
