source_problems: Garwood 2007, pp. 220-222 is the ONLY support for the one thing E04 grades positively, and it is read at second hand via the Wikipedia Samuel Shenton article. I confirmed the wikitext: the 'instant convert' paragraph is footnoted {{harvnb|Garwood|2007|pp=220-222}}, and I confirmed independently that the book cannot be reached from here (archive.org item flatearthhistory0000garw exists, but its search-inside endpoints return 502 / connection reset through the proxy; books.googleapis.com returns quota_limit_value 0; the books.google.com in-volume search page returns no snippet). A verdict of confidence 'medium' rests on a Wikipedia sentence reporting a book.

Schadewald, The Plane Truth, is tagged kind='scholarly' on three of the ten sources and carries the decisive negative plus most of the report's dating corrections. Its own Preface, by Lois Schadewald, says the book 'has been a work in progress since at least 1984', is 'unfinished in places', and 'remained unfinished because Bob felt that it never met his standards closely enough to be published' (https://www.cantab.net/users/michael.behrend/ebooks/PlaneTruth/pages/Preface.html). It is an author-unpublished, non-peer-reviewed, posthumously web-posted manuscript by a science writer, hosted on a private site. It is the best available history and I found it accurate everywhere I checked it, but the house rule is to say what a source is.

The report asserts of the movement's own wiki: 'Even the movement does not assert an institutional handover from the UZS to Shenton.' That is an unscoped absence and it is false. The sibling page on the same wiki, https://wiki.tfes.org/Universal_Zetetic_Society (raw text retrieved), opens 'The Universal Zetetic Society (UZS) was the precursor to the Flat Earth Society' and states 'In 1971, the UZS was revived as The Flat Earth Society when Samuel Shenton became its leader.' The reviewer sampled only wiki.tfes.org/Flat_Earth_Society and generalised. This does not make the handover documented — the page is movement-internal and its date is wrong — but the rhetorical point built on it collapses.

Patrick Moore is used selectively: the circular, the 23 November meeting, the 'It will die' quotation and 'not the same as those of the Flat Earthers of the early twentieth century' are all taken as authoritative (I verified each verbatim in the PDF), while the same author's adjacent sentence, 'Following a period of comparative inactivity, the British branch of the I.F.E.S. was revived in 1956', is discounted as 'a memoirist's loose phrase'. Same page, same eyewitness. Moore also writes that the November meeting 'put the Society back on a really firm footing', and Schadewald independently says Shenton was 'trying to revive the British flat-earth movement'. Two independent sources use revival language; the report should record that conflict rather than dissolve it.

The 1906 back-cover notice is dismissed as retrospective self-description that 'Schadewald contradicts'. Schadewald in fact corroborates both of its dates: ch. 7 has de Lacy Evans as 'vice president of the original Zetetic Society when it formed in December 1883', and ch. 4 refers to 'the original Zetetic some twenty years earlier' than 1892, i.e. c. 1872-73, matching the notice's 'New York in Sept., 1873'. The sources agree on dates and disagree only about continuity of the body. Reported as a flat contradiction, it picks a side.

record_problems[0] says Blount was 'one of twenty-four committee members' of the founding body, cited to Schadewald ch. 4. 'twenty-four' does not appear in ch. 4; it is ch. 7's count of the 1906 reorganised committee. Ch. 4 names a nine-member founding Committee (Williams, Albert Smith, Perry, Isaac and John Smith, Adams, Naylor, Skellam, Lady Blount).

new_person_needed calls John Williams 'the founder of record'. Schadewald never says that: he calls him 'the founding Secretary' and writes that the founding meeting 'was apparently held' at his home — a hedge, carrying ref. 4.2. The same chapter elsewhere writes 'the UZS (as reorganized under Lady Blount)', and ch. 7 has her 'now president', bankrolling it, over 'the new Universal Zetetic Society'. So the repo's shorthand 'Lady Elizabeth Blount's Universal Zetetic Society' needs its date fixed (1892, not 1893), not the flat correction the report demands. This inverts the project's own hedge rule: the report beats the repo's compressed phrasing using a hardened version of the source's hedge.
refutations.reasoning: WHAT I VERIFIED, AND IT HELD. I fetched the sources rather than reasoning about the summary. Schadewald ch. 4 verbatim: "The Universal Zetetic Society (UZS), founded late in 1892, was dominated by flat-earthers having little connection to the previous organizations"; "The Zetetic Society, founded only a year before he died, soon faded into oblivion". Ch. 7: "a mere shadow of its former self"; the back-cover notice, in full, reads "Founded in New York in Sept., 1873, and in London in Dec., 1883 (ten years after the American), as The Zetetic Society, by 'Parallax,' and others". Ch. 9: "Shenton and William Mills founded the International Flat Earth Society on December 20, 1956"; Mills "provided one of the links with the past"; the only inheritance language is "Johnson's Flat Earth Society was a spiritual inheritor of the Universal Zetetic Society". I extracted Moore's PDF and read the reproduced circular end to end: it is dated "December 20th, 1956", names Mills as President and Shenton as Organizing Secretary, and names no predecessor body — the report's decisive-document claim is correct. Shenton's "It will die ... just as at the turn of the century the great organization set up by Lady Blount died" verifies verbatim. I pulled the Samuel Shenton wikitext: the "direct descendant" sentence does indeed carry no inline footnote, while the Garwood-cited paragraph is the sourced one. I also confirmed by keyword sweep that Schadewald ch. 9 never mentions Blount or the UZS in connection with Shenton. So the negative half is properly scoped and, within the texts named, correct. The research is good. WHERE IT BREAKS IS THE LABEL. Both clauses of the posed claim failed. The reviewer then re-typed the edge as "textual_descent" and graded that instead. "not_documented" was available and was used zero times across all twelve edges; E04 is the clearest case on the board where it was earned, and awarding "partly_documented" instead is precisely the pattern of a researcher asked to establish a link finding one. The one positive component is single-sourced and second-hand. TWO THINGS THE REPORT UNDER-REPORTS, both cutting toward continuity: (a) Schadewald ch. 9 records that a son of Mills died 18 December 1957 and "left £500 to be used to finance publication of his uncle's unpublished flat-earth manuscript" — Cook's 382-page Our Earth Flat, Not Spherical, completed c. 1947. Money plus an Edwardian-generation author's manuscript entering the 1956 society is the strongest material continuity in the reviewer's own source, and the scope note's blanket "no transfer of funds, records" survives only because it is scoped to the UZS as a corporate body. (b) Schadewald documents officer-level continuity across hop one — de Lacy Evans was VP of Rowbotham's 1883 Zetetic Society and VP of the UZS — so grading hop one and hop two as equally undocumented flattens a real asymmetry. ALTERNATIVES the report does not test: on Garwood's own account (as relayed) Shenton reached Rowbotham via Archbishop Stevens, a Blount associate, so the carrier was UZS-era print, not a bare Rowbotham volume; the E02 reviewer's unidentified St Petersburg, Florida 1955 reprint is an untested mid-century channel for Victorian text into 1956; and both Schadewald ("Shenton's view differed slightly from previous flat-earthers") and Moore ("not the same as those of the Flat Earthers of the early twentieth century") say the system Shenton built was not Rowbotham's — so even the surviving line should read "read Rowbotham and was converted", not "descends from Rowbotham". DIRECTION is not the failure here: Rowbotham died 1884 and his editions run 1849-1881; Shenton was born 1903 and read in the British Museum before 1956. No later-author/earlier-author trap. The date trap on this edge is retrospective self-dating (a 1906 notice claiming 1873/1883), and the reviewer caught it — though he did not notice that Schadewald independently corroborates both dates. RECOMMENDATION: record E04 as not_documented for the claim as posed; split the Garwood anecdote out as its own low-confidence, second-hand textual edge with the Garwood-unread caveat attached to the edge and not buried in a scope note; keep the Mills-Cook intermediary recommendation, which is better supported than the report says; strike the "even the movement does not assert" sentence; and do not let E04 be counted as a hold in any 12-of-12 headline.

I tried to break E05 and could not. It is the one edge on this board that was already downgraded against the movement's interest, and my checks pushed it further in that same direction rather than restoring it.

WHAT I VERIFIED FIRST-HAND (not from the summary):
1. The Schadewald quote is verbatim. I pulled https://www.cantab.net/users/michael.behrend/ebooks/PlaneTruth/pages/Chapter_09.html, stripped tags and grepped: "The mantle of leadership along with a small but precious library of flat-earth books was passed on to Johnson in 1972." Also confirmed in that chapter: "Before he died in 1971"; Lillian's "brief false start"; "Shenton, himself, had picked Ellis Hillman to become president, but it wasn't meant to be"; the 1995 house fire destroying "most of the Flat Earth Society's records and its fine collection of flat-earth literature". Every quotation the record attributes to ch. 9 is accurate.
2. NCSE/Cole re-fetched: it gives NO date for the fire and NO year for the succession. The record's charge that Wikipedia mis-cites Cole for "1997" is correct.
3. Wikipedia's Ellis Hillman article re-fetched: no mention of the Flat Earth Society or the Science Fiction Foundation. Correct as recorded.

DIRECTION. Secure, and secured by dates rather than plausibility. Shenton died 2 March 1971 (Garwood-based Wikipedia; Schadewald "before he died in 1971"; NY Press "died in Dover in 1971"); Johnson leads from 1972. Reverse transmission of an office from a dead man is not available. The only bidirectional window is 1967-71, when Johnson was a corresponding member — and E05 already refuses textual_descent, which is the correct call there.

WHERE I HURT IT (three real objections, none fatal):

(a) SOURCE CLASS, Schadewald. The sources array labels The Plane Truth "scholarly". Per its own preface, it is an unfinished manuscript its author "felt... never met his standards closely enough to be published", assembled posthumously by his sister and widow and hosted on a private website in 2015. It is primary research (he travelled to England, interviewed principals) but it is not peer-reviewed, and the preface records that Johnson "once nominated me to Outstanding Young Men of America." Worse, the handover passage is agentless and Johnson-framed: "Johnson believed that America would be more hospitable... and so the transfer to America was made... was passed on to Johnson." No transferor is named, no document cited. E05's line "Schadewald, who knew Johnson personally, states it plainly" reads acquaintance as corroboration when it is a dependency on the interested party.

(b) ONE UNVERIFIED PAGE CARRYING TWO OPPOSITE LOADS. Garwood 2007 p. 320, reached only through Wikipedia, supplies both the "inherited part of Shenton's library from Shenton's wife" transferor correction AND the "Hillman added most of Shenton's library to the SFF archives" finding that kills the archive half. I independently failed to verify it too: archive.org scrape endpoints returned empty, the Google Books API is still 429 over daily quota, and searches turned up no independent secondary repetition — HandWiki and markfoster.net are Wikipedia mirrors, and Bob Forrest's flat-earth page (a Johnson correspondent) does not mention Shenton's library, Hillman or Garwood. The scope note discloses this honestly, but record_problems item 6 ("should not be published in any form") is a hard directive resting on an unverified encyclopaedic relay.

(c) ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATION NOT EXCLUDED. Nothing I found rules out self-assumption into a vacuum — Lillian's failed interregnum, Hillman declining, Johnson picking up the name and incorporating his own California body, then 29 years of unchallenged press repetition. That is exactly the move his 1984 flyer makes on Dowie, Voliva and a claimed 6,000-year zetetic pedigree. No contemporaneous 1971-72 document of conferral was located: no Flat Earth News masthead, no letter from Lillian, and the California Secretary of State business search (bizfileonline) was blocked by an Incapsula WAF on my POST attempt, so the incorporation filing remains unchecked.

TWO THINGS THE RECORD DOES NOT HAVE (new source: NY Press obituary, 2001, https://www.nypress.com/news/charles-k-johnson-president-of-the-international-flat-earth-research-society-icnp1020010404304049996):
- A FOURTH SUCCESSION STORY, conflicting: "before Samuel died in Dover in 1971, he requested that Johnson succeed him. And so it came to pass." That contradicts both Schadewald and Garwood/Wikipedia, which agree Shenton's designated successor was Hillman. Report the conflict; it cuts the same way E05 already cuts — the flattering version is the one the two better sources contradict. (Same piece also credits the 1956 founding to Samuel and Lillian, where Schadewald says Shenton and William Mills — a second, looser conflict.)
- INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF THE FIRE DATE: "a fire swept through their home in late September 1995". That makes 1995 three-sourced (Schadewald, Irish Times, NY Press) against Wikipedia's 1997, which mis-cites a source that gives no date. The record's "use 1995, footnote 1997" can be firmed up.

THE ABSENCE CLAIM SURVIVES MY RETEST, still scoped. I chased the Shenton papers past where the record stopped: the SFF collection moved to the University of Liverpool, so I read Liverpool Special Collections' Science Fiction Foundation Archive guide (libguides.liverpool.ac.uk/library/sca/SFFarchive) — it describes correspondence, Foundation typescripts, notices, agendas and minutes, with no flat-earth, Shenton or Hillman material listed, and no accession history. An Archives Hub/Liverpool site-scoped search was blocked by robots.txt. So: not located in the Liverpool SCA guide pages, the SFF-related libguides, or the searches run here — which is where a future pass should knock next (a direct enquiry to Liverpool SCA, or Garwood's own acknowledgements).

VERDICT STRENGTH. "Partly documented" is right and is if anything conservative for an institutional_continuity edge. What is well documented is that Johnson held and was universally recognised in the office from 1972; what is thin is the mechanism of conferral, which rests on Johnson-proximate narration plus one unverified page. I would leave the verdict, downgrade confidence from "high" to "medium" on the conferral mechanism (high only on post-1972 leadership), soften the reasoning's header "THE SUCCESSION IS DOCUMENTED" to name that no contemporaneous 1971-72 document was located, and reclassify Schadewald as an unpublished primary-research manuscript rather than "scholarly". NCSE/Cole is likewise an advocacy-organisation newsletter obituary, not scholarship.

I set survives=true because every objection I could state concretely makes the edge weaker in the direction the record already chose, and none of them restores the claim's "inherited the society and its archive" wording.
refutations.strongest_objection: The mechanism of conferral has no source that is independent of Charles K. Johnson. Schadewald's sentence is the load-bearing one, and it is agentless passive ("the transfer to America was made... was passed on to Johnson"), written from Johnson's stated beliefs, by a researcher whose preface records that Johnson nominated him for an award, in a manuscript its own author refused to publish. The only assertion of a transfer from the Shenton side — "inherited part of Shenton's library from Shenton's wife" — exists for this review only as unverified Wikipedia relay of Garwood 2007 p. 320, which I also could not verify (archive.org scrape empty, Google Books API 429, no independent secondary repetition found). Self-assumption into a vacuum, later ratified by 29 years of obituary repetition, is not excluded by any source located — and a fourth, conflicting story (NY Press 2001: Shenton personally "requested that Johnson succeed him") shows the succession narrative was already unstable in the press. This lowers confidence in the mechanism; it does not overturn partly_documented, because Johnson's uncontested tenure of the office from 1972 is multiply attested.
source_problems: Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch. 9, labelled 'scholarly' in the sources array: per its own preface it is an UNFINISHED manuscript the author 'felt... never met his standards closely enough to be published', assembled posthumously by his sister and widow and web-hosted privately in 2015. Primary research, yes; peer-reviewed scholarship, no. Relabel as unpublished primary-research manuscript.

Schadewald is not independent of the beneficiary. The preface records Johnson 'once nominated me to Outstanding Young Men of America'; ch. 9's handover passage names no transferor, cites no document, and is narrated from what 'Johnson believed'. E05's reasoning treats personal acquaintance as corroboration when it is a dependency.

Garwood 2007 p. 320 is reached only through Wikipedia and was NOT verified first-hand by the original pass or by me (archive.org scrape endpoints empty; Google Books API 429 over daily quota; no independent secondary repetition located — HandWiki and markfoster.net are Wikipedia mirrors). That single unverified page supplies BOTH the 'from Lillian' transferor correction AND the SFF-archive finding that kills the 'its archive' claim. One unverified relay carrying two loads in opposite directions.

NCSE/Cole is labelled 'scholarly'. It is an obituary in Reports of the NCSE, an advocacy organisation's newsletter — better than press, not scholarship. Re-fetched: it gives no succession year and no fire date, so it corroborates the succession only, not '1972'.

Smithsonian is a popular magazine blog post containing a demonstrable error ('Johnson's good friend Samuel Shenton', contradicted by Schadewald's account of Johnson learning of Shenton from a press article). It is obituary-cycle derivative, not an independent witness to 1972.

The record's 'independent confirmation' framing overstates the NCSE / Irish Times / Smithsonian trio: two are 2001 obituaries from the same news cycle and one is a 2016 popular retelling. What they jointly establish is that Johnson's leadership from 1972 went unchallenged for 29 years — consistent with, but not proof of, a conferred transfer.

MISSING SOURCE, new conflict: the NY Press obituary (2001) says Shenton 'requested that Johnson succeed him' before dying in 1971, contradicting Schadewald and Garwood/Wikipedia, which both name Ellis Hillman as Shenton's designated successor. Same piece also miscredits the 1956 founding to Samuel and Lillian Shenton where Schadewald says Shenton and William Mills. Not in the record; should be reported as a conflict, not silently dropped.

No contemporaneous 1971-72 document of conferral was located by either pass — no Flat Earth News masthead, no Lillian Shenton correspondence, and the California Secretary of State business search for the incorporation filing was blocked by an Incapsula WAF on my attempt, so the one genuinely contemporaneous record on this edge remains unchecked.

refutations.reasoning:
I fetched all five texts the report cites (Gutenberg 55387 Carpenter 1885; Gutenberg 69892 Rowbotham 1865; the two archive.org djvu OCRs for Rowbotham 3rd ed. 1881 and Winship 1899; the archive.org Dubay OCR) and re-parsed them myself rather than reading the summary, then added a sixth text the report did not test.

DIRECTION — cannot be broken. Carpenter's title page reads "BALTIMORE: Printed and Published by the Author ... 1885"; Dubay's list is 2015 (project doc; the OCR closes with his own AtlanteanConspiracy.com / ifers.boards.net promo, so it is authentically his). Direction is not merely chronological: Dubay 96 opens by naming Carpenter's book and author, and Dubay 129 opens "To quote William Carpenter". The arrow is inside the later text. Carpenter died 1896. No reversal is available.

TEXT — verified word by word, not summarised. Carpenter proof 36 (index title "Chesapeake Bay by night") reads "If we take a journey down the Chesapeake Bay, by night, we shall see the 'light' exhibited at Sharpe's Island for an hour before the steamer gets to it ... the astronomers' theory of 'curvature' demands a difference ... of 112 feet 8 inches!" Dubay 96 reproduces this with exactly the two drifts the report names ("will not vary" to "won't vary", "112 hair's breadths" to "100 hair's breadths"). Dubay 129 is confirmed as a splice: its first half is the tail of Carpenter 98 (granite pillars, lynx-eyed astronomer, "a shot from a cannon is a very slow coach") and its second half is the tail of Carpenter 80 (same corner of the same pane of glass, North Star). 98 and 80 are not adjacent in Carpenter, which is real evidence that whoever made the splice had the whole list.

INTERMEDIARY TEST — the report's key discriminator holds, and is actually stronger than it says. Winship 1899 does quote "100 Proofs that the Earth is not a Globe" on the Chesapeake, and I identified the passage: it is Carpenter proof 7, "a trip down the Chesapeake Bay, in the day-time" (index title "A trip down Chesapeake Bay"), a different proof from the one Dubay uses. Carpenter has two Chesapeake proofs; Winship excerpts one, Dubay the other. Scott's Terra Firma contains "Chesapeake" zero times. Neither Rowbotham edition contains it. The Winship route for Dubay 96 is genuinely closed.

Dubay 42 also survives an expanded distinctiveness test: "69,000" occurs in Carpenter and in none of Rowbotham 1865, Rowbotham 1881, Winship 1899 or Scott 1901 (Scott's Challenger figure is 70,000 and lacks "indirect"; Rowbotham's Challenger in both editions is the 1845 frigate wreck; Winship's is Spry's Cruise).

WHERE I BROKE IT. The report ran its distinctiveness test against three rivals and omitted a fourth that it names in its own new_person_needed field as "a documented Victorian source feeding 200 Proofs directly": David Wardlaw Scott, Terra Firma (1901). I fetched two independent scans (archive.org cu31924031764594 and terrafirmaearthn0000scot; identical on every term counted). Scott p.126-27 runs two consecutive sentences: the Mississippi over 3,000 miles "would have to ascend 11 miles before it reached the Gulf of Mexico", then "Again, in one portion of its long route, the great river Nile flows for a thousand miles with a fall of only one foot". Dubay's proofs 4 and 5 are consecutive and track those two sentences in order. Word-level longest-common-run: Dubay 5 shares 12 consecutive words with Scott ("flows for a thousand miles with a fall of only one foot") and only 3 with Carpenter proof 4 ("a thousand miles"), whose actual wording is "notably, the Nile, which, in a thousand miles, falls but a foot". Dubay 4 shares 9 consecutive words with Scott's preceding sentence. So the report's second "CONFIRMED, UNATTRIBUTED, CARPENTER-DISTINCTIVE" pair fails: the textual ancestor of Dubay 5 is Scott, not Carpenter, and Dubay 5 then splices in Winship's Congo/Parana/Paraguay. This is precisely the error class the report catches in the existing record — crediting Carpenter with material carried by another Victorian — committed one rival short of a complete panel. Note the origin/transmission distinction: Scott 1901 postdates Carpenter 1885 and knew him personally (Terra Firma names "the late Mr. William Carpenter, then of Lewisham"), so Carpenter may still have originated the Nile argument; what fails is the claim that Dubay got it from him.

WHY THE VERDICT STILL STANDS. Losing Dubay 5 costs the edge one unattributed corroborator. The edge does not rest on unattributed paraphrase — it rests on two explicitly attributed, near-verbatim, title-naming quotations that I verified character-run by character-run against the primary text, with the only competing intermediary excluded on a different-proof basis. "Documented" is not doing work only "partly documented" earned; this is about as strong as a textual-descent edge can be, and the report is unusually disciplined in refusing the doc's "quarter of Carpenter's hundred" figure and in labelling Pannofino as asserting structure rather than documenting transmission and the archive.org bundle as movement-internal.

I also independently reproduced, from the primary texts, the report's corrections to the existing record: Carpenter 40 contains none of Dubay 8's distinctive content (locks, 26-foot datum, several lakes) while Rowbotham 1881 contains all of it; Winship's Natal Mercury Cape L'Agulhas passage (33 feet high, 238 feet above sea level, over 50 miles, 1,400 feet below the line of sight) is verbatim the ancestor of Dubay 89; "Hatteras" occurs 0 times in the Dubay OCR; Dubay 19 is Tycho Brahe on stellar parallax, not Rowbotham; Dubay 119 is "spherical terra firma" generically, not Scott; Earth Review is cited at 9 and 12; and my own count of items naming Victorian zetetic sources is 15, matching the report's correction and not the doc's mapping.

An intermediary that reproduces Carpenter verbatim would leave identical evidence, and the 98+80 splice could itself have been inherited. The Dubay edition is unspecified. The record does not say whether the archive.org OCR corresponds to the 2015 free PDF or the 2018 print edition, and every proof number cited is edition-dependent. refutations.reasoning:
VERDICT SURVIVES; TWO LOAD-BEARING PIECES OF ITS REASONING DO NOT.

What I did: refetched and re-read every source in the record rather than reasoning about the summary — history3.html, no066/editor.html, no067/aberration.html (raw HTML, tag-stripped), Schadewald Appendix D (raw), the ABA history page, and I downloaded both PDFs (no084 obits.pdf, md5 834b0118c6205d0c8f15c3f1bf1e5add, 3,283 words after pdftotext — matching the record's own count; de_labore.pdf, 2,885,158 bytes, md5 1132e04145f9d9cc960ad53a0b3556fc, 44,004 words) and grepped them.

1. DIRECTION — the succession half is genuinely secure, and I found one more confirmation the record does not have. Both parties describe the same dated event in the same terms; van der Kamp: "in the Bulletin of March 1984 I handed over its editorship to a trustworthy successor, my friend Gerry Bouw" (verbatim, confirmed). Bouw's editorial pins it to an issue number ("until March, 1984, when he produced No. 37 as his last"). Schadewald says it from outside. New: the back matter of van der Kamp's own 1988 book prints "Editor: Gerardus D. Bouw, 4527 Wetzel Avenue, Cleveland, Ohio 44109" — an edition-level confirmation, in the founder's book, that as of 1988 the successor holds the chair. This is a dated handover event, not an inference from shared material, so it cannot be knocked down the way an argument-descent edge can. I could not break it and I tried.

2. DIRECTION — the argument half is NOT secure, and the record's own cited document reverses it. The record's source #11 is filed as "primary (queried, negative result)" and states that De Labore Solis has "no mention of Gerardus Bouw anywhere" and concludes: "The flow of citation between these two men does not run backwards from the founder to the successor." That is false against the PDF at the URL the record cites. Endnotes 20-22 of the Airy chapter read: 20 = Airy's own 1871 Proceedings paper; 21 = "Quoted in Gerardus D. Bouw, With Every Wind of Doctrine. privately published, 1984, p.187"; 22 = "Ibid. p.188". Those two notes carry the Arago experiment and Fresnel's dragging coefficient — i.e. the standard explanation of Airy's null, the core apparatus of the chapter. So the founder's 1988 book, subtitled "Airy's Failure Reconsidered", sources part of its Airy material through the successor's 1984 book. The only documented citation between these two men that I located runs successor -> founder, the opposite direction to the edge.

3. That destroys the record's one positive strand. The verdict draws "a thin, named strand of argument-level descent (the Airy framing)". It does not hold. (a) The label's direction was resting on "earliest documented use is 1988" (van der Kamp's subtitle) vs Bouw's ~1994 use — but Bouw's With Every Wind of Doctrine (1984) is explicitly not consulted by the record, and is now shown to have been in van der Kamp's hands and quoted by him while writing that very chapter. It is the one text that could settle whether the Airy frame was Bouw's before it was van der Kamp's printed subtitle, and it is the one text nobody opened. (b) The record says No. 67 shows "the LABEL descends from van der Kamp". Reading No. 67: Bouw uses the phrase in the passive — Airy's failure to detect the added aberration "is called 'Airy's Failure'" — credits the experiment's design to Boscovich, and does not mention van der Kamp anywhere in the "Airy's Failure" section. The descent is the reviewer's inference, not the article's statement. (c) The remaining support is Bouw's eulogy sentence, discussed next.

4. SOURCE CLASS — the against-interest discount is applied selectively. The record's stated justification for leaning on movement-internal parties is that "they testify AGAINST their own lineage story, which is the direction that makes internal testimony strong rather than weak." That is sound for the refutation of the corpus half — van der Kamp disowning the succession's intellectual content in Bouw's own bulletin is strong. But the record then takes its single positive argument-credit ("Through Walter's pioneering work in pointing out the geocentric nature of Airy's failure ... Walter may truly be called the father of modern geocentricity") from Bouw's editorial in the Spring 1998 MEMORIAL issue, published weeks after van der Kamp's death, alongside a Don Quixote tribute and an obituary. That is a eulogy — the genre in which founder-credit costs nothing and runs WITH the lineage story. It is evidence of what the movement says about its own descent, which is interesting, but it is not documentation of textual transmission, and the record's own discount rule does not cover it.

5. ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATION, from the same PDF. Bouw's editorial gives an entry account in which the arguments are his own, not inherited: Armstrong alerted him; as an undergraduate he had "taken enough relativity theory to know that neither heliocentrism nor geocentricity could be proven or disproven"; he wrote asking "which Scriptures?"; he found van der Kamp's answer "rather weak"; so he ran a three-week study and printed his own analysis in Bulletin No. 13 (1976). That is common-ancestor / parallel-derivation, in the successor's own words, and it directly contradicts the one source (Wikipedia) that phrases the influence as textual ("reading the works of Walter van der Kamp"). The record flags Wikipedia as weakest but does not report this head-on conflict. The repo's own scripts/_b11_R11.py independently notes Bouw credits the equivalence claim upstream to Hoyle and Mach — same pattern.

6. VERDICT STRENGTH. "partly_documented" stands, but note what it conceals: half of this claim is not merely undocumented, it is REFUTED, by both parties in print and now by a counter-flowing citation. The parent's observation that "none came back negative" is partly an artefact of aggregate labelling — E07 contains a refutation filed under a positive-sounding label. The record's own recommendation (relabel the diagram line "succeeded him as editor, 1984") is the right fix and should be treated as mandatory, not optional.

Net: the edge is not a manufactured link. A researcher told to find a connection found a genuinely adversarial result and reported it. But the specific negative it rests on is wrong in the direction that flatters its own conclusion, and the one positive strand it draws should be withdrawn.
refutations.strongest_objection: The record's source #11 asserts, as a checked negative result, that van der Kamp's De Labore Solis (1988) contains "no mention of Gerardus Bouw anywhere", and infers from it that "the flow of citation between these two men does not run backwards from the founder to the successor." The PDF at the URL the record cites contains exactly that mention, twice, in the Airy chapter's own endnotes: "21. Quoted in Gerardus D. Bouw, With Every Wind of Doctrine. privately published, 1984, p.187" and "22. Ibid. p.188", attached to the Arago/Fresnel passage that explains Airy's null — plus "Editor: Gerardus D. Bouw" in the back matter. The founder quotes the successor's 1984 book inside the book subtitled "Airy's Failure Reconsidered". So the only citation between these two men that I could document runs successor -> founder, and the one strand of argument-level descent the verdict draws (the Airy framing, van der Kamp -> Bouw) is not date-secured against a 1984 Bouw text that the record never opened and that van der Kamp demonstrably had in hand.
source_problems: FALSE NEGATIVE, load-bearing and directionally convenient. Source #11 (geocentricity.com/bibastron/ts_history/de_labore.pdf, filed as 'primary (queried, negative result)') claims 'no mention of Gerardus Bouw anywhere'. Checked: file downloaded 2026-08-10, md5 1132e04145f9d9cc960ad53a0b3556fc, pdftotext = 44,004 words; two hits for 'Bouw' — endnote 21 ('Quoted in Gerardus D. Bouw, With Every Wind of Doctrine. privately published, 1984, p.187'), endnote 22 ('Ibid. p.188'), plus 'Editor: Gerardus D. Bouw' in the back matter. The conclusion drawn from the false negative is reversed by the document.

UNCONSULTED TEXT IS THE DECIDING TEXT. Bouw, With Every Wind of Doctrine (1984) — the record notes it was not consulted but treats that as a footnote-level gap. It is not: it is now known to be quoted inside van der Kamp's 1988 Airy chapter, so it is the single text that would settle the direction of the 'Airy's failure' frame. Schadewald's Appendix D bibliography gives it as 'Cleveland: Tychonian Society, 1984'; van der Kamp's note 21 says 'privately published, 1984' — a minor imprint conflict worth recording, not resolving.

EULOGY READ AS DOCUMENTATION. The sole positive argument-credit ('Walter's pioneering work in pointing out the geocentric nature of Airy's failure ... the father of modern geocentricity') is from Bouw's editorial in the Spring 1998 memorial issue of Biblical Astronomer No. 84, printed with Elmendorf's Don Quixote tribute and Byl's obituary. Movement-internal, posthumous, running WITH the lineage story — outside the against-interest justification the record uses to license its internal sources. Evidence of what the movement says about its descent; not evidence of textual transmission.

INFERENCE ATTRIBUTED TO A SOURCE THAT DOES NOT MAKE IT. The record says Biblical Astronomer No. 67 shows 'the LABEL descends from van der Kamp'. No. 67 uses the phrase impersonally — Airy's failure to detect the added aberration 'is called “Airy’s Failure”' — credits the experiment's design to Boscovich, and names van der Kamp nowhere in that section. Bouw there explains the null by Fresnel drag and says Airy 'saw what he expected so it was a success and not a failure', which is the mainstream reading, not the geocentric one the eulogy credits to van der Kamp.

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION / CONFLATION in new_person_needed. It states Bouw learned of van der Kamp 'from Armstrong's 1976 remark in that newsletter, and from van der Kamp's Jan 1976 article “I Make Its Pillars Firm” in it.' Checked against no084 obits.pdf: the Jan 1976 Bible-Science Newsletter reading is R. G. Elmendorf's, in a signed tribute (Glenshaw PA, 17 March 1998), not Bouw's — as the record's OWN record_problems item 1 correctly states. Bouw's editorial names only Armstrong and gives no venue for his 1976 remark. The recommendation that the Bible-Science Newsletter is 'the channel' by which the lane recruited therefore rests on a venue no source states; Armstrong was first editor of the Creation Research Society Quarterly (Schadewald, App. D), so CRSQ is at least as likely.

INDEPENDENCE OVERSTATED. 'Documented, and from four independent directions' is soft. Van der Kamp and Bouw are the two parties, publishing in the same organisation's serial; the ABA history page is that organisation's own record (a third item from the same house); Faulkner (AiG, 2020) and Wikipedia are tertiary and neither shows independent sourcing. Schadewald is the only outside line, and his Appendix D selected bibliography lists no Society bulletins — so whether he is an independent witness or a careful reader of the same internal record is not shown. CONFLICT REPORTED, NOT RESOLVED: the repo's own scripts/_b8_D02.py asserts Schadewald 'wrote the movement's history from its own bulletins'; if that is right he is not an independent direction at all. I did not locate a statement of sourcing in Appendix D either way.

UNREPORTED CONFLICT WITH THE ONE TEXTUAL-INFLUENCE SOURCE. Bouw's own editorial has him arriving with the equivalence argument from undergraduate relativity coursework, finding van der Kamp's scriptural answer 'rather weak', and printing his own study in Bulletin No. 13 (1976). That flatly contradicts Wikipedia's 'reading the works of Walter van der Kamp ... became convinced'. The record downgrades Wikipedia but does not report the contradiction, which is the strongest available common-ancestor/parallel-derivation evidence against the corpus half.

SCOPE. My own negatives are bounded: I searched the de_labore.pdf and no084 obits.pdf text layers named above, the four geocentricity.com HTML pages, Schadewald Appendix D and the ABA history page. I did NOT locate With Every Wind of Doctrine (1984) or Geocentricity (1992) in any form, and did not read the Bulletin run 1-53. Nothing here should be read as 'no earlier use of “Airy’s failure” exists'.

refutations.reasoning:
I tried to break this and could not. I did not reason about the report: I downloaded the two Internet Archive OCR files it cites (2006 CD-ROM Vol. I, 3.34 MB; complete Vol. 1-3, 5.50 MB), reproduced its counts exactly (48 and 68 occurrences of "Bouw"), and read every Bouw context in the 2006 file plus the relevant ones in the complete text.

DIRECTION. Secure by dates and by the citing side, not by plausibility. Bouw's Geocentricity is 1992; the 2006 Vol. I introduction is signed 25 April 2006; Sungenis cites the 1992 book by page 30+ times and Bouw's Bulletin of the Tychonian Society Nos. 46-47 (1988) as block-quote sources. There is no reverse-flow candidate: Bouw's own 2006 review of GWW (geocentricity.com/ba1/no117) makes no priority claim, which the report itself notes. Sungenis also sides with Bouw AGAINST van der Kamp ("Bouw's colleague, Walter van der Kamp, argued for a small universe and thus posited that stellar aberration and parallax were the same phenomenon. To that issue, Bouw writes..."), which kills the obvious alternative explanation — a common Tychonian-Society ancestor. It is not a common ancestor when the later author adjudicates between the two earlier ones and follows the named one.

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS, tested and mostly closed. (a) Shared third text for the Marinov aether figures: closed, Sungenis writes "the latter cited in Bouw, Geocentricity, p. 257" — textbook transmission-through. (b) Wheeler rather than Bouw for the Planck/firmament cosmology: the ultimate ancestor is indeed Wheeler's equation, but Sungenis reaches it through Bouw's prose, quoted at length across ch. 7 and ch. 11, and states the dependency outright — "requires the adoption of Bouw's overall understanding of how the universe is put together." Descent through Bouw stands; Bouw's own ORIGINATION of it does not, see below. (c) Common ancestor for the neo-Tychonic model: NOT closed, and this is the one place the report over-reads (see strongest_objection).

VERDICT STRENGTH. "Documented" is earned, and by an unusually good class of evidence: this is a primary text I read myself, containing an acknowledgement of live consultancy, a bibliography, page-level citation, and multi-paragraph block quotation. The movement-internal items (Bouw's endorsement blurb, his Biblical Astronomer no. 117 review) are correctly labelled and explicitly excluded from load-bearing — the report says the descent is established from Sungenis's citations, not from Bouw's assertion, and that is the right call. No wiki or dealer catalogue carries any weight on this edge.

WHAT THE STATED LIMIT ACTUALLY COSTS. The report concedes it never opened Geocentricity. For a transmission edge that is the correct limit and it is survivable: the citing side establishes that Sungenis drew on Bouw. But it does NOT license record_problem #6's suggestion that "the dependency runs the other way for the firmament/Planck cosmology, which is Bouw's throughout." Bouw as CONDUIT is proved; Bouw as ORIGINATOR is not, and the text itself shows the core equation is Wheeler's, quoted by Bouw. Do not let #6 upgrade a documented conduit into an unverified origin.

Net: a confirmation I fought for. The edge is real; two scoping statements attached to it are wrong and should be fixed before it becomes a diagram label.
refutations.strongest_objection:
The verdict survives, but the PRECISION paragraph — the one explicitly written to govern the diagram label — is wrong in both directions because it blends editions, and the report's own headline quote is the weakest citation in the file rather than the strongest.

(1) SCOPE OVER-READ. The quote chosen to represent the edge is a footnote: "In the last few years the same explanation for parallax has been promoted by astronomer Gerardus Bouw. He has also coined the term 'modified Tychonic model'..." That is an "also," not a "from." The main text it hangs off presents the neo-Tychonic model as pre-existing and mainstream, citing a University of Illinois Physics 319 lecture twice and saying "most geocentrists know" it. Sungenis credits Bouw with the TERM, not the model. So listing "the modified-Tychonic model" among what this edge carries is exactly the shared-third-source case the brief warns about. (Parallax-vs-aberration is different and does hold — Bouw's four arguments for a large universe are set out and block-quoted.)

(2) AIRY EXCLUSION IS FALSE FOR THE LATER EDITION. The report states Airy and Michelson-Gale have "no Bouw citation in proximity (I checked a 2,400-character window around every occurrence of 'Bouw')." I ran that exact test. True for the 2006 Vol. I: zero hits. NOT true for the complete three-volume text, where one hit sits inside the Airy's-failure argument — "Thus, as Bouw notes: 'Physically speaking, if they are real, both effects must be contributing so that in actuality we must either conclude that Fresnel drag and the Fitzgerald contraction are one and the same thing...'" So Bouw is quoted on the Fresnel-drag/Fitzgerald-contraction rebuttal within the Airy material. The Airy argument itself still traces to van der Kamp, not Bouw — but the categorical exclusion is edition-dependent and stated without that scope.

(3) EDITION BLENDING inside the same paragraph. It lists "p. 363 (Keeler redshift)" among the 2006 citations. Keeler appears zero times in the 2006 Vol. I OCR, and the only "p. 363" there is Dreyer's History of Astronomy. Geocentricity pages actually cited in 2006: 232, 257, 309-310, 324-325, 325, 326, 329 — exactly what the report's own SOURCES entry says. Pages 244, 248-49, 249, 258, 363, 60-80 appear only in the complete text. Same slip for point (4): "Endorsement" and "magnificent" appear zero times in the 2006 file; the Endorsements page is the later edition. And "Miller" — in 2006 the "as cited in Bouw" tag attaches to Marinov's Eppur Si Muove, with Miller named only as a comparison; the Miller/Shankland-via-Bouw material (Bouw on Shankland's temperature explanation, the 23.75-degree figure, Geocentricity p. 258) is in the later text. Given that edition dates have caught this project out twice, the narrative contradicting its own source record is the finding to act on.
source_problems: Faulkner, Answers in Genesis, 4 Sept 2020 is the report's only non-movement source for the causal/biographical narrative, and it is presented as 'independent (non-movement) confirmation of the causal direction'. I fetched it: the sentence 'Around 2002, Sungenis read Bouw's book Geocentricity: The Biblical Cosmology and became an advocate for geocentrism a few years later' carries no citation, no source, no documentation. In the same breath it mis-titles Bouw's book (every citation inside GWW, including Bouw's own endorsement line, gives the plain title Geocentricity) and dates GWW to 2007. It is an uncorroborated secondary narrative from a partisan in an intra-creationist dispute, not confirmation. It should be labelled as such. This costs the verdict nothing only because direction is independently established by Sungenis's own page citations — but the word 'confirmation' should go.

Bouw's endorsement blurb and his book report in The Biblical Astronomer no. 117 are movement-internal mutual endorsement, contemporaneous with a consultancy Sungenis thanks him for. The report labels them correctly and explicitly declines to rest descent on them, which is the right discipline — flagged here only so the labelling is not lost downstream.

The Biblical Astronomer citation is given as 'vol. 16 no. 117, Summer 2006'. The fetched page states neither journal name, issue number, nor date; only the URL path (/ba1/no117/) supports 'no. 117'. The volume and season are inferred from elsewhere and should be marked as such.

PER-BOUW's dataset sources are Wikipedia plus creation.com/geocentric-gobbledegook — a page the corrections log in claude/source-genealogy.md forbids citing for Bouw, since it is Faulkner reviewing Marshall Hall. WRK-BOUW-1992 carries the same URL as its only link. The report flags this; it remains true that Bouw's node currently rests on a wiki and a mis-cited review.

Minor: the report puts 'geo-lock' in quotation marks as the name of the Selbrede frame-dragging argument. The string does not occur in either OCR file. The Selbrede citation itself checks out verbatim in both editions ('Geocentricity's Critics Refuse to Do Their Homework,' The Chalcedon Report, 1994, p. 11), so only the coined term is unverified.

refutations.reasoning:
WHAT SURVIVED MY ATTACK. Two of the three legs are sound, and I re-ran them rather than trusting the summary.

(1) The edition question is handled correctly — better than the record claims for itself. I pulled the archive.org GWW text (3,335,538 bytes). Preface signed "Robert Sungenis / April 25, 2006"; ISBN 0-9779640-0-0; CD-version copyright notice. I then tested it independently of the front matter: every apparent post-2006 date in the whole file is a false positive (a page range "2001-2008", a DOI, and the Michelson-Gale rectangle "2010 x 1113 feet"). Zero cited literature later than April 2006 across 3.3 MB. This is not a later edition wearing a 2006 preface. The trap the brief warned about was avoided.

(2) The verbatim match is real. GWW ch.12, "Summary:" block, p.841: "Airy thought he needed to tilt his water-filled telescope more than the air-filled telescope to see a star. He did not. The starlight was already coming in at the correct angle, so no change was needed." Dubay carries it. That much is exactly as reported.

WHERE IT BREAKS — ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATION, NOT DIRECTION. The record excluded Marshall Hall (two texts) and van der Kamp, and flagged Bouw and Wyatt as unchecked. It never tested the one man its own notes name twice: Malcolm Bowden.

Bowden, "A geocentrist replies to 'Geocentrism and Creation'", Journal of Creation 16(2), 2002, pp.79-82. I downloaded the PDF from creation.com and extracted the text myself. Section "(iv) 'Airy's failure'": telescopes have to be tipped very slightly in the direction of the Earth's travel; Airy filled a telescope with water, which slowed the light, but no change in the angle of the telescope was needed; this showed the light was already coming in at an angle from the moving star to a stationary telescope, and it was not the telescope that was moving. Same page carries the Michelson-Gale claim measured "to within 2% of the known speed", inside a numbered list of the same four experiments Dubay bundles (Michelson-Morley; Sagnac and Kantor; Michelson-Gale; Airy's failure). Dated 2002. Four years before GWW.

Then the stemma. The TFES wiki preserves Bowden's video description, which is his 2002 paragraph expanded — same sentences, same order — and which now also carries GWW's polished clause. Comparing Dubay against Bowden-video and GWW:
- "Airey" spelling: Bowden yes, Dubay yes (2x in Atlantean Conspiracy), GWW zero occurrences.
- "starlight ... down the axis of the tube": Bowden yes, Dubay yes, GWW zero ("axis of the tube" not present in the GWW file at all; GWW says the telescope is "tilted to keep the light from hitting the side").
- the earth's "speed around the sun", in scare quotes: Bowden yes, Dubay yes, GWW zero.

refutations.strongest_objection: Route 1 states an inference as a fact its own source does not contain. Schadewald's sentence (which I fetched and matched verbatim against the report's `quote` field) says only that *Earth Review* reprinted Schöpffer's lecture, and parenthetically that the lecture "had previously been reprinted in Scientific American, in a translation submitted by" Blavatsky. The same Schadewald chapter says *Earth Review* "reprinted material from earlier writers and occasionally from religious or even secular journals" — which makes SA plausible and identifies nothing. The report itself concedes it never obtained the *Earth Review* issue (Schadewald gives no issue or date). Compounding it: Schadewald writes "translation *submitted by*"; the only source that says she *translated* it is the kookscience wiki, which the report elsewhere correctly quarantines as a wiki. So the word making the text "hers" rests on the wiki. The documented fact is co-appearance of one lecture in two venues, not descent of a Blavatsky text into the zetetic press. The report's WHAT-TO-DRAW section hedges this correctly ("dashed", "must be labelled as a translation of Schöpffer"), so the defect is confined to the reasoning prose — but this project has been caught twice by exactly this class of slippage, and the prose is what a future writer will lift.

DIRECTION. Secure on both routes, by dates and by naming, not by plausibility. Isis Unveiled 1877 precedes Hall 1928 by fifty-one years and Hall names her and quotes her in quotation marks — there is no who-copied-whom question. On route 1 I checked the dates rather than assuming: SA Supplement 1878, UZS founded late 1892, Earth Review Jan 1893 – Apr 1897 (Schadewald, same chapter). The direction is not the weak point on route 1; the *existence* of the link is (see strongest_objection).

ONE MORE FINDING I FOUND ARGUING AGAINST THE REPORT'S EVIDENCE, THOUGH NOT ITS CONCLUSION. The report writes "the chain Blavatsky → Hall → specimen is real and demonstrable at the first hop" — and "at the first hop" is quietly doing a lot of work. Of the two legs offered, the one with actual verbatim reuse (the microcosm passage) lands on D06 items 159/161/177/186, whose recorded originator in our own dataset is Atkinson/The Kybalion 1908, not Hall. So the leg with real textual reuse is not a Hall-carried route into the specimen by this project's own attribution. The leg where Hall IS the recorded carrier — item 168, D07 — is the see-also, which as noted fails the report's own strict test and whose named source is Hippolytus. The second hop (Hall → specimen) is taken from the repo's prior record ("the twelve items track his chapter list"), not re-verified in this pass.

That said, the repair is easy and I found it: at djvu line 21922 Hall block-quotes Isis Unveiled by name on the Kether/Sephiroth emanation ("H. P. Blavatsky writes:" followed by a long quotation), in the same Qabbalah chapter as "four concentric globes called worlds" (21080) and "the forty concentric circles" (21962). That is real quoted reuse, in a D07 chapter, on concentric-sphere iconography. The cited evidence for leg (b) should be swapped for that one; the leg survives the swap.

VERDICT STRENGTH. This is where I most want to push. For the edge as literally posed — "whether Theosophical material reaches the flat-earth corpus by any documented route at all" — the report's own answer is no, three times over: no Theosophical doctrine travels, no flat-earth author among the 19 is documented naming her, and no item among the 461 traces to the Schöpffer reprint. "partly_documented" is earned only by re-reading the edge from Theosophy-the-doctrine to Blavatsky-the-person. That re-reading is announced in bold in the first two sentences and is not traded on anywhere — the recommendation is "do not draw Blavatsky → the corpus", which is the negative answer. So the label is generous while the content is not. If the operator wants the twelve verdicts to be comparable, this one should be recorded as not_documented for the edge as written, with a separate documented Blavatsky → Hall edge alongside; I have left proposed_verdict at partly_documented because the substance is right and relabelling is the operator's call, not a finding against the researcher.

WHY I DID NOT SET survives=false. The orchestrator's suspicion is that a researcher asked to find a link found one. This is the edge that most clearly did the opposite: it returns a substantive negative, it publishes three reasons against itself including that Blavatsky's own text is round-Earth and heliocentric, and it declines to draw the line the dataset currently implies. I can add a datum sharper than the one it used — at Isis Unveiled line 14691 Blavatsky describes the planet "as it turns about its axis" in the very sentence introducing the Hermetic axiom, so she is on record for rotation as well as for a round Sun-centred Earth, three lines from the passage our D06 cluster depends on. The direction of the line anyone would draw to her is refuted from the primary text twice over.

THE GAP THAT COULD STILL OVERTURN THIS, IN EITHER DIRECTION. The report declares it could not obtain the body text of Flatlantis or The Atlantean Conspiracy, nor the Earth Review issue, nor Isis Unveiled vol. II. That declaration is honest and it matters more than the report lets on: Hall block-quotes Blavatsky *on Atlantis* at djvu 4423–4434 ("H. P. Blavatsky thus sums up the causes which precipitated the Atlantean disaster:", closing "(See Isis Unveiled.)"), and Dubay wrote two Atlantis books. That is precisely where a genuine Theosophy → corpus route would surface, and it is the one place nobody has looked. The negative half is correctly scoped to the searches actually run, but it is unrun in the direction most likely to break it.

people.name: Joseph Steer Christopher (signs himself "J. Steer Christopher"; "J. S. Christopher" on Gleason's map)
people.dates: b. Dartmouth, Devon, 15 April 1805 (day/month from the Earth Review obituary); d. Morden College, Blackheath, 31 December 1894; interred Charlton Cemetery, 3 January 1895. Active as a Natal emigration promoter and merchant c.1850 (address 18a Basinghall Street, London; firm "J. S. Christopher & Co." at Pietermaritzburg and Durban, per his own 1850 book). Map "Entered at Stationers' Hall, August 1885"; Library of Congress copy stamped "168821 / MAY 2 1887 / SMITHSONIAN DEPOSIT" and again "Map Division MAY 7 1903".
people.lineage_evidence: Assigned on documented relationship to the zetetic literature and its organisations, not on resemblance, and with the specific gap named. (1) HIS OWN ARTEFACT: the map's printed legend states the seas are "all uniformly and perfectly level, Without any Rotundity" and the heading reads "SCIENTIFICALLY, PRACTICALLY AND INTELLIGIBLY CORRECT. WITHOUT ANY ANTIPODES" — Christopher himself asserts a plane Earth in print (primary, read off the LoC copy photographed at archive.org/details/1885-joseph-steer-christophter-loc-gov). (2) DISTRIBUTION LINK: that copy carries a purple rubber stamp "JOHN HAMPDEN, BALHAM, S.W." twice — head and foot — with the engraved line "To be obtained of the Author as above" struck through in blue ink. Balham was John Hampden's address (Schadewald ch.3, quoting the December 1883 Cosmos notice), and Hampden signed himself Rowbotham's "grateful disciple and fellow-worker" when he launched Parallax in March 1885. My reading of the artefact: Hampden was retailing Christopher's map, over-stamping the author's own sales line. That is an inference from the object, not a document saying so. (3) MOVEMENT RECEPTION: the Universal Zetetic Society's Earth (not a Globe) Review printed a zetetic's testimonial to "The map of the world designed by Mr. J. Steer Christopher, of Morden College, Blackheath, near Greenwich" (Thomas Whittle, Croydon, May 1894, p.162) and an In Memoriam calling him "our esteemed friend" (v.2 n.5, p.96, 1895) — movement-internal primary, i.e. evidence of what the movement said about him. (4) SECONDARY: Schadewald describes the map as "still the zetetic standard". WHAT IS NOT DOCUMENTED: I located no statement by Christopher citing Rowbotham, no record of his membership of the Zetetic Society or UZS, and no appearance of his name in the Earth Review other than the Whittle letter and the obituary (printed twice in the scan) — searched: full text of the 1893–97 Earth Review scan, Schadewald's Plane Truth chs. 1,3,4,5,6,8, his own 1850 Natal book, loc.gov search for "J. S. Christopher"/"Steer Christopher", and open web. So: zetetic by his own printed cosmology and by documented reception inside the zetetic institutions; the specific claim that he took the system FROM Rowbotham rests on an uncited dealer sentence.
people.role: CARRIER — not an originator of any argument. He introduced no claim: the plane-Earth cosmology is Rowbotham's, and the north-polar plane map predates him inside the movement (Rowbotham's world map appears in the 1873 edition of Earth Not a Globe; E. E. Middleton issued a "Pioneer Map of the World" in 1876; Hampden had his own "Circular Chart of the World" by March 1885, on a different scale — 57½ degrees equator-to-pole, against Christopher's 90). The projection is not his invention either: the polar azimuthal equidistant projection is described by al-Biruni in the 11th century, used by Mercator as a 1569 inset and by Postel in 1581 — "the projection of J. S. Christopher" is a credit line on a chart, not a claim of authorship of a projection. What he did originate is a physical object, narrowly and demonstrably: the 1885 engraved chart that Alexander Gleason copied and credited on the face of his own 1892 map. Originator of an artefact, carrier of the argument. INSTITUTIONAL is wrong — he held no office in any zetetic body that I located.

The phrase matches the obituary's description of Christopher's map ('his Map of the World as a Plane') but the advertisement does not name him.
people.summary: Joseph Steer Christopher (1805–1894) was a Devon-born merchant and Natal emigration promoter who drew "The New Map of the World", a north-polar azimuthal equidistant chart entered at Stationers' Hall in August 1885, whose printed legend denies antipodes and rotundity. Alexander Gleason's 1892 "New Standard Map of the World" credits that chart on its face — "ON THE PROJECTION OF J. S. CHRISTOPHER, MODERN COLLEGE, BLACKHEATH, ENGLAND" — where Christopher's own map reads "Morden College Blackheath", so "Modern College" is Gleason's misprint, reproduced ever since by library catalogues transcribing his title faithfully. The Library of Congress copy of Christopher's map carries John Hampden's Balham stamp over a struck-out "To be obtained of the Author" line, and the Universal Zetetic Society's Earth Review printed a testimonial to the map in 1894 and his obituary in 1895. He introduced no argument: the plane cosmology, the polar plane map format and the projection itself all predate him.
conflicts: DATE OF CHRISTOPHER'S MAP — four sources, three answers, report all. (a) The map itself: 'Entered at Stationers' Hall, August 1885. All rights reserved.' — read off the artefact. (b) Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch.4: 'Published as early as 1880' — he attaches no reference to that sentence, though he references the adjacent facts. (c) Boston Rare Maps: 'some time in the 1880s'. (d) The archive.org uploader (a flat-earth account) titles it 1885. An earlier state may exist; the 1885 imprint dates only the copy I examined. Related: the Earth Review testimonial says the late Lady Brassey wrote thanking Christopher for a copy — she died 14 September 1887, which bounds circulation before that date and is consistent with either 1880 or 1885.

THE ROWBOTHAM CLAIM — the load-bearing one, and it is uncited. Boston Rare Maps writes 'At some time in life Christopher got hooked on Samuel Birley Rowbotham's "zetetic astronomy"' with no footnote; their reference list is Ancestry.com, Schadewald ch.4, a Flat Earth Society forum thread and three 1844–50 newspapers. Schadewald — their own cited source — does NOT say Christopher adopted Rowbotham's system; he says the map 'is still the zetetic standard' and prints the Earth Review obituary. I located no document in which Christopher names Rowbotham. Chronology cuts both ways: Rowbotham died 23 December 1884, eight months before the Stationers' Hall entry, so if the map is 1885 there was no living Rowbotham to be adopted from; if Schadewald's 1880 is right, there was.

'MODERN' vs 'MORDEN' — resolved in favour of error, but note who says what. Gleason's 1892 map prints 'MODERN COLLEGE' (verified on the Leventhal/Boston Public Library copy at 3000px via IIIF). Christopher's own 1885 map prints 'Morden College Blackheath' (verified on the LoC copy). Morden College, Blackheath, founded by Sir John Morden, exists from 1695 (AIM25 archival authority record). Library catalogues (Leventhal, Digital Commonwealth, DPLA, UWM) transcribe Gleason's spelling faithfully because that is what the object says — they are not endorsing it. Incidental: booksellers list T. Frank Green's monograph on the almshouse as 'Modern College, Blackheath', so the slip is a recurring one, not unique to Gleason.

RESIDENCE FROM 1875 — Boston Rare Maps dates his residence at Morden College from 1875, sourced to an Ancestry.com timeline (a genealogy database, not scholarship); I could not check it. Independently confirmed: he died there on 31 December 1894 (Earth Review obituary; Schadewald cites the same). The 1885 map's own imprint already gives 'Morden College Blackheath' as his address.

BANKRUPTCY AND EAST INDIA CHAMBERS — Boston Rare Maps' 1844 bankruptcy and East India Chambers details rest on The Exeter Flying Post (4 Apr 1844), The Morning Post (22 Oct 1845) and The Morning Chronicle (8 Mar 1850), which I did not see; a London Gazette API query for 'Steer Christopher' 1840–60 returned nothing, which given that interface's indexing is not evidence of absence. His own 1850 book gives a different address, 18a Basinghall Street, and a firm trading in Natal — not a contradiction, but it is the only primary I verified.

THE FELLOWSHIP — the Earth Review obituary says he was made a 'Fellow of the Society of Science, Art and Literature' on account of his map. The London body of roughly that description is usually styled the Society of Science, Letters and Art. I did not verify which body, or the fellowship itself, and have not silently corrected the movement's wording.

THE UZS MAP FUND — Schadewald ties the Universal Zetetic Society's £15 lithographic-block fund to a plan to republish Christopher's map. The fund appeal I located in the Earth Review scan ('those who are desirous of having a good Map of the World as a Plane... the purchase of a block... about £15') does not name Christopher. The connection may rest on Earth Review text outside the 1893–97 scan; treat it as Schadewald's, not as something I confirmed.
NAME — flatearthprints.com gives his middle name as 'Streep'. Every primary I saw (the map, the 1850 book, the obituary) reads 'Steer'.

people.reasoning:
TASK 1 — verify the load-bearing claim (Boston Rare Maps: he adopted Rowbotham's zetetic astronomy). VERDICT: the lineage holds on other evidence; the specific sentence does not verify. Boston Rare Maps states it without a citation, and Schadewald — the one substantive source they list — does not say it. What I can document instead, and it is stronger than the dealer's sentence: (a) Christopher's own map asserts a plane Earth in his own words ("Without any Rotundity", "WITHOUT ANY ANTIPODES"), so his cosmological commitment needs no third party; (b) the LoC copy is stamped twice by John Hampden of Balham, Rowbotham's self-declared disciple, over a struck-out author's-address line, which places the object in the Rowbotham network by 1887; (c) the UZS's own Earth Review printed a testimonial to the map (1894) and an affectionate obituary (1895). I have labelled (c) as movement-internal — it is evidence of what the zetetics said about him, not independent documentation. The residual gap, which I have not papered over: nothing located shows Christopher himself invoking Rowbotham, and if the 1885 imprint is the true first publication, Rowbotham was already dead.

TASK 2 — "Modern College". CONFIRMED, from both artefacts rather than from commentary. Christopher's own 1885 map prints "Morden College Blackheath"; Gleason's 1892 map prints "MODERN COLLEGE, BLACKHEATH, ENGLAND". Morden College is a real 1695 foundation in Blackheath (AIM25 authority record; Schadewald describes it as an almshouse for retired Turkey merchants). So the error is Gleason's, introduced in transcription, and the library catalogues that carry it are correctly transcribing his sheet.

TASK 3 — his own map and its date. FOUND: "The New Map of the World, on the Projection of J. Steer Christopher", lithographed by J. R. King, "Entered at Stationers' Hall, August 1885", Library of Congress accession 168821, Smithsonian Deposit 2 May 1887. Boston Rare Maps wrote in their catalogue entry that they had found references to such a map but no image; the image exists — a photograph of the LoC copy — and I read the imprint, the legend, the Hampden stamps and the accession stamp off it directly at full resolution rather than trusting the uploader's caption. That is also how the date conflict got caught: Schadewald's "as early as 1880" is unreferenced and disagrees with the sheet in front of me, so both are reported.

ORIGINATOR DISCIPLINE. I nearly wrote "originator of the flat-earth map". That fails the rule. Rowbotham's Earth Not a Globe already carried a north-polar plane map in its 1873 edition; Middleton issued one in 1876; Hampden had his own circular chart by March 1885; and the projection itself runs back to al-Biruni, Mercator's 1569 inset and Postel 1581. Christopher introduced no argument and no projection. He made one well-drawn sheet that Gleason copied and credited, and that the UZS treated as its standard. So: CARRIER, with the artefact-level origination stated narrowly and separately.

SCOPE OF WHAT I SEARCHED, so the absences are not read as claims about the world: full text of the 1893–97 Earth (not a Globe) Review scan; Schadewald's Plane Truth chapters 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and its reference list; his 1850 Natal book in full text; loc.gov's JSON search API for "J. S. Christopher", "Steer Christopher" and date-filtered map searches; the LoC flat-earth research guide (its maps tab 404s); Open Library; Digital Commonwealth/Leventhal; Wikimedia Commons. HathiTrust full-text search returned 403 (bot wall) and the Google Books API was over quota, so those two corpora are untested — an 1880s periodical notice of the map could well be sitting in either. The Flat Earth Society forum thread that both Boston Rare Maps and MCToon rely on returned 403 and I could not read it; that means the ultimate source of the "resident from 1875" and possibly the Rowbotham line is a document I have not seen.

people.name: Alexander ("Alex.") Gleason
people.dates: b. 28 November 1827, d. 13 March 1909 (Find a Grave memorial 75244128, buried Darien Cemetery, Genesee Co., NY; same dates given by Kook Science). NEITHER SOURCE IS SCHOLARSHIP — Find a Grave is user-contributed genealogy and its memorial does not mention the map, the book or the patent, so the identification of that man with the mapmaker rests on name + Buffalo residence + engraving trade + matching dates. Boston Rare Maps, which worked the Buffalo City Directory and Ancestry, gives no birth/death dates at all. Treat 1827-1909 as probable, not established. Active dates that ARE documented from artefacts: Lake Erie observation 4 July 1887 (his own narrative); book copyright 1890; map deposited 1892 ("Map 10.4.1892" in the LoC/BPL deposit hand) and "PATENT ALLOWED November 15, 1892" printed on it; patent filed 15 Aug 1892, granted 23 May 1893; second edition of the book 1893.
people.lineage_evidence: Documented relationship to the zetetic literature, not resemblance — four independent strands. (1) PRIMARY, his own book: he quotes Rowbotham under the pen-name "Parallax" repeatedly and by page — "The quotations will be found on pages 375-406 of his work, 'Zetetic Astronomy'" — plus citations to "Zetitic Astronomy, by Parallax, pages 36-38", "Parallax, pp. 81-87" and "Parallax's Earth not a Globe, pps. 105-107". He announces at ch. IV that his conclusions use "the sentiments largely of Parallax and his words verbatim", promises "a synoptical biography of this noted philosopher... to whom the world owes a tribute far greater than to a Newton, Galileo, Copernicus or Kepler", and runs a whole section headed "The Horizon Line, by Dr. Wm. Rowbotham" (OCR: "Hobotham"; note Gleason's own initials for Rowbotham are wrong — Samuel Birley, not Wm.). (2) SELF-IDENTIFICATION: he writes of "the Zetetic faith", "the zetetic astronomers", and "Zeteticism and the Bible is most likely right". (3) THE PARENT MAP: the Library of Congress deposit copy of the 1885 Christopher map from which Gleason's derives has the printed line "To be obtained of the Author as above" struck out in ink and overstamped "JOHN HAMPDEN, BALHAM, S.W." at head and foot — Hampden being Rowbotham's patron and the Bedford Level wagerer. Schadewald independently reports Gleason accepting Hampden's 57.5-degree pole-to-equator figure (I could NOT confirm "Hampden" anywhere in the OCR of the 1893 second edition — 0 hits — so that link is Schadewald's, not verified by me in Gleason's own words). (4) SECONDARY: Schadewald places him in the American zetetic chapter, and the movement's own later author Goudey lists his debt to "Dr. Samuel B. Rowbotham, Prof. Wm. Carpenter, Prof. Alex. Gleason..." — i.e. the movement itself canonises him inside the zetetic line. He also cites "Carpenter's 'Common Sense Astronomy,' p. 47". NOT located: any mention of Lady Blount, the Earth Review or the Universal Zetetic Society anywhere in the OCR of the 1893 edition (0 hits each) — so no documented tie to the Blount organisational wing.
people.role:
CARRIER, with two narrow and specifically sourced origination candidates that must not be upgraded without a corpus check.

CARRIER is the correct headline and he says so himself: at the head of his summary chapter he states he will use "the sentiments largely of Parallax and his words verbatim". The map is the same story — the projection is J. S. Christopher's, published in London in 1885; Gleason renamed it "Gleason's New Standard Map of the World", bolted a patented mechanical time-dial onto it, and mass-published it in Buffalo. He is the vector that carried an English zetetic map into America and into the twentieth century (Voliva is photographed pointing at Gleason's map on the cover of Leaves of Healing, 10 May 1930, per Schadewald ch. 8). He also Americanises Victorian examples the way Carpenter did — the Suez Canal argument reappears as the 52-mile lockless level of the Erie Canal between Syracuse and York Mills.

ORIGINATION CANDIDATES (documented, but narrow):
(a) The sun's altitude/distance of 1,725 miles, geometrically computed. Primary: "1725 miles equal the altitude of both the Sun and the North Star; and four times 1725 miles equal 6900...", followed by "Some of the Zetetic faith had given the sun's altitude 2500, some 3500, and some even less than I have given it. By what process they have arrived at the various results I do not know, but I know of no other geometrical process than the last herein given." He explicitly distinguishes his figure from other zetetics'. Downstream carry is attested: Goudey quotes "Professor Alex. Gleason gives the distance however, geometrically computed, as being only 1,725 nautical miles" (via Schadewald ch. 8).
(b) A diagram. Schadewald says flatly that Goudey "reproduced the deceptive diagram Gleason invented to rebut sphericity" — Schadewald is a critic, and "invented" is his word, so this is a hostile secondary attribution of origination, not Gleason's own claim.
(c) Weaker: his own field tests — the Lake Erie / Silver Creek sighting of 4 July 1887, where he hired A. E. Arnold, "a civil engineer of the Nickel Plate Railroad", and his two transits. This is an American Bedford Level analogue, i.e. a new instance of an inherited argument, which is carriage with local substitution rather than a new argument.

CAUTION FOR THE DATASET: grep of scripts/ and data/ in this repo returns ZERO occurrences of "Gleason", "Silver Creek" or "Nickel Plate", so no item in the 461-list is currently attributed to him and I have not checked the corpus for a 1,725-mile sun item. Do not promote him to originator of any cluster on the strength of this record alone.

RE-COPYRIGHTED AND RE-WRITTEN, REVISED AND ENLARGED, 1893") and independently by Schadewald ch. 5, who describes it as a softcover of about 95 pages.
