people.summary: Alexander Gleason of Buffalo, New York, published Is the Bible from Heaven? Is the Earth a Globe? (1st ed. 1890; 2nd, 402-page ed. 1893), issued Gleason's New Standard Map of the World in 1892, and held US patent 497,917 for the "Time-Chart" mechanism built around that map. His book quotes Rowbotham ("Parallax") verbatim by page and describes his own levelling tests on Lake Erie and the Erie Canal; it also teaches the seventh-day Sabbath, the 2300-day prophecy, the 1844 cleansing of the heavenly sanctuary and the investigative judgment, and quotes Uriah Smith of Battle Creek with permission — the distinctive doctrinal package of Seventh-day Adventism. His 1892 map is not an independent design: it reproduces the projection of J. S. Christopher of Morden College, Blackheath, published in London in 1885, whose Library of Congress copy is overstamped with the name of John Hampden of Balham.
conflicts: OCCUPATION — THREE-WAY, AND THE PROJECT'S OWN BEST SOURCE IS ON THE 'CIVIL ENGINEER' SIDE. Schadewald (Plane Truth ch. 5), which this project already relies on elsewhere, calls him "civil engineer Alexander Gleason, of Buffalo, New York"; Kook Science says "machinist and civil engineer" and is probably downstream of Schadewald. Against that, Boston Rare Maps worked the primary record: "Secondary sources on the internet describe him as a civil engineer, but in the Directory he is listed variously as a solicitor (1882-1883), machinist (1889), engraver (1893) and patternmaker (1898)... never as a civil engineer." A third line, Find a Grave, gives "a Die Sinker, Stencil maker, Carriage painter" who struck Civil War tokens in Hillsdale County, Michigan. Two further scraps cut the same way: on the 1892 map the trade credit is the Buffalo Electrotype and Engraving Co., an engraving house; and in his own Lake Erie narrative Gleason HIRES a civil engineer (A. E. Arnold of the Nickel Plate Railroad) and his instruments rather than using his own. My read of the weight of evidence is skilled metal/engraving trades, not a civil engineer — but Schadewald says otherwise and I am reporting both. Note also that Goudey called him "Prof. Alex. Gleason", a movement honorific with no located institutional basis. NOT LOCATED: the Buffalo City Directory entries themselves; I am relying on the dealer's reading of them.

THE 1885 MAP — DEALER SAYS GLEASON, THE ARTEFACT DOES NOT. Boston Rare Maps: "His initial effort was The New Map of the World on the Projection of J. Steer Christopher, Morden College, Blackheath...Without Any Antipodes. Published in 1885, this map closely resembles the 1892 map offered here, though it lacks the indicator arms" — and elsewhere refers to "the two maps", so this is a real attribution to Gleason, not loose phrasing. But I read the map. The digitised Library of Congress deposit copy carries NO Gleason and NO Buffalo anywhere: "THE NEW MAP OF THE WORLD. ON THE PROJECTION OF J. STEER CHRISTOPHER. Morden College Blackheath, Lithographed by J. R. King... WITHOUT ANY ANTIPODES", "Entered at Stationers' Hall, August 1885. All rights reserved", the printed line "To be obtained of the Author as above" struck through in ink, and "JOHN HAMPDEN, BALHAM, S.W." rubber-stamped at head and foot. LoC copyright stamp MAY 3 1887; Map Division MAY 7 1903. On its face this is an English publication of Christopher's, later distributed by Hampden. So: Gleason republished Christopher ONCE that is documented on the object — in 1892 — not twice. An 1885 Gleason issue may exist and simply not be the copy digitised, but I did not locate any catalogue record for one in the loc.gov search API, Open Library, or web search. SCOPE OF MY EVIDENCE: the 1885 scan I examined is a user upload to archive.org by an apparent flat-earth account claiming LoC provenance; the LoC copyright and Map Division stamps visible in the image corroborate that it is a LoC sheet, but I could not find the LoC catalogue record itself.

BOOK DATE — 1893 vs 1890. Library of Congress / Open Library / most dealers and auction listings date the book 1893 and catalogue it as "2d ed. Rev. and enl." Schadewald ch. 5 and the Leventhal Map Center exhibition both say the first edition was 1890. The book settles it in its own front matter: title page "SECOND EDITION ... REVISED AND ENLARGED", copyright page "CopyRIGHT, 1890. By ALEX. GLEASON. RE-COPYRIGHTED AND RE-WRITTEN, REVISED AND ENLARGED, 1893." Anything citing 'Gleason 1893' as the work's date is citing the second edition. No 1890 copy located in the searches named above.

"MODERN COLLEGE" vs "MORDEN COLLEGE". Christopher's 1885 map reads "Morden College Blackheath" — Morden College is the real 17th-century almshouse in Blackheath. Gleason's 1892 map prints "MODERN COLLEGE, BLACKHEATH, ENGLAND", and every library catalogue (BPL/Leventhal, Yale, Digital Commonwealth, DPLA) faithfully reproduces the error because it is on the sheet. Boston Rare Maps silently corrects it to Morden. This is not a trivial spelling point: it is direct textual evidence of the direction of copying, and it means the two spellings identify two different objects.

SEVENTH-DAY ADVENTIST AFFILIATION — the newspaper claim and the doctrinal evidence are different things and should not be merged. Boston Rare Maps: "According to contemporary Buffalo-area newspapers in 1889 he helped establish a Seventh-Day Adventist Church there"; Schadewald calls him "The most important Seventh-day Adventist flat-earther"; Kook Science lists the affiliation flatly. I could NOT read those Buffalo newspapers (Chronicling America and NYS Historic Newspapers API calls both failed from this environment; Kook Science is unreachable to WebFetch behind a robots/TLS error). What I CAN evidence, from the primary text: the 1893 edition teaches the seventh-day Sabbath (a chapter head reads "Seventh Day vs. the First"), the 2300-day prophecy terminating in 1844, the cleansing of the heavenly sanctuary, and the investigative judgment — and cites "Synopsis of Present Truth, by U. Smith, Battle Creek, Mich.", noting "Prof. U. Smith has given us permission". That is Uriah Smith, the denomination's leading author, at its headquarters. The doctrinal commitment is beyond doubt from the book itself; formal membership and the 1889 church-founding remain on newspaper testimony I have not seen. Separately, Schadewald quotes Carpenter reporting a Seventh Day Adventist minister EXCOMMUNICATED in London for flat-earth teaching — so the denomination did not own the position, and the page should not imply it did.

GLEASON vs THE ZETETIC MAINSTREAM ON THE SUN. He puts the sun at 1,725 miles; he records that "Some of the Zetetic faith had given the sun's altitude 2500, some 3500, and some even less". Schadewald reports Goudey adopting 2,700 nautical miles instead and attributes Gleason's lower figure to his acceptance of Hampden's 57.5-degree pole-to-equator claim. I did not locate "Hampden" in the OCR of the 1893 edition (0 hits), so that causal explanation is Schadewald's and is not confirmed in Gleason's own words.

sources.kind: primary artefact — patent facsimile (public domain, 1893)
sources.says: ANSWERS THE PATENT QUESTION: NO. The specification of US 497,917 'Time-Chart' nowhere asserts, argues or implies that the earth is flat. I read the printed facsimile, p. 3, col. 2, and transcribed it directly: 'The extorsion of the map from that of a globe consists, mainly in the straightening out of the meridian lines allowing each to retain their original value from Greenwich, the equator to the two poles.' Immediately before, p. 3 col. 1: 'The map is not so extorted as to lose the relative latitude and longitude of any places on the land or sea, but retains all latitudes and longitudes of places agreeing with other recognized authors'. The opening reads 'My invention has reference to certain mechanical devices and geographical illustrations, to be used on a flat circular map of the world'. Claim 1 claims only the mechanism — circular time dial, graduated disk, two pivoted indicating arms held by friction. The whole pitch is pedagogical: computing time differences for 'the school child'. In short, before the Patent Office Gleason described his sheet as a globe flattened out, and the word 'flat' in it describes the paper, not the earth. Google Patents OCR of this document is noisy ('limeChart', 'sufiieient'); the quotations above are from the page images, not the OCR.

sources.kind: primary source — the book, full text (public domain, 1893)
sources.says: Title page: 'SECOND EDITION ... REVISED AND ENLARGED BY ALEX. GLEASON', published by The Buffalo Electrotype and Engraving Co. Copyright page: 'CopyRIGHT, 1890. By ALEX. GLEASON. RE-COPYRIGHTED AND RE-WRITTEN, REVISED AND ENLARGED, 1893.' Dedicated to 'that class of citizens who are known as "Honest Skeptics"'. Zetetic dependence: 'we shall use the sentiments largely of Parallax and his words verbatim'; 'The quotations will be found on pages 375-406 of his work, "Zetetic Astronomy."'; section 'The Horizon Line, by Dr. Wm. Rowbotham'; also cites 'Carpenter's "Common Sense Astronomy," p. 47'. Own experiment: 'I will now give my own experimental tests as to the convexity of the waters of Lake Erie. On July 4th, 1887...' — Silver Creek / Lighthouse Point, with 'Mr. A. E. Arnold, a civil engineer of the Nickel Plate Railroad' and 'his two transits or theodolites'. Erie Canal: the 52-mile lockless level between Syracuse and York Mills. Sun: '1725 miles equal the altitude of both the Sun and the North Star'. Adventist doctrine: 2300 days ending '1844', 'the cleansing of the sanctuary, the investigative Judgment', chapter head 'Seventh Day vs. the First', and 'Synopsis of Present Truth, by U. Smith, Battle Creek, Mich.' Contributions by R. E. L. J. Lovell of Vadis, W. Va. Term counts in this OCR: zetetic 6, Parallax many, Sabbath 186, Adventist 0, Christopher 0, antipodes 0, Hampden 0, Blount 0, Earth Review 0.

sources.says: 'THE NEW MAP OF THE WORLD. ON THE PROJECTION OF J. STEER CHRISTOPHER. Morden College Blackheath, Lithographed by J. R. King. SCIENTIFICALLY, PRACTICALLY AND INTELLIGIBLY CORRECT. WITHOUT ANY ANTIPODES.' Subtitle: 'All Oceans and Seas perfectly level ... all uniformly and perfectly level, Without any Rotundity.' Imprint: 'Entered at Stationers' Hall, August 1885. All rights reserved.' Foot: 'To be obtained of the Author as above' struck through in blue ink, with 'JOHN HAMPDEN, BALHAM, S.W.' stamped in purple at head and foot. sources.kind: primary artefact — the 1892 map, BPL/Leventhal copy (IIIF image examined directly)
sources.says: Head of sheet: 'GLEASON'S NEW STANDARD MAP OF THE WORLD / ON THE PROJECTION OF J. S. CHRISTOPHER, MODERN COLLEGE, BLACKHEATH, ENGLAND / SCIENTIFICALLY AND PRACTICALLY CORRECT / AS "IT IS" / PATENT ALLOWED November 15, 1892'. Foot: 'ALL RIGHTS RESERVED / ALEX. GLEASON / BUFFALO, N.Y.' and 'PUBLISHED BY THE BUFFALO ELECTROTYPE AND ENGRAVING CO., BUFFALO, N.Y., U.S.A.' Deposit hand: 'Map 10.4.1892'; shelfmark G3201.B71 1892. THE MAP ITSELF, UNLIKE THE PATENT, CARRIES ZETETIC COSMOLOGY: the June note has the sun moving 'round the Tropics in a spiral circle', and the December note reads 'There is no "sunlight" beyond 80 degrees south, but unknown regions of ice' — i.e. the Antarctic midnight sun denied on the face of the sheet. Catalogue note: 'Map of the globe stretched and flattened into a circular plane... Text on verso.' The verso is NOT digitised in this IIIF manifest (one canvas only), so the line Boston Rare Maps quotes from the map — 'the earth a globe or a plane—take your choice' — I could not verify against the object.

sources.kind: secondary — Robert Schadewald, The Plane Truth (posthumous, web edition), chs. 5 and 8. A critic writing history of the movement; the best secondary source this project uses.
sources.says: Ch. 5 calls him 'The most important Seventh-day Adventist flat-earther... civil engineer Alexander Gleason, of Buffalo, New York', dates the first edition to 1890 (about 95 pp.) and the second to 1893 (402 pp.), and credits him with experiments on the Erie Canal. Ch. 8 documents the downstream carry: Charles Morse's reading list includes Gleason alongside Rowbotham, Carpenter and Winship; Goudey acknowledges a debt to 'Dr. Samuel B. Rowbotham, Prof. Wm. Carpenter, Prof. Alex. Gleason...', cites the Erie Canal and Lake Erie tests, and quotes 'Professor Alex. Gleason gives the distance however, geometrically computed, as being only 1,725 nautical miles'; Schadewald adds that Goudey 'reproduced the deceptive diagram Gleason invented to rebut sphericity' and attributes Gleason's low sun figure to Hampden's 57.5-degree claim. Ch. 8 also records Voliva photographed on the cover of Leaves of Healing, 10 May 1930, pointing at Gleason's map. Ch. 5 separately reports, via Carpenter, a Seventh Day Adventist minister excommunicated in London for flat-earth teaching.

sources.says: 'Gleason himself is very hard to pin down... Secondary sources on the internet describe him as a civil engineer, but in the Directory he is listed variously as a solicitor (1882-1883), machinist (1889), engraver (1893) and patternmaker (1898)... never as a civil engineer.' Also: 'According to contemporary Buffalo-area newspapers in 1889 he helped establish a Seventh-Day Adventist Church there and in 1898 broke his hip in a bicycle collision.' Attributes the 1885 map to Gleason as 'His initial effort'. Reads the patent's globe sentence as Gleason 'unwittingly fessing up that his map is... a projection of a globe'. Census: 'I find record of but one other having appeared on the antiquarian market... and but three holdings in institutional collections' (BPL-Leventhal, National Geographic Society, Yale). Cites Rowbotham, Schadewald, Garrett Dash Nelson, the Buffalo Commercial, Ancestry and OCLC. Does NOT mention John Hampden.

Its companion page on the book says 'first privately published in 1890 and republished as an expanded edition in 1893'. Its listed references are newspaper citations (Buffalo Commercial Nov 1890 and Mar 1893; Wichita Democrat Feb 1897) which I could not retrieve; the 'civil engineer' field carries no visible citation and most likely descends from Schadewald. Dates the book to 1890, agreeing with Schadewald and the copyright page against the catalogue date of 1893.

The memorial does not mention the map, the book or the patent — the identification with the mapmaker is inferential.

people.reasoning:
METHOD. I read the artefacts rather than the write-ups, because the brief flagged that this project has taken dating from movement genealogy three times and been wrong. Specifically I pulled the full OCR of the 1893 second edition from the Internet Archive and grepped it; I downloaded and visually read the header and footer of the 1885 Christopher map at full resolution; I read the header and footer of the 1892 Gleason map from the BPL IIIF image; and when the patent's globe sentence turned out to be load-bearing (a dealer is using it as a gotcha) I stopped trusting Google's OCR, downloaded the patent PDF facsimile and read the type off page 3. That is what turned up the 1890 copyright line, the John Hampden stamp, the Morden/Modern split, and the spiral-sun and 80-degrees-south notes on Gleason's own sheet.

WHAT THE BRIEF ASKED, ANSWERED.
1. School: Zetetic, on documented citation and self-identification, not resemblance — see lineage_evidence. He quotes Rowbotham by page, calls his own position "Zeteticism", and his map descends from a sheet distributed by John Hampden.
2. Republication of Christopher: YES for 1892, and the object proves it — the 1892 sheet names Christopher's projection on its face and even inherits the Blackheath address, garbled to "Modern College". NO for 1885 on the evidence I could reach: the LoC deposit copy of the 1885 map bears Christopher, J. R. King and John Hampden and no Gleason at all. Boston Rare Maps says otherwise. Reported as a conflict, not resolved.
3. Occupation: the "civil engineer" claim does NOT originate with Kook Science — it is Schadewald's, which matters because this project leans on Schadewald elsewhere. Against it stand the Buffalo directory entries (four different trades, none of them civil engineer), the Find a Grave trade description, the engraving-house imprint, and the fact that Gleason hired a civil engineer for his own Lake Erie test. I have given my read of the weight and reported both sides. I did not see the directories myself.
4. SDA: the doctrinal evidence is primary and decisive (1844, investigative judgment, heavenly sanctuary, seventh-day Sabbath, Uriah Smith of Battle Creek by permission). The 1889 church-founding is newspaper testimony I could not retrieve. Also worth carrying to the page: Carpenter reports a London SDA minister excommunicated for flat-earth teaching, so the denomination should not be painted as owning the position.
5. Patent: NO. It never mentions flat-earth views, and it describes the sheet as a globe unrolled — "The extorsion of the map from that of a globe..." — verified off the printed facsimile.

ROLE DISCIPLINE. I have written him as CARRIER because he says so himself ("the sentiments largely of Parallax and his words verbatim") and because the map is Christopher's projection with a patented dial on it. I have flagged, but deliberately not promoted, the 1,725-mile geometric sun distance — for which he explicitly distinguishes himself from other zetetics and which Goudey later attributes to him by name — and Schadewald's claim that he invented a diagram. Neither should be turned into an originator credit until somebody checks them against the 461-item corpus; grep shows the repo currently contains no reference to Gleason at all.

SCOPE OF ABSENCES. Every negative above is scoped to what I ran: term counts are from the archive.org OCR of the 1893 second edition only (zero hits does not exclude the 1890 edition, which I never located, and OCR of this scan is poor — it renders Rowbotham as "Hobotham"). No 1890 printing and no 1885 Gleason-imprint map were found in the loc.gov search API, Open Library, or web search. The Buffalo Commercial and other Buffalo newspapers were not reachable: the Chronicling America and NYS Historic Newspapers JSON endpoints both failed from this environment, and Kook Science is unreachable to WebFetch. The 1892 map's verso text is not digitised.

REPO. I read README.md and searched scripts/ and data/; I edited nothing and ran no tests, build or git.

people.name: John Hampden
people.lineage_evidence: Assigned on a documented relationship to the zetetic literature, not on resemblance. Four separate documented links: (1) Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch.2, states Hampden "chanced upon a copy of Rowbotham's Earth Not a Globe" in 1869 and was "converted at the first reading"; (2) his first publication was a pamphlet of extracts from Earth Not a Globe issued with Rowbotham's own permission (The Popularity of Error, and the Unpopularity of Truth); (3) after losing the 1870 wager he paid Rowbotham £10 to return to the Old Bedford Canal and re-run the experiments, and a further £10 to printer Alfred Bull for more (Schadewald ch.3); (4) the signed wager agreement — text reproduced verbatim in the Queen's Bench judgment, Hampden v Walsh, 1 QBD 189 — names "Mr. W. Carpenter, of 7 Carlton Terrace, Lewisham Park" as Hampden's referee, i.e. he appointed the other leading Rowbotham disciple to act for him. Independent corroboration of the conversion from Bob Forrest (amateur essayist, who credits Schadewald): "It was in 1869, when Hampden was fifty years old, that he became converted to Rowbotham's theories." Contra-evidence worth carrying: the relationship ran only one way at the end. Schadewald's note 3.1 records that Rowbotham "was obviously miffed at Hampden for stealing some of his thunder," published Experimental Proofs that the Surface of Standing Water Is Not Convex, but Horizontal (1870) backhanding Hampden over the wager, and "treated Hampden unkindly in the 1873 edition of Earth Not a Globe." The lineage is documented; the founder's endorsement is not.
people.role: CARRIER / distributor — with a proprietary and organisational layer. No argument was located that originates with him. Positive evidence for carrier status, not merely absence of evidence for origination: (a) his first publication was literally extracts from Rowbotham printed under licence; (b) he bought the remaining stock AND the copyright of William Carpenter's Theoretical Astronomy Examined and Exposed for £100 — he acquired and redistributed another man's arguments as property (Schadewald ch.2, sourced at ref. 2.3 to Carpenter's own statement in the introduction to The Delusion of the Day); (c) the arguments he gives in his own words in the longest verbatim record of his reasoning — the Chelmsford Chronicle gaol interview, 19 Feb 1875 — are Rowbotham's inventory item for item: ships hull-down explained by perspective ("it was merely a result of perspective"), the lamp/street-lamp analogy, a northern centre with no south pole ("having only the northern centre and a southern circumference"), the ice barrier, the immovable earth of Scripture, and circumnavigation dismissed by the walk-round-the-gaol analogy. He also repeats the Newton/Copernicus recantation trope, which long predates him. The organisational layer: he founded the New Geographical Society (Schadewald: headquarters seem to have been Hampden's home, and it is not clear it had more than one member) and from 1 May 1876 published The Truth-Seeker's Oracle and Scriptural Science Review, threepence monthly, also styled "Terra Firma" and "John Hampden's Monthly" — a distribution channel, not a research programme. ONE CANDIDATE ORIGINATION, deliberately NOT promoted to originator, flagged instead as a conflict below: Schadewald credits Hampden with introducing a rhetorical register rather than an argument — that Rowbotham and Carpenter "were generally circumspect in their language. Not Hampden!" Hampden's 1870 pamphlet opens on "the notorious rascality of the scientific world" and he branded Wallace a swindler, thief and felon in print for two decades. A tonal register is not an argument, and I could not show he was first even at that: I did not search pre-1870 zetetic periodicals, and the check is scoped to Schadewald chs 1–4 and the sources listed here. His money-challenge device (Scientific Opinion, 12 Jan 1870: "willing to deposit from £50. to £500. … and defies all the philosophers, divines and scientific professors in the United Kingdom") is likewise a device, not an argument; whether any zetetic offered a money wager before him was not tested.
people.dates: Born 1819 or 1820 — Schadewald gives both, biographical data cited (ref. 2.2) to Boase, Modern English Biography. Son of the Rev. John Hampden, Church of England clergyman, rector of Hinton Martel, Dorset from c.1829; Schadewald states he was related to Bishop Renn Dickson Hampden. Matriculated at St Mary Hall, Oxford, 14 February 1839; per Schadewald "apparently dropped out without graduating." Living at Swindon, Wiltshire at the time of the 1870 wager; at Croydon by February 1875 (Chelmsford Chronicle, 19 Feb 1875). Died 22 January 1891 of severe bronchitis (Schadewald ch.2 close; Forrest independently, though he credits Schadewald, gives "died of bronchitis in January 1891"). Schadewald ch.4 opens by noting his death "in the previous year" left the movement "without a visible leader." The flat 1819–1891 form appears in a dealer listing and in the movement's own wiki — see conflicts.
works: The Popularity of Error, and the Unpopularity of Truth (c.1869–70) — extracts from Rowbotham's Earth Not a Globe published with Rowbotham's permission, interleaved with Hampden's own commentary; Schadewald calls it "apparently Hampden's first publication"

God's Truth or Man's Science, Which Shall Prevail? (pamphlet, written and published c. March 1870) — Schadewald states this pamphlet has not survived; its contents are inferred only from Wallace's point-by-point reply of 20 March 1870. Do not describe its contents as known

Is Water Level or Convex After All? The Bedford Canal Swindle Detected and Exposed (Swindon, Wilts: Alfred Bull, 1870) — ATTRIBUTION CAVEAT: the title page names no author. Schadewald attributes it to Hampden on internal evidence only ("the style and tone are unmistakably Hampden's"). Scientific Opinion's editorial of 27 April 1870 also treats it as anonymous. Its subtitle became the movement's rallying phrase for three decades
A Few Scriptural Inconsistencies with the Newtonian Theory (New Geographical Society, June 1873, 4 pp.)

The Truth-Seeker's Oracle and Scriptural Science Review — monthly, first issue 1 May 1876, threepence; also identified as "Terra Firma", "John Hampden's Monthly" and "Organ of the New Geographical Society"

The New Manual of Biblical Cosmography; or, Outline of the General System of the Universe (London: Beaumont, [1877], 15 pp., fold. illus.) — catalogued at the Library of Congress, call number QB638 .H22. This is the only Hampden item in the LoC flat-earth research guide

A printed letter to T. H. Huxley as President of the Royal Society, 1885, with an appendix "Modern Education conducted on Wrong Principles" — known through Wallace's quotation of it in My Life (1905), vol. 2
Two-page leaflet, c.1885, one thousand copies circulated to residents and tradesmen of Godalming and masters of Charterhouse School — described and quoted by Wallace, My Life vol. 2
people.summary: John Hampden (b. 1819 or 1820, d. 22 January 1891) was an Oxford-matriculated gentleman of means who converted to Samuel Rowbotham's zetetic astronomy on reading Earth Not a Globe in 1869 and spent the next two decades as the movement's most conspicuous publicist. In January 1870 he advertised in Scientific Opinion offering to stake £50–£500 against anyone who could prove the Earth's rotundity; Alfred Russel Wallace accepted, and at the Old Bedford Canal on 1–5 March 1870 Wallace raised the sightline to roughly 13 ft 4 in and added a midpoint marker, and the umpire J. H. Walsh awarded him the stakes on 18 March. Hampden bought the remaining stock and the copyright of William Carpenter's Theoretical Astronomy Examined and Exposed for £100, published extracts of Rowbotham under licence, and ran a one-man New Geographical Society and its monthly from 1876. He stated his own motive in print: he "took up the subject, simply and solely relying on the fact that the Bible, or Scriptural evidence, as far as it went, uniformly ignored, if it did not directly oppose the notion of a globular earth."
conflicts: WHO REPAID WHAT — the project's own genealogy doc is wrong on the figure. claude/source-genealogy.md says the movement cites "the court voiding the wager and Wallace repaying the £1,000." The primary law report (Hampden v Walsh, 1 QBD 189, judgment 17 Jan 1876, Cockburn CJ with Mellor and Quain JJ) shows the action was brought against WALSH THE STAKEHOLDER, not Wallace, and was for recovery of Hampden's OWN £500 deposit, not £1,000. Headnote: "plaintiff having demanded his deposit back before it had been paid over by defendant, he was entitled to judgment." Wallace's own account reconciles the two but confirms the amount: he had signed an indemnity to Walsh, "so I had to pay back the money, and also pay all the costs of the action, about £200 more," then settled at costs plus £120, "amounting to £277," with £410 left nominally owing to him by Hampden. Wikipedia compresses this to "required that Wallace return the money to Hampden" (party wrong, amount unstated); the movement's own wiki says Hampden "sued Wallace" (party wrong). Recommend the page say: judgment against the stakeholder for Hampden's £500 deposit, borne by Wallace under an indemnity. Do not print £1,000.

GROUNDS OF THE RULING — all sources agree it was legal, not scientific, but they differ on which rule. Schadewald frames it as the Gaming Act 1845 having "made all wagers null and void." The judgment is narrower and the distinction matters: the court HELD the agreement was a wager and void, but held that s.18 did not bar recovery of a sum still in the stakeholder's hands where the depositor repudiated before payment over. The wager being void is not what won Hampden his money; his revocation before payment is.

BIRTH YEAR — Schadewald, citing Boase's Modern English Biography, writes "born in 1819 or 1820" and leaves it open. A dealer listing (Argosy Book Store, seen in search-result metadata only; the page itself returned HTTP 429 and was not read) and the movement's own tfes.org wiki both print a flat "1819–1891". Prefer Schadewald's hedge; the flat form has no visible source.

WHAT HAMPDEN WAS BEFORE 1869 — Schadewald: the thirty years after he entered Oxford "are lost to history," with only marriage and at least two children established. Bob Forrest states that at the time Parallax began lecturing "Hampden was busy studying Britain's coastal defences, with a view to improving them," giving no source. Unresolved; do not repeat Forrest's detail as fact.

MOVEMENT SELF-DESCRIPTION vs RECORD — tfes.org (The Flat Earth Wiki, movement-internal, and a wiki) opens: "John Hampden (1819-1891) was an English scientist of the Royal Academy." No credential of any kind is attested in Schadewald/Boase, in the 1875 newspaper interview, or in Wallace; Schadewald has him matriculating at St Mary Hall in 1839 and apparently leaving without a degree, and describes him as a gentleman of comfortable means. This is evidence of what the movement says about itself, not documentation. The same page states the court "deemed the bet to be invalid and Hampden's money was returned to him in full," which is closer to the law report than Wikipedia is.

IMPRISONMENTS — the counts differ by what is being counted, and the page should not print a bare number. Wallace's own chronology (My Life vol. 2): Old Bailey conviction on Walsh's prosecution 1871, bound over one year; a civil libel verdict of £600 to Wallace in 1871 (elsewhere £687 with costs), uncollectible because Hampden had assigned his assets to his solicitor son-in-law and declared bankruptcy; October 1872 and 13 January 1873 prosecutions respited on published apologies (the second, a full recantation, is quoted verbatim); then two months in Newgate; then Chelmsford Assizes 6 March 1875, one year plus two years' recognizances, released after about six months. Schadewald adds a week in gaol in July 1871 for want of sureties after Hampden wrote to Annie Wallace. Forrest says "no less than three jail sentences." Wikipedia gives "12 months' imprisonment … and keep the peace for two years," which is the 1875 sentence only.

THE CARPENTER PURCHASE IS SINGLE-SOURCED AND INTERESTED. The £100 for stock plus copyright of Theoretical Astronomy Examined and Exposed rests entirely on Schadewald's ref. 2.3: "Carpenter gives the amount in the introduction to The Delusion of the Day." That is Carpenter — a party to the transaction and the man whose stock was bought — reporting it himself. I could not locate a digitised text of The Delusion of the Day in the searches run (WebSearch on the title plus Hampden/copyright; Wikipedia's Carpenter article does not mention Hampden at all). Publish the £100 as "Carpenter's own account, relayed by Schadewald," not as an established figure. Also note the work bought has itself an unstable imprint: Wikipedia lists both an 1866 (London: Job Caudwell) and an 1869 printing.

PAGINATION OF WALLACE'S ACCOUNT — the LoC guide cites My Life v.2, pp. 381–393 for the Hampden chapter; the Internet Archive copy I read (myliferecordofev02walluoft) carries the same passage at printed pp. 372–375 in ch. XXXIX, "Hampden and the Flat Earth." Different printings. Cite the chapter, not a page, unless the specific copy is named.

DATE OF THE EXPERIMENT — Schadewald's chapter opens "On March 5, 1870" but his own narrative has the party assembling from 28 February, markers set 1 March, the first inconclusive observations 2 March and the decisive run on Saturday 5 March. Walsh's award is dated 18 March 1870 and was published in The Field on 26 March 1870. The repo's B03 currently pins nothing here, but if the page ever dates "the 1870 experiment" it should say 1–5 March 1870, award 18 March.

BEARS ON AN OPEN REPO ITEM (B03 / Manea Fen). The project state doc records Schadewald as saying 1839 for Rowbotham's first canal trials. Schadewald ch.3 in fact writes that Rowbotham's April 1870 party "reported the canal still as flat as it was when Rowbotham lived there in 1838" — i.e. Schadewald prints 1838 here, matching the repo's B03 rather than the state doc's summary of him. Someone should read ch.1 before treating "Schadewald says 1839" as settled.

BEARS ON THE PAGE'S JOHNSON ATTRIBUTION. The genealogy doc credits Charles K. Johnson with THE CONSPIRACY FRAME on the formula "Rowbotham and Carpenter said astronomers were wrong; Johnson said they were lying." Hampden, in 1870, said they were lying: his pamphlet opens on "the notorious rascality of the scientific world," and Schadewald explicitly marks this as the point where Hampden "broke new ground" against Rowbotham's and Carpenter's circumspection. The two claims are not flatly contradictory — Hampden's target was named individuals in a specific dispute, Johnson's was an institutional cover-up of a faked space programme — but the Johnson line as currently worded is too strong and should be narrowed, or it will be broken by anyone who reads chapter 2. I am NOT proposing Hampden as originator of anything; the fix is to the Johnson wording.

Hampden of Croydon, committed for want of sureties over a libellous postcard. people.reasoning:
METHOD. I worked from the primary record outward rather than from the movement's genealogy inward, because the brief warned this project has been burned three times by taking dating from the movement's own account. Order: Schadewald's The Plane Truth chs 2–4 plus his Notes and References pages (which name his own sources, so his claims could be graded); then the actual Queen's Bench law report; then Wallace's autobiography; then the 1875 newspaper interview; then library catalogues; then the wikis and the dealer listing last, as the weakest tier. Two of the four load-bearing documents (the law report and the 1875 interview) turned out to be hosted on Charles H. Smith's Wallace Page at WKU, which is a scholar-curated archive of primary texts rather than a commentary.

ORIGINATOR TEST — WHY HE FAILS IT, POSITIVELY. The strict rule requires showing a person INTRODUCED an argument. Hampden fails it on evidence rather than on silence: his first publication was Rowbotham's text reprinted under licence; he purchased another author's copyright rather than writing his own case; and the fullest verbatim record of his own reasoning — a hostile-but-fair newspaper interview conducted in gaol in 1875, where he had every incentive to make his best case and where the reporter says he answered every question directly — contains Rowbotham's arguments and nothing else. That is the strongest available form of a carrier finding: not "we could not find an origination", but "here is him arguing at length, and every argument is somebody else's". The one novelty a source does credit him with is tonal, not propositional, and I have deliberately left it as a flagged conflict against the page's Johnson attribution rather than promoting him. The money-challenge device is the other candidate; I did not test whether any earlier zetetic offered a wager, so I have scoped that rather than claiming a first.

WHAT THE BRIEF SAID THAT CHECKED OUT, AND ONE THING TO SOFTEN. "Rowbotham convert" — confirmed, 1869, with four independent kinds of link. "The 1870 Bedford Level wager" — confirmed to primary documents including the signed agreement text in the law report. "Bought the stock and copyright of Carpenter's Theoretical Astronomy" — confirmed as a claim, but it rests on a single interested witness, Carpenter, in the introduction to The Delusion of the Day, which I could not locate digitised. The brief's phrase "a material carrier on the Rowbotham–Carpenter edge" is exactly right and is in fact better supported by the referee appointment (in the court record) than by the copyright purchase (Carpenter's own word).

THE ERROR I WENT LOOKING FOR AND FOUND. The genealogy doc's line about "Wallace repaying the £1,000" is wrong on both party and amount as a description of the ruling, and the true story is more useful to the page than the false one: a court found the agreement WAS a wager and void, then ordered the stakeholder to return Hampden's own £500 because he had revoked before payment over. Wallace bore it only because he had indemnified Walsh. Nothing in that touches the measurement. The movement's compression is thus doubly wrong — it treats a stakeholder-revocation rule as a reversal of a survey — and the page can say so from the law report rather than from a secondary summary. Note that Hampden himself supplied the £1,000 figure that is probably the root of the confusion: his 1885 leaflet charged Wallace with obtaining "a cheque for £1,000 by fraud".

WHAT I DID NOT ESTABLISH. Whether The Delusion of the Day survives digitised anywhere (searched by title with Hampden/copyright terms). Whether any zetetic offered a money wager before January 1870 (not searched — pre-1870 periodicals not consulted). Hampden's exact birth date or a probate/death record independent of Boase and Schadewald (Jisc Library Hub was Cloudflare-blocked; the Argosy dealer page returned HTTP 429 and I read only its search-result title, so its "1819-1891" is uncorroborated metadata from a dealer catalogue). The first-edition date of The Popularity of Error. Whether the 1870 pamphlet's anonymity was ever resolved by anyone other than Schadewald on style.

BIO_STATUS RECOMMENDATION for people.py: this is enough for a "worked" record rather than a stub — formation, had, ignored, kernel and legacy are all evidenced — but the kernel field will be the hard one. His defensible kernel is procedural, not observational: he was right that the question "is this water surface curved?" is a matter of measurement rather than authority ("There is engineering science enough in the world to determine the exact surface of water, and it ought not to be left as a mere private squabble between myself and Mr. Wallace"), and right that it ought to be settled publicly by competent surveyors. Why it does not save the claim: he got precisely that — a public test, his own choice of canal, his own choice of referee, a stakeholder of agreed repute — and when the measurement came back he declined to look through the telescope, then litigated the custody of the stake for six years. He is the cleanest case in the dataset of a demand for a decisive test being met and then abandoned, which is the same stopping-rule failure the Rowbotham record already names, in its most documented form.

people.name: Albert Smith ("Zetetes"), first editor of The Earth—Not a Globe!—Review
people.lineage_evidence: Documented relationship to the zetetic literature, not resemblance. (1) He edited the Universal Zetetic Society's own organ, titled "The Earth—Not a Globe!—Review", and signed himself "Zetetes" in its pages (primary: mastheads and signed editorial matter, Internet Archive scan of the bound run, e.g. No. 1, January 1893, price 2d, and the resignation notice in No. 8, July 1894). (2) The Review's own "Advertizer" pages sold Rowbotham's "Zetetic Astronomy, by 'Parallax'" (7s.) and Carpenter's "100 Proofs the Earth is not a Globe" (3½d) by post from Hon. Sec. John Williams, 32 Bankside, London S.E. — i.e. the periodical he founded-as-editor was the distribution channel for both Victorian originators (primary: advertiser pages in the same scan). (3) Schadewald, "The Plane Truth" ch. 4 (movement history by an outside critic, published posthumously on the web, not peer-reviewed) reports Smith claimed Rowbotham as a personal friend, "suggesting that he had met the great 'Parallax' but never learned to spell his name" (Smith wrote "Rowbottam"). NOTE: this is a lineage assignment for a periodical editor, not a claim that he held any position Rowbotham did not.
people.role: CARRIER / INSTITUTIONAL. He is an editor and distributor, not an originator. No argument in the 461-item specimen family was found to originate with him in the sources searched. He is the person who put Rowbotham- and Carpenter-derived material, reader-supplied "engineer's testimony" quotations, and one Tychonian text into a subscription periodical with an international correspondence network — the mechanism by which Victorian zetetic claims left Britain. One possible originator claim exists and is NOT settled: Schadewald states "Albert Smith (and to a lesser extent Lady Blount) developed the 'two poles' version of the flat-earth theory," but the evidence Schadewald prints for it is Smith's own self-credit, written under his pseudonym in part two of his son Carl Albert Smith's book — "It was left for 'Zetetes' principally to carry on the war, and to be the first zetetic to acknowledge the proved existence of two so-called 'poles.'" That is a movement-internal self-claim carried by a later historian; it should not be published as originator status without independent corroboration, and the two-pole variant is in any case not the model used by the modern lists (which use the Gleason-style monopole azimuthal chart).
people.dates: PERIODICAL — "The Earth—Not a Globe!—Review" (mastheads also "The Earth — not a Globe — Review"; universally called "the Earth Review" or "E.R."). Old series: No. 1, JANUARY 1893, price 2d; No. 2, April 1893; No. 4, October 1893; No. 5, January 1894; No. 6, March 1894; No. 7, May 1894; No. 8, July 1894 (Nos. 3 and 5 headers not recovered by the OCR of the scan; the quarterly Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct 1893 pattern and Schadewald's account of a July 1893 and a January 1894 issue fill them in). New Series: No. 1, SEPTEMBER 1894 (headed "UNDER NEW MANAGEMENT"), No. 2 January 1895, No. 3 April 1895, No. 4 July 1895, No. 5 October 1895, No. 6 January 1896 — still 2d. Monthly Series, price cut to 1d: "Vol. I. No. 1 (Monthly Series). APRIL, 1896"; then "Vol. III. No. 2, MAY 1896", "No. 3, JUNE 1896", "No. 4-5, JULY-AUGUST 1896", "No. 6, SEPTEMBER to DECEMBER 1896" (the volume numbering jumps I. → III. in the scan; whether that is a masthead error or OCR damage was not determined). END DATE DISPUTED — see conflicts. EDITORSHIP — Albert Smith ("Zetetes") edited Nos. 1–8, January 1893 to July 1894 inclusive; John Williams ("Leo Castle", and per Schadewald also "Excalibur") edited from New Series No. 1, September 1894. Smith's own farewell, in No. 8: "With this issue 'Zetetes' will cease to be the editor of the E.R. Two months ago we placed our resignation (to take effect after No. 8 was issued) in the hands of the Secretary of the U.Z.S." — reason given: "failing health, and the pressure of other work." The September 1894 successor issue confirms: "our late Editor (Zetetes) Mr. Albert Smith … owing to continued illhealth, obliged to give up the Editorial Work of our Magazine." PERSON — birth and death dates NOT located in any source searched (Schadewald ch. 4 and ch. 7, the LoC flat-earth guide, the Internet Archive scan of the Review, the TFES wiki). Attested activity: a public flat-earth debate at Blackburn, Lancashire in 1884; a twopenny tract advertised 15 January 1887; UZS committee member and Review editor from 1892/93; address "Plutus House", Leicester, later "23, East Park Road, North Evington, Leicester" (announced in the Review's own notices and matching the address on a Smith letter reprinted by Winship in 1899); co-author with Lady Blount of "Zetetic Astronomy", 1906; contributed part two of his son's book, 2nd ed. Northampton [1918].
works: The Earth—Not a Globe!—Review ("the Earth Review"), organ of the Universal Zetetic Society. Editor, Nos. 1–8, January 1893 – July 1894. Sold at 2d; orders and monies to Hon. Sec. & Treasurer John Williams, 32 Bankside, Southwark, London S.E.

"Is the Earth a Globe and Has It Axial and Orbital Motion?" — twopenny tract reporting an 1884 Blackburn debate, advertised in the 15 January 1887 issue of Hampden's Earth and Its Evidences (per Schadewald ch. 4; the tract itself was not located)

Tracts and pamphlets listed by Schadewald as written before January 1893: The So-Called "Mistakes of Moses"; "Cranks"; The Sundial; Discussion on "Modern Astronomy" (the first two also appear for sale in the Review's own advertiser pages)
Socialism versus Christianity, published by "The Faith" Press (per Schadewald ch. 4; not independently located)
Zetetic Astronomy, with Lady Blount, 1906, 91 pp. (per Schadewald ch. 7)

Part two of Carl Albert Smith, "Is the Earth a whirling globe?" — LoC guide records the 2nd ed., rev. and enl., Northampton [1918], 112 pp., held by the British Library at 8562.aaa.35. This is where Smith's "two poles" self-credit appears.
people.summary: Albert Smith, who wrote as "Zetetes", was the founding editor of The Earth—Not a Globe!—Review, the Universal Zetetic Society's periodical, which ran from No. 1, January 1893; he edited Nos. 1–8 to July 1894 and resigned through ill health, John Williams ("Leo Castle") taking over from the New Series of September 1894. Under Smith the Review reprinted, in two installments in May and July 1894, the English text of Carl Schöpfer's Berlin lecture "Definite Conclusions of Science — Our Earth Motionless", crediting it "From the 'Scientific American,' April 27th, 1878" — the issue of the Scientific American Supplement whose own archive bylines the piece "Madame Blavatsky & Shcepfer"; the Review did not name Blavatsky. The Review is a documented intermediary between Rowbotham's literature and Thomas Winship in Natal: it answered Winship's letters from the Cape in its correspondence columns in 1894–95 and forwarded him pamphlets, and Winship's Zetetic Cosmogony (2nd ed. 1899) quotes the Review by issue at least six times, including three issues Smith edited. Its most consequential single carriage is the "W. Winckler, C.E." engineer's-testimony quotation, printed in the October 1893 issue and still circulating in modern proof lists — for which the Review's own contributor later admitted in print he could not say where he got it.

sources.kind: PRIMARY SOURCE (public-domain periodical, scanned bound run; OCR text at /stream/..._djvu.txt). Movement-internal — this is the movement speaking about itself — but as mastheads and dated editorial notices it is documentary for dates and editorship.
sources.says: Mastheads: "No. i. JANUARY, 1893. Price 2d"; "No. 7. MAY, 1894"; "No. 8. JULY, 1894"; "No. I (New Series). SEPTEMBER, 1894"; "Vol. I. No. 1 (Monthly Series). APRIL, 1896. Price Id"; last recovered masthead "Vol. III. No. 6 (Monthly Series). SEPTEMBER to DECEMBER, 1896". Smith's farewell in No. 8: "With this issue 'Zetetes' will cease to be the editor of the E.R. … This gave the Society ample time to find a fresh editor, and us an opportunity to conclude Dr. Shoepfer's important lecture." September 1894, "UNDER NEW MANAGEMENT": "our late Editor (Zetetes) Mr. Albert Smith … owing to continued illhealth, obliged to give up the Editorial Work of our Magazine." Correspondence thereafter addressed to "Leo Castle, c/o Mr. J. Williams, 32, Bankside, London, S.E.", with items "forwarded to us by the late Editor".

sources.kind: PRIMARY SOURCE (same scan, full text) — the Schöpfer/Blavatsky carriage
sources.says: Headline in No. 7 (May 1894) and continued in No. 8 (July 1894): "OUR EARTH MOTIONLESS. DEFINITE CONCLUSIONS OF SCIENCE. A popular lecture proving that our earth neither rotates upon its axis nor around the sun. — Delivered at Berlin by Dr. Shoepfer." Credit lines: "From The Scientific American. (To be Continued)" and "From the 'Scientific American,' April 27th, 1878." Editorial note signed Ed. E.R. treats the geocentrist as a half-convert: he "should first ascertain experimentally and definitely the shape of the earth we live on." A correspondent's letter of 7 May 1894 confirms serial publication under Smith and his impending resignation: "Am sorry you intend to give up the editorship of the 'E. R.' … Am much pleased that a man of Dr. Schcepfer's standing and ability should attack the twirling mass." Blavatsky is not named: no occurrence of "Blavatsky", "Blava" or "Madame" was located anywhere in the OCR text of this scan.

sources.says: "Definite Conclusions of Science—Our Earth Motionless", byline "By Madame Blavatsky & Shcepfer", Scientific American Supplements Vol. 5, No. 121supp, 27 April 1878, p. 1925. Scientific American's own author index also lists the piece under "Madame Blavatsky".

sources.kind: SECONDARY — Robert Schadewald, The Plane Truth, ch. 4. A researched history by a critic of the movement, posthumously published on a private web archive; not peer-reviewed, no scholarly apparatus beyond its own reference notes. Best single secondary source on the UZS.
sources.says: The UZS's "principal publication was to be the Earth—Not a Globe!—Review, edited by 'Zetetes' (Albert Smith)"; "the most ambitious flat-earth periodical ever". Smith lived in Leicester at the founding, called his headquarters Plutus House, was excommunicated from the Seventh-day Adventists for "upholding the Bible-Earth", had debated at Blackburn in 1884, and claimed "Rowbottam" as a friend. "Leo Castle" and "Excalibur" were John Williams's pseudonyms as editor. The Review "reprinted a lecture 'Our Earth Motionless,' originally delivered in Berlin by a follower of Ptolemy, one Dr. Schoepfer. (It had previously been reprinted in Scientific American, in a translation submitted by Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, founder of Theosophy.)" "After a long struggle under three editors, it folded with the April 1897 issue."

sources.says: Lady Blount "made her Earth Review debut in the second issue" — as a contributor, not editor. "Albert Smith (and to a lesser extent Lady Blount) developed the 'two poles' version of the flat-earth theory", evidenced by Smith's self-credit in his son's book, ending "He was the first editor of The Earth—Not a Globe—Review." In 1906 Blount and Smith published Zetetic Astronomy, 91 pp.

The piece is therefore not located in Collected Writings vol. I as searched; that is not evidence it is absent from the Collected Writings as a whole, which I did not search beyond vol. I.

conflicts: END DATE OF THE PERIODICAL — three-way, unresolved. (a) Schadewald ch. 4: "After a long struggle under three editors, it folded with the April 1897 issue." (b) The Internet Archive scan of the bound run (item titled 1893-1897) contains an "IN MEMORIAM" noticing the death of James Heywood on 17 October 1897 and of Henry George on 29 October 1897, alongside a reference to "The Universal Zetetic Society" — text that cannot have appeared in an April 1897 issue. The masthead of that page did not survive the OCR, so I could not identify its issue number or date. (c) Wikipedia's Universal Zetetic Society article says the magazine "remained active well into the early 20th century." I report all three and pick none.

WHO RAN THE PERIODICAL — the project's own source-genealogy doc currently reads "Lady Elizabeth Blount … Earth Review from Jan 1893" under her originator row, and Wikipedia credits Blount with founding the society and its publications. The primary mastheads and Schadewald both make Albert Smith the editor from No. 1 and Blount a contributor who debuted in issue 2 and later funded the society. This looks like a live error in our own doc and should be corrected there rather than silently reconciled here.

THE THIRD EDITOR — Schadewald says the Review ran "under three editors". I identified two by name: Smith ("Zetetes", Nos. 1–8) and John Williams ("Leo Castle"; Schadewald says "Excalibur" was also Williams). The identity of a third editor was not located in Schadewald ch. 4 or ch. 7, in the recovered OCR of the scan (which ends its recoverable mastheads at September–December 1896), or in the LoC guide.

BLAVATSKY'S EXACT ROLE — Schadewald says the Scientific American printing was "in a translation submitted by Helena Petrovna Blavatsky"; the Kook Science wiki says it was "translated by Madame Blavatsky"; Scientific American's own archive metadata bylines the item "By Madame Blavatsky & Shcepfer", which is a byline, not a statement of who did the translating. Submitted-versus-translated is not settled by any of these, and the piece is not located in Blavatsky's Collected Writings vol. I as searched. Do not publish "Blavatsky translated it" as settled.

WHICH TEXT THE EARTH REVIEW USED — Schadewald's parenthesis notes only that the lecture "had previously been reprinted in Scientific American" in Blavatsky's translation; it does not say the Review used that translation. The Review's own credit lines ("From the 'Scientific American,' April 27th, 1878") and a correspondent's note thanking a reader for sending copies of Scientific American — "You will see that we are making good use of the former" — make it strongly likely the Review reprinted the Scientific American English text verbatim, but I did not collate the two texts word-for-word, and the Review never names Blavatsky. State the chain as sourced, not as collated.

DATE OF THE WINSHIP CORRESPONDENCE ITEM — the reply "T. Winship. — Thanks for The Cape Magazine…" appears twice in the scan at page 96, once inside the July 1895 issue block and once inside the October 1895 block. The bound volume's page order is disturbed and the OCR duplicates pages, so I can place it in 1895 but not in a specific issue. A separate, cleanly placed item — "Thos. Winship. — Thanks for your letter and cuttings from Cape Argus. Hope you have received letter and pamphlets, forwarded." — sits in New Series No. 1, September 1894.

VOLUME NUMBERING OF THE MONTHLY SERIES — the scan shows "Vol. I. No. 1 (Monthly Series). APRIL, 1896" followed by "Vol. III. No 2 (Monthly Series). MAY, 1896". Whether the jump is a masthead error by the publisher or OCR damage was not determined; do not publish a volume number for this series.

NAME COLLISION, flagged so it is not reintroduced — "Albert Smith" is also the name of a well-known Victorian writer and Mont Blanc showman (Albert Richard Smith, 1816–1860), who has a Wikipedia article and no connection to any of this. Our man is Albert Smith of Blackburn and then Leicester, pseudonym "Zetetes", whose birth and death dates I could not establish in any source searched.
people.reasoning:
METHOD. I read the repo README and the project's source-genealogy doc first, then worked from the periodical itself rather than from the movement's account of it: I pulled the OCR text of the Internet Archive scan of the bound run of The Earth—Not a Globe!—Review (1893 onward), indexed every recoverable masthead by byte position, and located each finding inside a dated issue. Secondary framing came from Schadewald chs. 4 and 7 (fetched raw and read directly, not via summariser), with the LoC guide and Scientific American's own archive used for catalogue-level facts.

WHAT THE TASK ASKED, ANSWERED. (1) DATES OF PUBLICATION: No. 1, January 1893, 2d, through an old series of eight numbers to July 1894; a New Series of at least six numbers from September 1894 to January 1896; a Monthly Series at 1d from April 1896, last recovered masthead September–December 1896. End date disputed — see conflicts. (2) EDITORSHIP: Smith edited Nos. 1–8, January 1893 – July 1894. This is established from his own signed farewell in No. 8 and from the successor editor's "UNDER NEW MANAGEMENT" notice in September 1894, not from anyone's later recollection. (3) WHAT IT REPRINTED: Rowbotham- and Carpenter-derived matter and pamphlet advertising; older zetetic texts (Rowton, Middleton); reader-supplied engineers' testimony; and one Tychonian import, Schöpfer's Berlin lecture, taken from the Scientific American Supplement of 27 April 1878 that Scientific American bylines to Blavatsky.

WHY CARRIER AND NOT ORIGINATOR. I looked specifically for an argument that starts with Smith and did not find one. Everything traceable in his run is either older (Rowbotham, Carpenter), supplied by correspondents, or lifted from another periodical. The one thing anyone credits to him — the two-pole variant — rests on his own pseudonymous self-credit printed in his son's book, and Schadewald repeats it. That is exactly the pattern the originator rule exists to catch, so I have recorded it as an unsettled self-claim in the role field and left him a carrier. He matters here as plumbing, not authorship: he is how the material moved.

TWO FINDINGS THAT ARE WORTH MORE TO THE PROJECT THAN THE BIOGRAPHY. First, the "W. Winckler, C.E." engineer's-testimony quotation — "As an engineer of many years experience, I say that this absurd allowance [for curvature] is only permitted in school books…" — is still a staple of modern proof lists. Its earliest appearance I located is the Review's October 1893 issue, under Smith's editorship, in an article on "Scientific Falsehoods" by the pseudonymous "A Hottentot"; Winship reprints it from there in 1899. And the Review published its own failure to source it: a reader, John Bradley, wrote in asking for "the title, etc., of the work by Mr Winckler in which this quotation appears", adding that without it "the value and convincing force of quotations [is] seriously diminished" — and "A Hottentot" replied in print, "I am unable to say where I got the quotation from." A named-witness quotation whose supplier admitted, in the movement's own journal in the 1890s, that he could not say where it came from, and which is still being cited as testimony in 2015–2026, is a provenance result in its own right. It should be checked against the specimen's surveyor/engineer items before it is published.

Second, the editorial note attached to the Schöpfer reprint shows the two lineages were not one movement in 1894. The Review's editor printed the geocentrist's lecture and then told him he had "made great advance on the way to Truth" but "should first ascertain experimentally and definitely the shape of the earth we live on." That is the zetetic organ treating the Tychonian as an incomplete convert — a contemporaneous, primary-source instance of the "two lineages that were never reconciled" claim the page already makes, and stronger than an inference from doctrine.

BONUS FOR THE NOT-VERIFIED LIST. Item 3 of the source-genealogy doc's NOT-VERIFIED section ("Winship's 1st edition date") can now be moved: the LoC guide's catalogue note reads "First published in 1897 (46 p., QB638.W769)". That is a library catalogue record, so cite it as such — it establishes an LoC holding, not an independently examined copy.

SCOPE OF MY NEGATIVES. Where I say something was not found, I mean: not located in Schadewald chs. 4 and 7; not located in the OCR text of the Internet Archive scan of the bound Review run; not located in the LoC flat-earth guide; not located in the extracted text of Blavatsky's Collected Writings vol. I; not located in the TFES wiki page. I did not consult the printed originals, the Cape Magazine or Cape Argus, British census or civil-registration records (which is where Smith's dates would most likely be settled), or Scientific American's paywalled 1878 text — which is the single check that would confirm word-for-word that the Review reprinted Blavatsky's English rather than a fresh translation.

people.name: John Williams (also "Jno. Williams"), founding Secretary and Treasurer of the Universal Zetetic Society
people.dates: No birth or death dates located. Documented active range: 20 August 1892 (his letter to *The Faith*, written from 32 Bankside) to the closing issues of the *Earth (Not a Globe) Review*, which Schadewald says folded with the April 1897 issue. Addresses, in sequence: 32 Bankside, Southwark, London S.E. (1892 – c.1896, his home and the Society's registered meeting place under Rule 10); later 96 Arkwright Street, Nottingham (later issues in the same bound run; POs "payable at Nottingham"). NOT LOCATED IN: Schadewald, *The Plane Truth*, chs. 4, 7 and 9 plus the Notes and References pages; the archive.org OCR of the *Earth Not a Globe Review* 1893–1897 (1.49 MB, searched for "Williams", "Secretary", "Hon. Sec", "resign", "late Secretary"); English Wikipedia; and four targeted web searches. Treat his dates as unestablished, not as absent from the record.
people.role: INSTITUTIONAL, with CARRIER activity. He is not an originator of any argument I could document. Primary evidence of the institutional role: the Society's own masthead in *Earth Review* v.1 n.5 (January 1894), p.110 lists "UNIVERSAL ZETETIC SOCIETY. Treasurer and Secretary. John Williams, 32, Bankside, London, S.E." above a separately-listed Editor and a seven-member Committee; the printed Rules are signed "Signed on behalf of the Committee, John Williams, Secretary"; Rule 10 fixes the Society's meetings at his home address; Rule 6 routes all subscriptions to him; he ran the Society's funds, its lending library, its local-branch recruitment and its pamphlet mail-order. He later became editor of the Review. What he actually argued in print is inherited: his signed compass letter ("if the world was a globe of what use would the compass be?") restates Carpenter's *One Hundred Proofs* (1885) nos. 10, 11 and 13, which are the mariners'-compass proofs; his standing-water/quicksilver piece, quoting Airy's *Six Lectures*, restates Rowbotham's level-water argument and Carpenter's proof no. 2; his £1,000 challenge to *Science Siftings* reprises the Hampden–Wallace wager and Carpenter's "they won't debate me" move. Schadewald credits him with an article "Globe Tinkering, or Gas Meteorites" in issue no. 1 ridiculing meteorites-from-space; I could not locate that article in the OCR run I searched, and I did not establish priority for the anti-meteorite argument, so it should not be scored as an origination on this evidence. He contributes no argument to the 461-item corpus: `scripts/corpus.py` has no Williams-, compass- or meteorite-derived item traceable to him.
people.lineage_evidence: Zetetic by documented relationship to the zetetic literature, not by resemblance. (1) The Society he ran adopted Rowbotham's programme as its constitution: object "The propagation of knowledge relating to Natural Cosmogony in confirmation of the Holy Scriptures, based upon practical investigation", Rule 2 directing that the "so-called 'sciences,' and especially Modern Astronomy" be handled "from practical data" — printed over his signature as Secretary in *Earth Review* v.1 n.5 (Jan 1894), p.110. (2) He was the retail channel for the founding texts: the "Earth Review Advertizer" pages repeatedly run "The following Pamphlets and Leaflets may be had from Mr John Williams, 32 Bankside, London, S.E.", the revised list heading with "Zetetic Astronomy, by 'Parallax.'" and "100 Proofs the Earth is not a Globe" — i.e. he physically distributed Rowbotham and Carpenter from his own front door. (3) He was in correspondence with Carpenter himself; the Review prints an editorial reply to "W. Carpenter" and defers a point to "Mr. Carpenter to answer". Source for all three: the primary periodical, archive.org, *Earth not a Globe Review 1893-1897*. NOTE: I deliberately did not use Schadewald's ref. 4.5 for this — I checked it, and the 1890 Rowbotham sale it records was made by John Hampden, not Williams.

people.summary: John Williams was the founding Secretary and Treasurer of the Universal Zetetic Society, which was constituted in the autumn of 1892 and met at his home at 32 Bankside, Southwark. He ran the Society's money, rules, membership, library and pamphlet trade, signed its Rules on behalf of the Committee, and later edited its journal, the *Earth (Not a Globe) Review*; Lady Blount sat under him as one of seven ordinary Committee members in the January 1894 masthead. Every argument he published over his own name is a restatement of Rowbotham or Carpenter, and none of it reaches the 461-item corpus. Schadewald describes him as an Adventist; that specific claim carries no citation and I could not corroborate it.
conflicts: FOUNDING DATE — 1892 vs 1893, and BOTH sides need caveats. Schadewald ch. 4 says the UZS was 'founded late in 1892' and that the founding meeting was 'apparently' held Wednesday 21 September 1892 at Williams's home. HIS OWN NOTE [4.2] SAYS: 'The date is inferred. It is known that UZS was founded in September, and its financial year began on September 21. The location is also inferred.' So 21 Sept 1892 is Schadewald's inference from Rule 7, not a minuted date. Our project doc `claude/source-genealogy.md` item 10 presents it as a documented founding meeting and should be corrected to say 'inferred by Schadewald'. Against it: English Wikipedia ('Modern flat Earth beliefs') states 'After Rowbotham's death, Lady Elizabeth Blount established the Universal Zetetic Society in 1893' and cites Patrick Moore, 'Better and Flatter Earths', in *Can You Speak Venusian?* (1972) — a popular-astronomy humour essay, not archival work. Blount's own Wikipedia article makes the same 1893 claim and carries {{Sfn|Garwood|2007|pp=146-147}}, i.e. the standard scholarly monograph may also say 1893; I DID NOT READ GARWOOD DIRECTLY and cannot confirm what she says. Independent primary support for 1892, from the periodical itself: (a) *Earth Review* no. 1, January 1893 already describes 'The Universal Zetetic Society' as existing and directs subscriptions to 'the Secretary, Mr. John Williams, 32, Bankside'; (b) printed Rule 7, 'The financial year to commence on September 21st'; (c) Williams's own Secretary's Statement in v.1 n.5 (Jan 1894) — 'When, twelve months ago, some of us came together to consider the advisability of continuing our united public testimony' — against accounts closed 26 November 1893. 21 September 1892 was in fact a Wednesday (checked), which makes Schadewald internally consistent but does not validate the inference.

FOUNDER IDENTITY — Williams vs Blount. Schadewald and the primary masthead put Williams as founding Secretary–Treasurer with Blount as one of seven Committee members; Wikipedia (and possibly Garwood) say Blount established the society. Our own `source-genealogy.md` row for Blount reads 'Universal Zetetic Society (founding meeting 21 Sept 1892 ...)' as though she convened it — that framing is not supported by the primary officer list and should be revised.

BLOUNT'S PRESIDENCY — start date. Wikipedia says she became president 'After Samuel Rowbotham's death in 1884', which is impossible if the society dates from 1892 and is contradicted by the January 1894 masthead listing her as an ordinary Committee member under Secretary Williams. Schadewald ch. 7 has her as president only by 1904, and the 1906 *Zetetic Astronomy* rear cover names her President with C. de Lacy Evans as vice president. Note also that the 1890s UZS had NO president or vice-president at all — the structure was Secretary–Treasurer, Editor, and Committee.

MOVEMENT-INTERNAL GENEALOGY vs THE RECORD — label this one carefully. The inside rear cover of Blount and Smith's *Zetetic Astronomy* (1906) claims the UZS was 'Founded in New York in Sept., 1873, and in London in Dec., 1883 ... as The Zetetic Society, by "Parallax," and others' and is 'now firmly established, by E.A.M.B., (Lady Blount)'. John Williams is not named. This is the movement's own account of itself, not documentation, and it is the likeliest root of the 'Blount founded it after Rowbotham died' story. It is not pure invention: Schadewald ch. 7 independently records a Zetetic Society formed in December 1883 with de Lacy Evans as its vice president. The defect is conflation of that 1883 body with the 1892 UZS.

'LEO CASTLE' — one man or two? Schadewald ch. 4 states that 'Leo Castle' and 'Excalibur' were pseudonyms used by John Williams after he took over as editor. The Review's own correspondence masthead reads 'All letters must be prepaid and addressed to Leo Castle, c/o Mr. J. Williams, 32, Bankside, London, S.E.' — which on its face reads as two distinct people. This matters for authorship: the serial 'Universal Gravitation, a Pure Assumption' is signed Leo Castle. Unresolved.

WILLIAMS'S ADDRESS — the TFES wiki quotes 'John Williams, 96 Arkwright Street, Nottingham' with no date, which appears to conflict with Southwark. It does not: the primary run shows 32 Bankside through c.1896 and the Nottingham address in later issues, with POs 'payable at Nottingham'. Sequential, not contradictory — but the wiki gives no date and would mislead anyone citing it. (The TFES wiki is a movement wiki, not scholarship.) The Review itself notes 'several letters have been delivered opened by other Mr Williams' living on Bankside', so the surname was locally common.

JAMES NAYLOR — 'of Birmingham' in the January 1894 committee list and in Schadewald, but 'Mr. James Naylor, of Leeds' elsewhere in the same periodical. Minor internal inconsistency in the primary source.
BLOUNT'S JOURNAL *Earth* — 'published between 1901 and 1904' (Wikipedia, citing Garwood 2007 pp. 155–159) vs 'she edited from at least January 1900 to November 1904' (Schadewald ch. 7).
BLOUNT'S FATHER'S NAME — 'James Zecharias Williams' (Schadewald ch. 7) vs 'James Zacharias Williams' (Wikipedia). Trivial, but see the conflation warning in `reasoning`.

INSTITUTIONAL BRIDGE TO SHENTON — weaker than 'institutional'. Wikipedia, citing Moore 1972, calls Shenton's 1956 IFERS 'a successor to the Universal Zetetic Society'. Schadewald ch. 9 calls Johnson's society a 'spiritual inheritor' of the UZS and identifies the concrete link to the past as William Mills's marriage relation to Frederick Henry Cook plus an inherited library — not corporate continuity. The *Earth Review* folded in April 1897 and the society was reconstituted around Blount. The Rowbotham→Shenton chain is textual and personal descent plus asserted succession; it is not a documented unbroken institution, and the page should not say it is.
