people.reasoning:
HOW I WORKED. I did not take the dating from any genealogy. I downloaded the archive.org OCR of the society's own periodical (*Earth not a Globe Review* 1893–1897, 1.49 MB of text), stripped it, and searched it directly for Williams, "Secretary", "Committee", "Adventist", "President", "1892", "founded", "Blount" and "Nottingham". Everything in the officer list, the Rules, the addresses and the August 1892 letter is read off that primary text, not off a summary. I then went back to Schadewald's own References page rather than his prose, which is where I found that his 21 September 1892 date is explicitly an inference.

WHY HE IS INSTITUTIONAL AND NOT AN ORIGINATOR. He is the administrative spine of the only Victorian flat-earth organisation that mattered — the money, the rules, the membership, the branch network, the book trade and eventually the editorship all pass through one Southwark address. But the originator test is about introducing an argument, and he fails it on every piece of writing I could attach to his name: the compass letter is Carpenter's proofs 10/11/13, the level-water piece is Rowbotham's and Carpenter's proof 2, and the £1,000 challenge is the Hampden–Wallace move plus Carpenter's dedication-and-dare. Schadewald credits him with an anti-meteorite article in issue no. 1; I could not find that article in the OCR run I searched and did not establish that the argument was new with him, so I have not scored it. He also contributes nothing to our 461-item corpus. INSTITUTIONAL, with CARRIER activity, is the honest call.

DOES BLOUNT BELONG ON THE PEOPLE TAB? Yes — but as a later leader and as the originator of the movement's photographic evidentiary turn, not as founder. The primary masthead settles her 1890s status: she is one of seven ordinary Committee members, listed under Secretary–Treasurer Williams, in the January 1894 issue. The 1890s society had no president at all. Her presidency belongs to the reconstituted society of c.1904–06. Two further things I would put on her card, both documented: her flat-earth debut was in an outside Seventh-day Adventist paper in 1892, before the UZS existed, so she did not come out of it; and Schadewald's chapter 7 records that her own photographer Edgar Clifton described the shimmering vapour over the canal — the refraction layer — in the very experiment her publicity used.

A TRAP I WANT TO FLAG EXPLICITLY. Lady Blount's maiden name was Williams and her father was James Zecharias/Zacharias Williams, an architect and land surveyor with an interest in astronomy. John Williams of 32 Bankside is a different man, and I found no source connecting them; the Review itself complains that other Mr Williamses lived on Bankside and opened his post. If anyone later drafts these two cards together, the surname will invite a family link that no source supports.

WHAT I COULD NOT SETTLE. (1) Williams's Adventism. Schadewald asserts it in a sentence carrying no citation. I could not corroborate it in the 1893–97 run: "Adventist" occurs three times there and none of them is about Williams, and the Review's editorial voice is doctrinally hostile to Seventh-day Adventists as "this American sect". That is not a refutation — Schadewald wrote "Adventist", not "Seventh-day Adventist", and nineteenth-century British Second Adventism is a wider category, and the editorial voice at that date was Albert Smith's, not Williams's. But the descriptor should be published as Schadewald's characterisation, not as established fact, especially since Williams's one surviving letter on the subject is addressed to an Adventist editor who was refusing to print him. (2) Garwood. The 1893 date and the Blount-as-founder claim may rest on the standard scholarly monograph (Garwood 2007), which I could not access; I am inferring its content from Wikipedia's footnote placement and say so rather than characterising a scholar's book I have not opened. That gap is the single thing most worth closing before this goes on the page.

people.name: Lillian J. Shenton
people.lineage_evidence: Zetetic BY INSTITUTIONAL AFFILIATION ONLY — and the distinction is load-bearing, so do not publish it unqualified. What is documented: (1) she was the wife of Samuel Shenton, founder of the International Flat Earth Research Society, and is placed by name inside the movement's own zetetic pedigree — Johnson's IFERS flyer reads "We have absorbed the Universal Zetetic Society ... Samuel Shenton, Lillian J. Shenton of England 1971" (talkorigins.org/faqs/flatearth.html, movement-internal self-genealogy, and the same passage claims "Our Society of Zetetics have existed for at least 6,000 years", which shows what that assertion is worth on its own); (2) the IFERS-of-America membership card prints "Hon. Pres. & Sec. Samuel Shenton, Lilian Shenton, Dover, Eng." (primary artefact, Schadewald's own card, reproduced in The Plane Truth ch. 9). What is NOT documented: any relationship between her and the zetetic literature. I located no text by her, no evidence she read or cited Rowbotham, Carpenter, Winship or Blount, and no statement of belief attributed to her in any source. Her lineage placement therefore rests on organisational office and on the movement naming her in its pedigree, NOT on the documented relationship to zetetic texts that this project's standard normally requires. If the People tab's lineage field is meant to assert textual descent, the honest value for her is "none"; "Zetetic" is correct only if the field admits institutional membership.
people.dates: Birth date and birthplace NOT LOCATED. Death: December 1974, per Charles K. Johnson, "When the Light went out in England", Flat Earth News, December 1978, p. 2 — "In December of 1974, the Last of the True Nobility of England ... passed out of the vale of sorrow ... I'm speaking of Mrs. Lillian J. Shenton." This is a single movement-internal source (Johnson, writing four years after the fact) and I found NO independent corroboration. The death date appears to be absent from the project's existing record, from Schadewald, and from the Wikipedia articles on Samuel Shenton and Charles K. Johnson. Marriage to Samuel Shenton (30 March 1903 – 2 March 1971, Dover) is documented; the marriage date was not located. Widowed 2 March 1971.
people.role: INSTITUTIONAL. Not an originator of any argument, and not a carrier of one either — no text, lecture, article, letter or argument authored by or attributed to her was located in any source searched, including the movement's own literature. Her documented functions are entirely organisational and relational: (a) named honorary secretary of Johnson's US body on its membership cards, alongside Samuel as honorary president, a listing still printed on a card paid up to 1977, i.e. after her death; (b) named in Johnson's IFERS flyer among the bodies and persons his society "absorbed"; (c) per Schadewald, she "tried to keep it going" after Samuel's death, which he calls "a brief false start"; (d) per Wikipedia citing Garwood 2007 p. 320, Johnson "inherited part of Shenton's library from Shenton's wife" — the sole basis for calling her the transferor; (e) per Wikipedia (sentence carries no inline footnote; article bibliography is Garwood 2007), she was "suspicious of [Ellis Hillman's] motives" when Samuel designated Hillman as successor, which is the only documented instance of her holding a position on the succession; (f) Johnson states he held "a bundle of letters from Lillian", establishing a Lillian-to-Johnson correspondence channel. Even Johnson, her warmest source, credits her with no doctrinal contribution: in his account she is Samuel's "Stalward right hand", and "Her Life was her Dear Husband."
people.summary: Lillian J. Shenton was the wife of Samuel Shenton, founder of the International Flat Earth Research Society, with whom she lived in Dover; her birth date was not located and Charles K. Johnson dates her death to December 1974. Schadewald records that after Samuel's death on 2 March 1971 she "tried to keep it going", which he describes as "a brief false start"; Wikipedia, citing Garwood 2007, is the only located source stating that Johnson "inherited part of Shenton's library from Shenton's wife". Johnson's American society printed her as honorary secretary beside Samuel as honorary president on its membership cards, a listing still in use on a card paid to 1977. No text, argument or publication authored by her was located in any source searched, including the movement's own newsletters and its founder's surviving correspondence.
conflicts: DATE OF THE HANDOVER, AND THEREFORE WHETHER AN INTERREGNUM EXISTED AT ALL. Schadewald: the mantle and library 'was passed on to Johnson in 1972'; the Irish Times, Independent and Guardian obituaries all give 1972. BUT Johnson himself dates it to 1971, twice and unambiguously: 'He departed for Heaven Above in 1971 ... I took the Mantle ... as he left, and wear it still' (Flat Earth News, Dec 1978) and 'till he passed up and I took the Mantle in 1971' (Flat Earth News, June 1979); his flyer likewise dates the absorption of the Shentons to '1971'. On Schadewald's dating the interregnum is roughly a year; on Johnson's own dating there was none. Report both.

WHETHER SHE RAN THE SOCIETY. Schadewald: 'there was a brief false start for the International Flat Earth Society as Shenton's widow, Lillian, tried to keep it going.' Johnson, by contrast, casts himself as leader from Samuel's death and her as a bystander to his succession: 'Lillian J. Shenton tarried for a while ... to see if the New Prophet ... could make the grade and to help' (Dec 1978). A third position: Patrick Moore, writing in England for 1972 publication and personally acquainted with Samuel, describes the society at that moment as having 'very few members, no organization, and no leader', and never mentions her.

WHOM SAMUEL DESIGNATED AS SUCCESSOR — this is what decides whether she is load-bearing. Wikipedia (bibliography Garwood 2007) and Schadewald both say Samuel picked Ellis Hillman, who then did little, leaving the succession to fall to Johnson via Lillian. All three 2001 British broadsheet obituaries say the opposite: 'Before his death ... Shenton decreed that Johnson should inherit his work' (Independent/Telegraph) and 'who specified before his death that Johnson should replace him at the society's head' (Guardian). If the obituaries are right, the edge runs Samuel-to-Johnson directly and Lillian is not on it. Weighting note, not a silent pick: the same obituaries date Samuel's death to 1972 (it was 2 March 1971) and the Guardian text has the Universal Zetetic Society 'founded in England in 1832 by Sir Birley Rowbotham' — both plainly wrong, so they are weak on detail.

WHETHER SHE TRANSFERRED THE BOOKS. Only Wikipedia, citing Garwood 2007 p. 320, makes her the transferor: Johnson 'inherited part of Shenton's library from Shenton's wife'. Schadewald uses the passive and names no transferor: 'The mantle of leadership along with a small but precious library of flat-earth books was passed on to Johnson in 1972.' Johnson's own accounts never mention receiving books from her — he mentions only letters ('I have a bundle of letters from Lillian'). So the single scholarly claim that makes her the pivot of this edge reaches us only as encyclopaedic relay, and I could not verify Garwood's own wording.

HER DEATH DATE. December 1974 per Johnson (Flat Earth News, Dec 1978). No other source located gives any death date for her at all — not Schadewald, not the Wikipedia articles on Samuel Shenton or Charles K. Johnson, not the Johnson obituaries. Uncorroborated and movement-internal; if published it must be labelled as Johnson's claim. It also creates a tension worth noting: Schadewald's membership card, paid up to 1977, still lists her as honorary secretary, so the title was posthumous decoration rather than an office she held.

SPELLING OF HER NAME. 'Lillian J. Shenton' in Johnson's newsletters (Dec 1978, June 1979) and in his IFERS flyer, and 'Lillian Shenton' in Wikipedia. But the IFERS-of-America membership card — the primary artefact — prints 'Lilian Shenton', with one medial L. Use 'Lillian J.' as the main form and footnote the card's variant rather than silently normalising a primary source.

sources.kind: scholarly (Schadewald, The Plane Truth, ch. 9; author knew Johnson personally)
sources.says: Fetched in full and keyword-swept. 'After Shenton's death, there was a brief false start for the International Flat Earth Society as Shenton's widow, Lillian, tried to keep it going. Shenton, himself, had picked Ellis Hillman to become president, but it wasn't meant to be.' Also: 'The mantle of leadership along with a small but precious library of flat-earth books was passed on to Johnson in 1972' — passive, no transferor named. Caption to the membership-card image: 'Samuel and Lillian Shenton are named as Honorary President and Secretary, though Samuel, at least, was no longer alive.' Gives no dates for Lillian and does not say she transferred anything.

sources.kind: PRIMARY ARTEFACT (Schadewald's own membership card, read directly, not via caption)
sources.says: Card reads: 'International Flat Earth Research Society of America / BOX 2533, LANCASTER, CA. 93534, U.S.A. / MISSION: To restore sanity to the world. / Hon. Pres. & Sec. Samuel Shenton, Lilian Shenton, Dover, Eng.' Signed at foot 'Marjory Johnson SECRETARY' and 'Charles Johnson PRESIDENT'; holder Robert J. Schadewald, 'Paid up member to 1977'. Three things this settles at artefact level: her honorific title is real and printed; the operating officers were the Johnsons, so her secretaryship was honorary, not functional; and the body issuing it is the American corporation, not the British society. Note the spelling 'Lilian'.

It is a tribute to Lillian and the source of her death date: 'In December of 1974, the Last of the True Nobility of England ... passed out of the vale of sorrow ... I'm speaking of Mrs. Lillian J. Shenton.' Also: 'From the passing of Mr. Shenton in 1971 to December of 1974, SHE stood ALONE in that Den of Serpants, England'; 'He departed for Heaven Above in 1971 ... I took the Mantle ... as he left, and wear it still. Lillian J. Shenton tarried for a while ... to see if the New Prophet ... could make the grade and to help. Her Life was her Dear Husband'; and 'I have a bundle of letters from Lillian, Mrs. Samuel Shenton, can't bear to look at them.' Establishes the correspondence channel, dates Johnson's own succession to 1971, and credits her with no doctrinal contribution.

sources.says: Johnson's lineage narrative, running Dowie to Voliva to Shenton to himself: 'Mr. Samuel Shenton, Fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society and Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society in England took the Mantle. Aided by his Stalward right hand Lillian J. Shenton, his Wife kept up the WITNESS TO THE NATIONS till he passed up and I took the Mantle in 1971.' Two uses: it is the strongest movement-internal claim that Lillian worked actively alongside Samuel during his lifetime, and it repeats the 1971 succession date. Separately it asserts F.R.A.S. and F.R.G.S. fellowships for Samuel Shenton — unverified, and adjacent to PER-SHENTON rather than to this record.

Shenton of England 1971.' Confirms the 'Lillian J.' form, names her in the pedigree, and dates the absorption to 1971. The same passage claims 'Our Society of Zetetics have existed for at least 6,000 years', which is the measure of how much this document's genealogical assertions are worth unsupported.

sources.kind: encyclopaedic (raw wikitext via Special:Export; article bibliography is Garwood 2007)
sources.says: Samuel Shenton 30 March 1903 – 2 March 1971, Dover. 'Samuel Shenton was a sign writer, who lived with his wife Lillian in a ginger-brick terrace in suburban Dover.' On the succession: Hillman 'agreed to be president of the IFERS, with the encouragement of Patrick Moore. Lillian Shenton was suspicious of his motives (he was developing a post-graduate course on the development of ideas about the shape of the earth) and in the event he did little for the society.' IMPORTANT: I checked the markup — that sentence carries NO inline footnote; the adjacent cited material is a Guardian piece of 2 Jan 1969 about membership numbers. The article never mentions Johnson, Lillian's death, or the fate of the library.

sources.kind: encyclopaedic relay of a scholarly source (cites Garwood 2007 p. 320)

Same passage: Hillman 'added most of Shenton's library to the archives of the Science Fiction Foundation he helped to establish', and Johnson 'incorporated and became president of the International Flat Earth Research Society of America and Covenant People's Church in California'. This is relay, not the book: I could not open Garwood to check the wording.

sources.kind: contemporaneous eyewitness (Patrick Moore, 'Better and Flatter Earths', Can You Speak Venusian?, 1972), hosted by the movement
sources.says: Downloaded and read in full. Moore knew Samuel Shenton, attended the society's meetings and reproduces its 1956 circular; he names Shenton 11 times and NEVER mentions a wife, Lillian, or any Mrs Shenton. Closing assessment, written for 1972 publication: the society 'has very few members, no organization, and no leader to match Lady Blount, Wilbur Glenn Voliva, or Samuel Shenton.' Handle precisely: 'no leader to match' is a comparative judgement, not a denial that anyone was administering the society. Still, the most contemporaneous English account of exactly this period does not record her stewardship.

sources.kind: PRIMARY (Samuel Shenton's outgoing correspondence, 3 volumes plus the 1963 Shenton-to-Hillman letter, scanned by Daniel Shenton; no text layer, so I rasterised and OCRed all 63 pages)
sources.says: Searched for Lillian, Lilian, wife, Mrs Shenton, secretary. She appears ONCE, as 'My wife and I are shocked' in a condolence letter of 9 April 1969. No letter in these volumes is signed by her, and none gives her a society office. The same letter shows Samuel's declining health and his own view of the succession problem: 'I'm always hoping that someone younger may take over.' Scoped negative: her institutional role is not evidenced in the founder's own surviving outgoing correspondence as digitised here.

sources.kind: press obituary (Tim Bullamore, The Independent, 30 March 2001)
sources.says: 'During that time he was in contact with an Englishman, Samuel Shenton ... Before his death in 1972, Shenton decreed that Johnson should inherit his work.' No mention of Lillian, of a widow, or of any intermediary. Contradicts the Hillman-designation account. Reliability caution: it dates Samuel Shenton's death to 1972 (he died 2 March 1971). SEPARATE RECORD PROBLEM: the TFES library's file labelled as the Daily Telegraph obituary of 6 April 2001 serves this identical Bullamore text — do not cite the two as independent corroboration.

sources.kind: press obituary (Christopher Reed, The Guardian, 8 May 2001)
sources.says: 'He took over in 1972 from the late Samuel Shenton of Dover' and 'He began corresponding with Shenton, who specified before his death that Johnson should replace him at the society's head.' Again no Lillian and no interregnum. Reliability caution: the same text has the Universal Zetetic Society 'founded in England in 1832 by Sir Birley Rowbotham', conflating Samuel Birley Rowbotham with a knighthood he never held and misdating the society by six decades.

sources.kind: in-volume full-text search of Garwood 2007 (Macmillan ebook edition) — INSTRUMENT, NOT A READING
sources.says: Attempt to reach Garwood's own wording rather than Wikipedia's relay. FAILED, and the failure should be recorded rather than the numbers: the endpoint is unstable, returning 20 hits, then 0, then a blank for the identical query 'Shenton' on consecutive tries, so no count from it is evidence. The one result stable across repeats was 'Lillian' returning 6 and 'Lilian' returning 0, weakly indicating that Garwood spells it 'Lillian'; I could retrieve no snippet text before being rate-limited. Archive.org search-inside for flatearthhistory0000garw is closed (item restricted) and HathiTrust is behind a Cloudflare challenge.

people.reasoning:
WHAT I DID. Read README.md and the project's source-genealogy doc first, then the repo's own prior work — review/edge-evidence-report.json edge E05 already flagged Lillian as a needed node and is the origin of the brief I was given. I treated that as a hypothesis to test, not a finding to dress up, and went to primary material: Schadewald ch. 9 raw, Wikipedia raw wikitext, the talk.origins reproduction of Johnson's flyer, Patrick Moore's 1972 chapter, and — new to this project as far as I can tell — the TFES library's scans of 18 issues of Johnson's Flat Earth News (1977-1981, 74 pages) and 3 volumes of Samuel Shenton's outgoing correspondence (63 pages). None of those scans has a text layer; I rasterised and OCRed all 137 pages, then read the two decisive pages off the images rather than trusting OCR.

WHAT IS NEW. (1) A death date: Johnson's Flat Earth News of December 1978 carries a tribute headlined "When the Light went out in England" that puts her death in December 1974. I have not seen this in our files or in any encyclopaedic source. It is Johnson's word alone, four years after the fact, and must be published as his claim, not as fact. (2) The membership card read at artefact level rather than through Schadewald's caption, which both confirms the honorary secretaryship and shows that the operating officers were Charles and Marjory Johnson — so her title was honorific, and the card carrying it was still being issued in 1977, after she was dead. (3) Johnson's own succession date, stated twice in his own paper: he took the mantle in 1971, "as he left".

THE ORIGINATOR QUESTION IS NOT CLOSE. I searched for anything authored by her and found nothing: no pamphlet, no article, no lecture, no signed letter, not a single sentence of doctrine attributed to her in Schadewald, in Wikipedia, in Garwood's relayed account, or in the movement's own newsletters and flyer. Johnson, who is fulsome about her, credits her with being Samuel's "Stalward right hand" and says "Her Life was her Dear Husband" — a tribute that itself contains no doctrinal claim on her behalf. She is INSTITUTIONAL, and she is not even a carrier, because carrying requires transmitting an argument and no argument passes through her hands in any source I found. What passes through her hands, on one source, is books.

WHERE THE BRIEF OVERSTATES, AND THIS MATTERS. I was told she "ran the society in the interregnum after March 1971 and handled the transfer to Johnson", and that the edge is "load-bearing" on her. The sources do not converge on that. "Ran the society" rests on one clause in Schadewald, which actually says she "tried to keep it going" and calls the episode "a brief false start" — trying and failing is not running. "Handled the transfer" rests on a single sentence in Wikipedia citing Garwood 2007 p. 320, which I could not verify against the book; Schadewald names no transferor at all, and Johnson never says he got books from her. Meanwhile three London broadsheet obituaries say Samuel designated Johnson directly, which if true removes her from the edge entirely, and Johnson's own paper dates his succession to 1971, which if true removes the interregnum. Patrick Moore, in England, writing for 1972 publication, says the society then had no leader and never mentions her. My recommendation is that the People tab keep her — she is real, documented, and the card and flyer prove the movement itself put her in its line of descent — but that the edge annotation be softened from "the edge is Shenton-to-Johnson only through her" to something like "on Garwood's account, relayed by Wikipedia, the books reached Johnson from Shenton's widow; Schadewald names no transferor and Johnson's own accounts mention only letters." I am reporting the disagreement rather than picking, per house rule, and I note that this is a case where our own prior pass's phrasing was firmer than its sources — the same failure mode the README documents for C02 and ARG-E13.

ON LINEAGE. I assigned Zetetic but the evidence is organisational, not textual, and I have said so explicitly in the lineage_evidence field rather than letting the label imply more. She held an honorary office in a zetetic body and the movement names her in its pedigree; there is no documented relationship between her and the zetetic literature. Given the Eliade precedent I would rather flag this than let a bare "Zetetic" stand on a page where that word means descent from Rowbotham's texts.

SCOPE OF EVERY ABSENCE ASSERTED ABOVE. Not located in: Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch. 9 (full text, swept for Lillian/widow/mantle/Hillman/library/1972/fire); Wikipedia raw wikitext for Samuel Shenton; the talk.origins FAQ reproduction of Johnson's IFERS flyer; Patrick Moore's "Better and Flatter Earths" as reproduced by TFES (full text, 11 Shenton mentions checked individually); the TFES library's 18 issues of Flat Earth News / Flat Earth Society Newsletter, July 1977 to December 1981, all 74 pages OCRed and grepped for Lillian/Shenton/honorary/secretary; the three volumes of Samuel Shenton outgoing correspondence plus the 1963 Shenton-to-Hillman letter, all 63 pages OCRed; the Independent, Telegraph and Guardian obituaries of Johnson as hosted by TFES; and the Schadewald membership-card image. Specifically NOT located in those: any writing by her; any independent record of her December 1974 death; her birth date, maiden name or birthplace; any statement of her own beliefs; any source other than Garwood-via-Wikipedia describing her as the transferor of the library.

WHAT I COULD NOT DO. Garwood 2007 itself — the one scholarly work that carries the load here — remains unread by this project. Archive.org search-inside for flatearthhistory0000garw is closed on a restricted item, HathiTrust returns a Cloudflare challenge, the Google Books in-volume search is demonstrably unstable (same query returning 20, then 0, then nothing), and the Google Books JSON API is disabled at quota 0. Google web search is robots-disallowed to the fetcher and DuckDuckGo served a bot challenge. My WebSearch allowance was exhausted (200/200) partway through, so the last stretch was direct fetches only; I did not attempt genealogical databases for her birth or death, and I would counsel care there anyway, since "Lillian Shenton" is not distinctive enough to identify safely without a corroborating detail. No Flat Earth News issue from the 1971-1976 interregnum is in the TFES holdings, which begin July 1977 — that gap is precisely the period at issue, and finding a 1972-74 issue is the single highest-value next step for this edge. Getting eyes on Garwood pp. ~315-321 is the second.

people.name: Robert J. Bennett
people.lineage_evidence: On evidence in his own authored text, not resemblance. Inside the chapter the book credits to him, Bennett sets out "Aberration models" under the headings "Neo-Tychonic view" and "The Tychonic view", writes that the Tychonic view "Posits that parallax, following Van der Kamp, is really stellar aberration", and rejects it on a phase-difference objection — i.e. he engages the Tychonian literature by name and takes Bouw's modified-Tychonic side against van der Kamp (GWW Vol. II 7th ed., Ch. 10, archive.org djvu text, lines ~11423–24990 of the scan; the whole book's Special Appreciation thanks "Gerardus Bouw and Martin Selbrede for providing their expertise and consultations", and its bibliography carries van der Kamp, De Labore Solis: Airy's Failure Reconsidered). Independent non-movement corroboration of the lane: Danny Faulkner (Answers in Genesis, 4 Sept 2020) frames the modern geocentric movement as van der Kamp → Bouw → Sungenis and names Bennett as co-author of Galileo Was Wrong. He is a spherical-Earth geocentrist, never a zetetic: his own viXra paper titles ("Reference Frames: If Inertial, then Geocentric", 2019) and his ALFA model argue a motionless Earth/laboratory frame, not a flat plane. Note that his co-author Sungenis published Flat Earth, Flat Wrong (2018) against the flat-earth position; I located no flat-earth advocacy by Bennett in the searches I ran.
people.role: CARRIER (with one origination that does not touch this list, plus an INSTITUTIONAL role). He introduced no argument in the 461-item specimen. What he did author is the *formulation that travelled*: the compressed "Summary" paragraph on Airy's water telescope, which sits in the chapter the book itself credits to him, and which reappears near-verbatim in Dubay (200 Proofs #16 / The Atlantean Conspiracy) and in the Flat Earth Society wiki. The underlying argument is van der Kamp's ("Airy's failure", De Labore Solis 1988) and is expounded in Sungenis's own Chapter 5 with van der Kamp cited by name; Bennett condensed it. He did originate the ALFA model (Absolute Lab Frame / Flexible Aether) — but scoped search of scripts/corpus.py (all 461 items) for "alfa", "absolute lab", "flexible aether", "dufour", "prunier", "ruyong", "hafele" returns zero hits, so nothing in this specimen descends from his one original construct. INSTITUTIONAL: per David Palm (geocentrismdebunked.org) he served as supervising professor/evaluator for Sungenis's Calamus International University dissertation, which became the first edition of Galileo Was Wrong, and the book lists him as "consultant for the entire ... project".
people.dates: Born 24 July 1940 per the Natural Philosophy Wiki profile — a self-submitted dissident-physics member wiki, not corroborated elsewhere in the searches I ran; treat as unverified. Physics instructor, Manhattan College and Bergen Community College, 1967–1983 (stated in the book's own About the Authors in both the 2006 and 2013 editions). Active in geocentrism from at least the 2006 first edition of Galileo Was Wrong through a viXra posting of 23 April 2025; no death notice located in the searches I ran.
works: Galileo Was Wrong: The Church Was Right — co-author with Robert A. Sungenis. CD first edition, ISBN 0-9779640-0-0, PDF metadata CreationDate 14 June 2006; Bennett authored Chapter 12 per that edition's About the Authors. In the 7th edition (2013, Vol. II) the same chapter is renumbered Chapter 10.
Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II (7th ed. 2013), Chapter 11, 'The ALFA Model: Absolute Lab Frame & Flexible Aether' — carries his byline and email in the body text.
Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II (7th ed. 2013), Appendix 3, 'Einstein's train derailed; the light clock smashed' — bylined 'By Dr. Robert Bennett'.
ALFA Challenge blog (alfachallenge.blogspot.com), posts 'Posted by Robert B' from December 2010, incl. the Airy water-telescope post of 19 Dec 2010.

viXra preprints, 13 items 2014–2025 (non-peer-reviewed archive), incl. 'A Landmark Experiment: The Linear Sagnac Test of Ruyong Wang' (2014), 'Reference Frames: If Inertial, then Geocentric' (2019), 'Sagnac(1913) Completed by Dufour & Prunier(1942)' (2020), 'Einstein Train Challenge' (2025).

Doctoral thesis, 'Relativistic Rigid Body Motion', Stevens Institute of Technology — cited only in the book's own author blurb and downstream copies of it; I did not locate an independent library/ProQuest record.
people.summary: Robert J. Bennett is the co-author of record of Galileo Was Wrong and, by the book's own statement, the author of its one technical chapter — Chapter 12 in the 2006 CD first edition, renumbered Chapter 10 in the 2013 seventh edition — which holds the Sagnac, Michelson-Gale, Hafele-Keating, GPS and parallax-versus-aberration material that this project currently files under PER-SUNGENIS. The compressed Airy paragraph that reaches Dubay's 200 Proofs #16 is in that chapter, verbatim, in the June 2006 edition; so are the two hedges the project's own hedge rule leans on (the Michelson-Gale "either the effect of the Earth's rotation or the ether's rotation around the Earth" disjunction, and the admission that the derivation is "obtained without explicitly invoking an ether, Lorentz transformations or General Relativity"). He introduced none of the arguments: the Airy case is van der Kamp's, expounded with van der Kamp cited by name in Sungenis's Chapter 5, and Bennett's own chapter credits A. G. Kelly for the stationary-lab Sagnac result and the Hafele-Keating critique. His one original construct, the ALFA model, appears nowhere in the 461-item specimen.

Chapter 10 opens with the byline 'Dr. Robert Bennett'. Chapter 10 cites A. G.
