conflicts: Chapter number — RESOLVED as an edition artefact, report it rather than picking: the 2006 CD first edition credits Bennett with CHAPTER 12 ('In Chapter 12, Robert has written a detailed, technical and mathematical explanation'); the 2013 seventh edition credits him with CHAPTER 10. I confirmed the text is the same chapter, renumbered. The edge agent's 'ch. 12' and my 'Ch. 10' are both correct for their respective editions. Any published wording must name the edition.

The book contradicts itself about how much Bennett wrote. About the Authors (2013) says Sungenis 'authored all the chapters and appendices ... except for Chapter 10', but in the same volume Chapter 11 ('The ALFA Model') carries 'Dr. Robert Bennett / e-mail: robert.bennett@rcn.com' as its byline and Appendix 3 is headed 'By Dr. Robert Bennett'. Bennett's authored share is therefore at least Ch. 10 + Ch. 11 + App. 3, not Ch. 10 alone.

Publication year, unchanged from the existing project note: the CD first edition's PDF metadata is dated 14 June 2006 and carries ISBN 0-9779640-0-0; Answers in Genesis (Faulkner 2020) says 2007; the NPA wiki says Vol. I 2007. Existing house rule (2006, footnote 2007) survives this pass.

Proximate route to Dubay is NOT settled. Two candidates, and I am not choosing. (a) Direct from Galileo Was Wrong: the wording is in the June-2006 edition under Bennett's chapter credit, six years before Dubay's earliest datable version. (b) Via Malcolm Bowden: the Flat Earth Society wiki and (per the edge report) Dubay's own IFERS forum credit a Bowden video for this material, and Bowden's video description carries the same sentences in a slightly altered form ('Airey', 'If it was the telescope moving he would have had to change the angle') — and Dubay's trailing sentence in The Atlantean Conspiracy matches BOWDEN's form, not GWW's. I could not date Bowden's original video: the only copy I could reach is a 2020 third-party Vimeo re-upload, the YouTube original (87M2i61N1cU) returned no usable metadata, archive.org CDX rate-limited me, and I did not locate this wording in Bowden's True Science Agrees with the Bible (1998), whose text I could not reach. So the direction Bennett→Bowden is likely on dates but NOT established; Bowden→Bennett is not excluded by anything I found.

Mark J. Wyatt remains an unresolved possible intermediary (edge report): Dubay names Wyatt's 'Is Geocentricism Possible?' in the same passage, and the 2006 edition's copyright page credits illustrations to Wyatt 'used by permission', so Wyatt sits inside the GWW project. I did not locate Wyatt's article.

ALFA's first presentation: NPA wiki says 2011; Todd Wood's first-hand attendance report puts an ALFA talk at the November 2010 conference and Bennett's own ALFA Challenge blog is posting from December 2010. Prefer 2010 on the eyewitness plus the dated blog, but report both.

Plagiarism allegation vs. what the chapter actually shows. Palm (2014) alleges Bennett paraphrased Ashby and Kelly without attribution at specific pages of the 9th edition. In the 7th-edition scan I searched, Chapter 10 credits 'A.G. Kelly' by name in the two places I inspected (Sagnac stationary-lab; Hafele-Keating) and returns zero occurrences of 'Ashby'. So attribution is present in some places and alleged absent at particular pages I could not check (I did not have the 9th edition). I located no response by Bennett to the plagiarism charge in the searches I ran, though he did post a substantive reply on the same site on a different point.
Bennett's dates rest on one self-submitted profile (NPA wiki, 24 July 1940). Not corroborated in any source I reached. Do not publish a birth date as fact.

NAME COLLISION — flag before any automated enrichment: there is a different, unrelated Dr Robert Bennett in physics at the University of Glasgow with a ResearchGate profile. Nothing about him belongs in this dataset.
people.reasoning:
VERDICT: yes, he deserves his own record — as a CARRIER, not an originator — and folding him into PER-SUNGENIS is now demonstrably wrong on the project's own primary source. Recommend PER-BENNETT with role CARRIER, lineage Tychonian, bio_status stub, and an explicit note that his single origination (ALFA) is absent from the specimen.

WHY HE NEEDS A RECORD. The book itself, in both the 2006 and 2013 editions, says the technical chapter is Bennett's and everything else is Sungenis's. That chapter is exactly the material this project attributes to 'Sungenis & Bennett': I verified by downloading both scans whole and searching locally that the Michelson-Gale disjunction and the 'without explicitly invoking an ether, Lorentz transformations or General Relativity' admission — the two sentences the README's hedge rule and claude/source-genealogy.md lean on — sit inside Bennett's chapter, in both editions (7th ed. Ch. 10 lines 13113 and 13164 of the scan; 2006 ed. Ch. 12, lines 38660 and 38615 of my extraction). The project's most-used concession about 'the source being more careful than its lists' is a statement about Bennett's prose specifically.

WHY HE IS NOT AN ORIGINATOR, TESTED THE WAY THE RULE REQUIRES. I asked what he INTRODUCED and the answer is: nothing in this list. (a) The Airy argument predates him and is not even his within his own book — Sungenis's Chapter 5 of the 2006 edition argues it at length citing van der Kamp 16+ times, and van der Kamp's De Labore Solis: Airy's Failure Reconsidered is in the bibliography; the phrase is van der Kamp's coinage per the existing genealogy. (b) The Sagnac stationary-lab result his chapter uses is credited in his own text to A. G. Kelly ('Kelly showed that the same result is found using the stationary laboratory'), and a critical source alleges further unattributed borrowing from Ashby and Kelly. (c) He DID originate the ALFA model — but a scoped search of scripts/corpus.py (all 461 items) for 'alfa', 'absolute lab', 'flexible aether', 'dufour', 'prunier', 'ruyong', 'hafele' returned zero hits, so his one original construct reaches this specimen not at all. What he authored is the COMPRESSION: the 100-word summary paragraph that is short enough to travel, and that is what Dubay's #16 reproduces. Authoring the formulation that travelled is a carrier fact, an important and specific one, but it is not introducing an argument — that distinction is the whole point of the rule.

CONCRETE RECORD CHANGES THIS IMPLIES. (1) ARG-A03's originator line should separate three roles that are currently collapsed: van der Kamp coined and argued it (1988); Sungenis expounds it citing van der Kamp (GWW Ch. 5, 2006); Bennett wrote the summary paragraph that actually reached the flat-earth lists (GWW Ch. 12/Ch. 10). (2) Every cluster carrying the byline 'Robert Sungenis & Robert Bennett' for Sagnac, Michelson-Gale, Hafele-Keating, GPS or parallax-vs-aberration material is pointing at Bennett's chapter and should say so. (3) The hedge-rule citations in claude/source-genealogy.md should name the chapter and its author, since our tone rule depends on whose hedge it is.

SCOPE OF THE NEGATIVES. Not located in: the archive.org OCR of GWW Vol. II 7th ed. (291,140 words, downloaded whole and grepped locally); the archive.org CD first-edition PDF (458,973 words, converted with pdftotext and grepped locally); scripts/corpus.py (461 items); the web searches listed in sources, run 2026-08-10. Specifically NOT located: any independent library or ProQuest record of the Stevens Institute thesis; any obituary or death notice; any flat-earth advocacy by Bennett; any Bennett response to the plagiarism allegation; any dating of Malcolm Bowden's original Airy video; the wording of the disputed passage in Bowden's 1998 book, whose text I could not reach. Volume I of the 2006 two-volume PRINT set and the 9th edition were not reachable this pass, so nothing here is a statement about what those printings hold. No print copies were consulted.

people.name: Carl (Karl) Schöpffer
people.dates: Born 13 March 1811, Göttingen. Died 1876 — year only in the German national authority file (GND 113667779); the kookscience wiki alone gives "December 1876, age 64", which is internally inconsistent with a March 1811 birth (that would be 65). Either way the death precedes both English translations: Blavatsky's (27 April 1878) and de Peyster's (New York, 1900) are posthumous, as is the Earth Review reprint (that periodical began January 1893). He therefore had no agency in any of the transmission this project cares about.
people.lineage_evidence: No lineage is assignable on evidence, and two candidate assignments both fail the project's test. (1) ZETETIC: rejected. The only documented contact is that Blount's Earth Review reprinted his lecture (Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch. 4) — at least 17 years after his death, in a periodical that did not exist in his lifetime, and Schadewald frames the reprint as the UZS taking material that was "not strictly flat-earth; sometimes geocentricity or Newton-bashing was close enough." That is the zetetic movement ingesting him, not a relationship he had with zetetic literature. I found no mention of Rowbotham, Carpenter, zetetic or flat Earth anywhere in the primary texts I read (his 1878 translated lecture; the full OCR of the 1900 English edition). His own text is expressly round-Earth: it reasons "from the spherical form of the earth", accepts polar flattening as measured, and the 1900 edition's epigraph is Psalm 93:2 "He hath made the ROUND WORLD so sure". (2) TYCHONIAN: rejected as resemblance. The dataset's "Tychonian" denotes van der Kamp's 1971 society and its descendants; I found no documented link from Schöpffer to van der Kamp, Bouw, Sungenis or the Association for Biblical Astronomy, and I could not run archive.org full-text search (endpoints returned HTTP 000) to test it further. Note the primary sources themselves disagree about which pre-modern system he belongs to — see conflicts. Best description without inventing a line: an unaffiliated German anti-Copernican of the 1850s–60s whose text was posthumously adopted, in Britain by the zetetic lineage's own periodical and in America by geocentrists.
people.role: AUTHOR of the source text; not an originator of anything in the 461-item specimen. On the Victorian route he is the author and Blavatsky is the translator/submitter, so a diagram that omits him silently attributes a Berlin schoolmaster's geocentrism to her. But by the strict rule he is not an originator FOR THIS DATASET either: no item among the 461 is traced to him, and the two clusters his lecture overlaps are credited elsewhere — ARG-A06 (Foucault pendulum) to Sungenis & Bennett 2006, ARG-A13 (no felt centrifugal force; equatorial bulge has another cause) to Rowbotham 1865. His versions are earlier in print than A06's recorded originator by 150 years and roughly contemporaneous with A13's, and his A13-parallel is close (he concedes the measured bulge, denies rotation causes it, and proposes tropical heat expansion plus polar cold contraction instead) — but I found no documented transmission from him to either cluster, so these are leads for the untraced-items pass, not attributions. The carriers around him are Blavatsky (translation, 1878), Blount's Earth Review (reprint, date unknown), and in America Brig.-Gen. J. Watts de Peyster and Frank Allaben (translation, notes and supplement, New York 1900).
works: Die Bewegungen der Himmelskörper: neue und unwiderlegliche Beweise, daß unsere Erde im Mittelpunkte des Weltalls steht, und Sonne, Mond und Sterne sich um dieselbe bewegen — Braunschweig: Oehme & Müller, 1854, 52 pp., ill. (K10plus)

Der Schein der Wahrheit: 20 neue Beweise, dass das copernicanische System eine Lüge und die Erde der ruhende Mittelpunkt des Weltalls ist — Braunschweig: Oehme & Müller, 1855, II+58 pp. (K10plus). NOTE FOR THE README'S CARPENTER CAVEAT: the title advertises an enumerated count of proofs 30 years before Carpenter 1885. The K10plus record carries no digitisation link and I could not open the book, so whether the 20 proofs are set out as a numbered list is UNVERIFIED, and it is geocentric, not flat-earth.

Die Erde steht fest: Beweise, dass die Erde sich weder um ihre Achse, noch um die Sonne dreht — Vorlesung, gehalten in Berlin. THIS IS THE LECTURE THAT TRAVELLED. K10plus holds a 4th and a 6th edition, Berlin 1868, 32 pp.; the 1900 New York edition states it was translated from the 7th edition, Berlin: A. Saco Nachf., Zimmerstrasse 94, 1868. Wikis date a first edition to 1853; rebuttal pamphlets of 1854–55 prove it circulated by then.

Uranos: populäre Vorlesungen über Sternkunde — Leipzig: Henning; K10plus holds the 2. Aufl., 1857, 188 pp. (digitised at SLUB Dresden, id336211465); wikis give 1856, which is consistent with that being the first edition.

Die Widersprüche in der Astronomie, wie sie bei der Annahme des Copernikanischen Systems entstehen, bei der entgegengesetzten aber verschwinden — Berlin: Beck, 1869, XVI+144 pp., with a preface by A. Frantz (K10plus).

Die Bibel lügt nicht! Erklärung der mosaischen Schöpfungs-Urkunde (1854); Lehrbuch der Physik für das weibliche Geschlecht (1854); Handwörterbuch der Fortschritte der gesammten Technologie (1865); Gartenlaube polemics (1873) — non-astronomical output, listed to show he was a jobbing popular author, per K10plus and GND (occupations: journalist, writer, pedagogue; the lecture itself refers to 'my pupils … in my geographical and physical lessons').

TRANSLATIONS OF THE LECTURE (carriers, not his works): (a) Russian — Zemlja nepodvižna, trans. P. Solov'ev, St Petersburg: Golike, 1876, 2nd corrected ed., 20 pp. (K10plus); (b) English — 'Definite Conclusions of Science—Our Earth Motionless', trans. Madame Blavatsky, F.T.S., Scientific American Supplement no. 121, 27 April 1878, pp. 1925–27; (c) English — The Earth Stands Fast, trans./ed. J. Watts de Peyster, notes and supplement by Frank Allaben, New York: Charles H. Ludwig, printer, 1900; (d) reprint in Blount's Earth Review, issue and date not located.
people.summary: Carl (Karl) Schöpffer (1811–1876) was a Berlin popular author, journalist and schoolteacher who published a run of anti-Copernican pamphlets in the 1850s and 1860s, the best-known being the lecture Die Erde steht fest, which reached at least a seventh edition by 1868 and drew printed refutations from Capaun-Karlowa (1854) and Fleischhauer (1855). That lecture, not any writing of Blavatsky's, is the text Blavatsky translated as "Definite Conclusions of Science—Our Earth Motionless" for Scientific American Supplement no. 121 of 27 April 1878, and which Lady Blount's Earth Review later reprinted; a separate American translation appeared as The Earth Stands Fast (New York, 1900), edited by J. Watts de Peyster with a supplement by Frank Allaben. The argument is a stationary-Earth case built on an attempted refutation of Foucault's pendulum and on an alternative cause for the equatorial bulge, and it is expressly a round-Earth argument — it reasons from the Earth's spherical form and accepts the measured polar flattening. He died in 1876, so every transmission of his text into the English-language movement is posthumous.
conflicts: SPELLING OF THE NAME — four forms, all documented, none obviously wrong. The German national authority file (GND 113667779) prefers 'Schöpfer, Karl'; the German book imprints catalogued in K10plus read 'Carl Schöpffer' (double f); Scientific American printed 'Dr. SCHŒPFER' on the article and 'Shcepfer' [sic] in its author index; the 1900 New York title page reads 'Professor C. SCHOEPFFER'. Schadewald writes 'Dr. Schoepfer'. Do not silently normalise — pick a house form and record the variants.

WHICH PRE-MODERN SYSTEM HE BELONGS TO. Schadewald (Plane Truth ch. 4) calls him 'a follower of Ptolemy'. Frank Allaben, in the 1900 edition, says he 'maintained the truth of the Tychonian theory, founded on the supposition that the earth stands still in space, that the sun revolves around the earth, and that the planets … revolve about the sun'. Those are different systems. I read only parts of the lecture (the surviving clipping and sampled passages of the 1900 translation) and did not settle it from his own text; the passages I did read defend the rotation of the celestial sphere, which fits Schadewald. Report both.

DATE OF THE LECTURE PAMPHLET. Wikis (de.wikipedia, kookscience) give 1853 for Die Erde stehet/steht fest. K10plus holds only Berlin 1868 printings, explicitly '6. Aufl.' and 'Aufl. 4'; the 1900 New York edition cites a 7th edition, Berlin 1868. The 1853 first-edition date is not confirmed by any catalogue record I retrieved, but an 1854 open-letter rebuttal (Capaun-Karlowa) and an 1855 chapter-length 'Kritik der Dr. Schöpffer'schen Theorie' (Fleischhauer) put the work in circulation by 1854 at the latest.

DEATH DATE. GND gives '1876' with no month; de.wikipedia gives 1876; the kookscience wiki gives 'December 1876, age 64', which does not reconcile with the 13 March 1811 birth all three agree on. Use '1876'; do not publish a month.

URANOS DATE. K10plus: Leipzig, Henning, 1857, marked '2. Aufl.' Wikis: 1856. These are probably the second and first editions rather than a contradiction, but I did not locate a catalogue record for an 1856 printing.

WHICH LANGUAGE BLAVATSKY TRANSLATED FROM — unresolved, and it changes who the intermediate carrier is. Her English title and subtitle track the Russian edition (St Petersburg 1876: 'Zemlja nepodvižna' = 'the Earth is motionless'; 'Populjarnaja lekcija, dokazyvajuščaja, čto zemnoj šar ne vraščaetsja ni okolo osi, ni okolo solnca' = 'a popular lecture proving that the terrestrial globe rotates neither about its axis nor about the sun') far more closely than the German ('Die Erde steht fest' = 'the Earth stands fast'; 'Beweise, dass …' = 'proofs that …'; no 'popular'). Blavatsky was Russian. That is suggestive, NOT documented: I have no statement from her or from Scientific American about the source text, and the correspondence could be coincidence. Flag it as a hypothesis if it is used at all.

sources.kind: primary (scanned clipping; user upload, from what appears to be Blavatsky scrapbook vol. 7 p. 117)
sources.says: The article itself. Masthead reads 'SCIENTIFIC AMERICAN SUPPLEMENT No. 121 / NEW YORK, APRIL 27, 1878'; headnote '[Translated by MADAME BLAVATSKY, F.T.S.] DEFINITE CONCLUSIONS OF SCIENCE.—OUR EARTH MOTIONLESS. A popular lecture proving that our globe neither rotates upon its axis nor around the sun.—Delivered at Berlin by Dr. SCHŒPFER.' I read the page image directly. Content: an attempted refutation of Foucault's pendulum ('I conclude that the deviation of the pendulum is not caused by the axial motion of the earth, but due to some other reason as yet unknown'); a rejection of rotation as the cause of the equatorial bulge, with tropical heat expansion and polar cold contraction offered instead; a defence of the rotating celestial sphere against the 'stars would move impossibly fast' objection. Round-Earth throughout ('the globe is flattened toward the poles').

sources.kind: primary — the publisher's own author index
sources.says: Independently confirms the item: one article under Madame Blavatsky, 'Definite Conclusions of Science—Our Earth Motionless', 27 April 1878, bylined 'Madame Blavatsky, Shcepfer', described as 'A popular lecture proving that our globe neither rotates upon its axis n., around the sun.—Delivered at Berlin'.

sources.kind: library union catalogue (K10plus SRU) — bibliographic authority, not scholarship
sources.says: 37 records. Establishes his geocentric bibliography with imprints: Die Bewegungen der Himmelskörper (Braunschweig: Oehme & Müller, 1854, 52 pp.); Der Schein der Wahrheit: 20 neue Beweise… (same publisher, 1855, II+58 pp.); Die Erde steht fest … Vorlesung, gehalten in Berlin (Berlin 1868, '6. Aufl.' and 'Aufl. 4', 32 pp.); Uranos (Leipzig: Henning, 1857, 2. Aufl., digitised at SLUB Dresden); Die Widersprüche in der Astronomie (Berlin: Beck, 1869, XVI+144 pp., preface by A. Frantz). Also the contemporary German rebuttals — Capaun-Karlowa, Die Erde steht nicht fest! Offener Brief an den Herrn C. Schöpffer (Wesel: Bagel, 1854); J. Sieberger, Und dennoch bewegt sich die Erde! (1854); J. H. Fleischhauer, 'Kritik der Dr. Schöpffer'schen Theorie: Die Erde steht fest…' (Langensalza, 1855) — and the Russian translation Zemlja nepodvižna, trans. P. Solov'ev (St Petersburg: Golike, 1876, 2nd corrected ed., 20 pp.).

sources.kind: national authority file (GND, via lobid)
sources.says: 'Schöpfer, Karl', GND 113667779, born 1811-03-13, died 1876 (year only). Occupations: Journalist, Schriftsteller, Pädagoge. Variant names include Schoepffer/Schöpffer/Schoepfer Carl/Karl and a long list of pseudonyms (Abenstein, Alvenstod, Scoper, Herold, Sheets, …). No biographical note. Note: the catalogue records for the astronomy titles carry '$4 aut' without a GND link, so the person-to-works identification rests on name form, place and period, not on a linked identifier.

sources.kind: primary (full OCR of a 1900 book)
sources.says: 'The Earth Stands Fast. A Lecture by Professor C. SCHOEPFFER. Translated for and Edited by J. WATTS de PEYSTER. With Notes and a Supplement by FRANK ALLABEN. NEW YORK: Charles H. Ludwig, Printer, 90 Walker Street. 1900.' Internal headnote: '[A Translation from the German of a Lecture delivered in Berlin, by Dr. C. Schoepffer. Seventh edition. Berlin: A. Saco, Successors, Publishers, Zimmerstrasse, No. 94. 1868.] Compared with the Original and Edited by J. W. de P.' The opening of this translation runs parallel to Blavatsky's ('It requires not a little courage to stand before you here…'; 'my pupils, boys and girls, in my geographical and physical lessons'), which is how I confirmed that the 1878 Scientific American piece and Die Erde steht fest are the same lecture. Allaben's framing letter calls it 'the Tychonian theory'. SCOPED NEGATIVE: the OCR contains no occurrence of Blavatsky, Scientific American, Earth Review, Rowbotham, zetetic or 'flat'.

sources.kind: secondary history (Schadewald, The Plane Truth — this project's standard history; a posthumously web-published typescript, not peer-reviewed)
sources.says: 'Thus, Earth Review reprinted a lecture "Our Earth Motionless," originally delivered in Berlin by a follower of Ptolemy, one Dr. Schoepfer. (It had previously been reprinted in Scientific American, in a translation submitted by Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, founder of Theosophy.)' — in a passage whose point is that Earth Review reprints were 'not strictly flat-earth; sometimes geocentricity or Newton-bashing was close enough'. No issue or date is given for the Earth Review reprint. I downloaded all 13 chapters and 4 appendices and grepped them: this is the only Schoepffer mention.

sources.kind: secondary history (same source)
sources.says: POSSIBLE SECOND ROUTE, worth a follow-up. Of the American flat-earther M. C. Morse (Unpopular Truth, 1913): 'He cited geocentrists John Watts de Peyster, Frank Allaban, and J. R. L. Lange.' Those are precisely the translator and annotator of the 1900 Schoepffer volume, alongside Winship, Rowbotham, Carpenter, Gleason and Blount in Morse's reading list. Schadewald names no title, and the only geocentric publication of theirs I located is the Schoepffer translation, so the inference is strong but unproven; Morse's book is not on archive.org under that title and I could not check it.

sources.kind: encyclopaedic wiki — not scholarship
sources.says: Georg Karl Ludwig Schöpfer (* 13 March 1811 Göttingen; † 1876), German writer, journalist and private scholar, who in the 1850s and 1860s published several works rejecting the Copernican world-picture. Lists 17 confirmed pseudonyms of 'at least thirty-one'. Dates the astronomy titles 1853 / 1856 / 1869. Cites A. G. Schmidt, Gallerie deutscher pseudonymer Schriftsteller (1840) and the Lexikon der Horrorliteratur (1999).

sources.kind: fringe-topics wiki — not scholarship; used only to pin the citation the other sources corroborate
sources.says: Gives the Scientific American Supplement citation as no. 121, pp. 1925–1927, 27 April 1878, 'translated by Madame Blavatsky of Theosophical Society fame'. Also asserts a death in 'December 1876, age 64' — the only source I found with a month, and it does not reconcile with the March 1811 birth.

people.reasoning: METHOD. I did not take the edge agent's evidence on trust; I re-derived the chain from primary and catalogue sources, then went looking for what it had not checked. Confirmed independently: the Scientific American item exists exactly as described (publisher's own author index, plus a scan of the printed page which I read directly); Schadewald's sentence about the Earth Review reprint is real and is the only Schoepffer mention across the whole of The Plane Truth (all 13 chapters and 4 appendices downloaded and grepped). NEW BEYOND THE EDGE REPORT. (1) The German original is identifiable: Die Erde steht fest … Vorlesung, gehalten in Berlin — the 1878 English subtitle is a near-verbatim rendering of the German subtitle, and the 1900 New York translation of that same pamphlet opens in parallel with the 1878 one, which is textual confirmation rather than title-matching alone. (2) Schöpffer died in 1876 (GND), so every transmission into English is posthumous, and he cannot be described as participating in anything. (3) A second, American carrier exists that this project did not have: The Earth Stands Fast, New York 1900, translated by Brig.-Gen. J. Watts de Peyster with notes and a supplement by Frank Allaben — and Schadewald ch. 8 records that the flat-earther M. C. Morse cited 'geocentrists John Watts de Peyster, Frank Allaban' in Unpopular Truth (1913). If that citation is to this volume, the movement absorbed Schöpffer twice by two independent routes, British and American. Not proven; Morse's book was not obtainable. (4) A Russian translation (St Petersburg 1876) exists whose title matches Blavatsky's English better than the German does — a hypothesis about her source text, explicitly not documented. (5) Der Schein der Wahrheit (1855) advertises '20 neue Beweise' in its title, which bears directly on the README's caveat that Carpenter 1885 is the earliest numbered proof-list IDENTIFIED rather than provably the first. It is geocentric, not flat-earth, in German, and I could not open it to see whether the proofs are enumerated — so it does not overturn the caveat; it is the kind of thing the caveat exists for. ORIGINATOR RULE APPLIED STRICTLY. He is the author of the text that travelled, which is the whole point of adding him — otherwise the diagram credits a Berlin schoolmaster's geocentrism to his translator. But he originated nothing IN THIS DATASET. His lecture overlaps ARG-A06 (Foucault) and ARG-A13 (bulge has another cause), which the dataset credits to Sungenis & Bennett 2006 and Rowbotham 1865 respectively; he is earlier in print than the former and roughly contemporaneous with the latter, and I found no documented transmission in either direction. Those are leads for the untraced pass, not attributions, and I would not publish them as anything else. SCOPE OF THE NEGATIVES. 'Not located' here means: not in the K10plus union catalogue (SRU queries by title and by author), not in the GND via lobid, not in archive.org's metadata search, not in the full text of the 1900 English edition, not in any of Schadewald's 17 files, and not in the repo's own dataset (which I scanned for foucault|pendul|centrifug|oblate|bulge). Specifically NOT located: the Earth Review issue and date of the reprint (Schadewald gives none, and I found no digitised run of the periodical); the 1853 first edition of the pamphlet; the text of Der Schein der Wahrheit; Morse's Unpopular Truth; any link from Schöpffer to van der Kamp, Bouw or Sungenis. The session's WebSearch budget was exhausted at the outset and archive.org's full-text-search endpoints returned HTTP 000, so a full-text sweep of twentieth-century geocentric literature for his name was NOT performed — that is the main gap, and it is the one that would decide the Tychonian question. I edited nothing and ran no tests.

people_conflicts.conflict: DATE OF CHRISTOPHER'S MAP — four sources, three answers, report all. (a) The map itself: 'Entered at Stationers' Hall, August 1885. All rights reserved.' — read off the artefact. (b) Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch.4: 'Published as early as 1880' — he attaches no reference to that sentence, though he references the adjacent facts. (c) Boston Rare Maps: 'some time in the 1880s'. (d) The archive.org uploader (a flat-earth account) titles it 1885. An earlier state may exist; the 1885 imprint dates only the copy I examined. Related: the Earth Review testimonial says the late Lady Brassey wrote thanking Christopher for a copy — she died 14 September 1887, which bounds circulation before that date and is consistent with either 1880 or 1885.

THE ROWBOTHAM CLAIM — the load-bearing one, and it is uncited. Boston Rare Maps writes 'At some time in life Christopher got hooked on Samuel Birley Rowbotham's "zetetic astronomy"' with no footnote; their reference list is Ancestry.com, Schadewald ch.4, a Flat Earth Society forum thread and three 1844–50 newspapers. Schadewald — their own cited source — does NOT say Christopher adopted Rowbotham's system; he says the map 'is still the zetetic standard' and prints the Earth Review obituary. I located no document in which Christopher names Rowbotham. Chronology cuts both ways: Rowbotham died 23 December 1884, eight months before the Stationers' Hall entry, so if the map is 1885 there was no living Rowbotham to be adopted from; if Schadewald's 1880 is right, there was.

'MODERN' vs 'MORDEN' — resolved in favour of error, but note who says what. Gleason's 1892 map prints 'MODERN COLLEGE' (verified on the Leventhal/Boston Public Library copy at 3000px via IIIF). Christopher's own 1885 map prints 'Morden College Blackheath' (verified on the LoC copy). Morden College, Blackheath, founded by Sir John Morden, exists from 1695 (AIM25 archival authority record). Library catalogues (Leventhal, Digital Commonwealth, DPLA, UWM) transcribe Gleason's spelling faithfully because that is what the object says — they are not endorsing it. Incidental: booksellers list T. Frank Green's monograph on the almshouse as 'Modern College, Blackheath', so the slip is a recurring one, not unique to Gleason.

RESIDENCE FROM 1875 — Boston Rare Maps dates his residence at Morden College from 1875, sourced to an Ancestry.com timeline (a genealogy database, not scholarship); I could not check it. Independently confirmed: he died there on 31 December 1894 (Earth Review obituary; Schadewald cites the same). The 1885 map's own imprint already gives 'Morden College Blackheath' as his address.

BANKRUPTCY AND EAST INDIA CHAMBERS — Boston Rare Maps' 1844 bankruptcy and East India Chambers details rest on The Exeter Flying Post (4 Apr 1844), The Morning Post (22 Oct 1845) and The Morning Chronicle (8 Mar 1850), which I did not see; a London Gazette API query for 'Steer Christopher' 1840–60 returned nothing, which given that interface's indexing is not evidence of absence. His own 1850 book gives a different address, 18a Basinghall Street, and a firm trading in Natal — not a contradiction, but it is the only primary I verified.

THE FELLOWSHIP — the Earth Review obituary says he was made a 'Fellow of the Society of Science, Art and Literature' on account of his map. The London body of roughly that description is usually styled the Society of Science, Letters and Art. I did not verify which body, or the fellowship itself, and have not silently corrected the movement's wording.

THE UZS MAP FUND — Schadewald ties the Universal Zetetic Society's £15 lithographic-block fund to a plan to republish Christopher's map. The fund appeal I located in the Earth Review scan ('those who are desirous of having a good Map of the World as a Plane... the purchase of a block... about £15') does not name Christopher. The connection may rest on Earth Review text outside the 1893–97 scan; treat it as Schadewald's, not as something I confirmed.
NAME — flatearthprints.com gives his middle name as 'Streep'. Every primary I saw (the map, the 1850 book, the obituary) reads 'Steer'.

OCCUPATION — THREE-WAY, AND THE PROJECT'S OWN BEST SOURCE IS ON THE 'CIVIL ENGINEER' SIDE. Schadewald (Plane Truth ch. 5), which this project already relies on elsewhere, calls him "civil engineer Alexander Gleason, of Buffalo, New York"; Kook Science says "machinist and civil engineer" and is probably downstream of Schadewald. Against that, Boston Rare Maps worked the primary record: "Secondary sources on the internet describe him as a civil engineer, but in the Directory he is listed variously as a solicitor (1882-1883), machinist (1889), engraver (1893) and patternmaker (1898)... never as a civil engineer." A third line, Find a Grave, gives "a Die Sinker, Stencil maker, Carriage painter" who struck Civil War tokens in Hillsdale County, Michigan. Two further scraps cut the same way: on the 1892 map the trade credit is the Buffalo Electrotype and Engraving Co., an engraving house; and in his own Lake Erie narrative Gleason HIRES a civil engineer (A. E. Arnold of the Nickel Plate Railroad) and his instruments rather than using his own. My read of the weight of evidence is skilled metal/engraving trades, not a civil engineer — but Schadewald says otherwise and I am reporting both. Note also that Goudey called him "Prof. Alex. Gleason", a movement honorific with no located institutional basis. NOT LOCATED: the Buffalo City Directory entries themselves; I am relying on the dealer's reading of them.

THE 1885 MAP — DEALER SAYS GLEASON, THE ARTEFACT DOES NOT. Boston Rare Maps: "His initial effort was The New Map of the World on the Projection of J. Steer Christopher, Morden College, Blackheath...Without Any Antipodes. Published in 1885, this map closely resembles the 1892 map offered here, though it lacks the indicator arms" — and elsewhere refers to "the two maps", so this is a real attribution to Gleason, not loose phrasing. But I read the map. The digitised Library of Congress deposit copy carries NO Gleason and NO Buffalo anywhere: "THE NEW MAP OF THE WORLD. ON THE PROJECTION OF J. STEER CHRISTOPHER. Morden College Blackheath, Lithographed by J. R. King... WITHOUT ANY ANTIPODES", "Entered at Stationers' Hall, August 1885. All rights reserved", the printed line "To be obtained of the Author as above" struck through in ink, and "JOHN HAMPDEN, BALHAM, S.W." rubber-stamped at head and foot. LoC copyright stamp MAY 3 1887; Map Division MAY 7 1903. On its face this is an English publication of Christopher's, later distributed by Hampden. So: Gleason republished Christopher ONCE that is documented on the object — in 1892 — not twice. An 1885 Gleason issue may exist and simply not be the copy digitised, but I did not locate any catalogue record for one in the loc.gov search API, Open Library, or web search. SCOPE OF MY EVIDENCE: the 1885 scan I examined is a user upload to archive.org by an apparent flat-earth account claiming LoC provenance; the LoC copyright and Map Division stamps visible in the image corroborate that it is a LoC sheet, but I could not find the LoC catalogue record itself.

BOOK DATE — 1893 vs 1890. Library of Congress / Open Library / most dealers and auction listings date the book 1893 and catalogue it as "2d ed. Rev. and enl." Schadewald ch. 5 and the Leventhal Map Center exhibition both say the first edition was 1890. The book settles it in its own front matter: title page "SECOND EDITION ... REVISED AND ENLARGED", copyright page "CopyRIGHT, 1890. By ALEX. GLEASON. RE-COPYRIGHTED AND RE-WRITTEN, REVISED AND ENLARGED, 1893." Anything citing 'Gleason 1893' as the work's date is citing the second edition. No 1890 copy located in the searches named above.

"MODERN COLLEGE" vs "MORDEN COLLEGE". Christopher's 1885 map reads "Morden College Blackheath" — Morden College is the real 17th-century almshouse in Blackheath. Gleason's 1892 map prints "MODERN COLLEGE, BLACKHEATH, ENGLAND", and every library catalogue (BPL/Leventhal, Yale, Digital Commonwealth, DPLA) faithfully reproduces the error because it is on the sheet. Boston Rare Maps silently corrects it to Morden. This is not a trivial spelling point: it is direct textual evidence of the direction of copying, and it means the two spellings identify two different objects.

SEVENTH-DAY ADVENTIST AFFILIATION — the newspaper claim and the doctrinal evidence are different things and should not be merged. Boston Rare Maps: "According to contemporary Buffalo-area newspapers in 1889 he helped establish a Seventh-Day Adventist Church there"; Schadewald calls him "The most important Seventh-day Adventist flat-earther"; Kook Science lists the affiliation flatly. I could NOT read those Buffalo newspapers (Chronicling America and NYS Historic Newspapers API calls both failed from this environment; Kook Science is unreachable to WebFetch behind a robots/TLS error). What I CAN evidence, from the primary text: the 1893 edition teaches the seventh-day Sabbath (a chapter head reads "Seventh Day vs. the First"), the 2300-day prophecy terminating in 1844, the cleansing of the heavenly sanctuary, and the investigative judgment — and cites "Synopsis of Present Truth, by U. Smith, Battle Creek, Mich.", noting "Prof. U. Smith has given us permission". That is Uriah Smith, the denomination's leading author, at its headquarters. The doctrinal commitment is beyond doubt from the book itself; formal membership and the 1889 church-founding remain on newspaper testimony I have not seen. Separately, Schadewald quotes Carpenter reporting a Seventh Day Adventist minister EXCOMMUNICATED in London for flat-earth teaching — so the denomination did not own the position, and the page should not imply it did.

GLEASON vs THE ZETETIC MAINSTREAM ON THE SUN. He puts the sun at 1,725 miles; he records that "Some of the Zetetic faith had given the sun's altitude 2500, some 3500, and some even less". Schadewald reports Goudey adopting 2,700 nautical miles instead and attributes Gleason's lower figure to his acceptance of Hampden's 57.5-degree pole-to-equator claim. I did not locate "Hampden" in the OCR of the 1893 edition (0 hits), so that causal explanation is Schadewald's and is not confirmed in Gleason's own words.

WHO REPAID WHAT — the project's own genealogy doc is wrong on the figure. claude/source-genealogy.md says the movement cites "the court voiding the wager and Wallace repaying the £1,000." The primary law report (Hampden v Walsh, 1 QBD 189, judgment 17 Jan 1876, Cockburn CJ with Mellor and Quain JJ) shows the action was brought against WALSH THE STAKEHOLDER, not Wallace, and was for recovery of Hampden's OWN £500 deposit, not £1,000. Headnote: "plaintiff having demanded his deposit back before it had been paid over by defendant, he was entitled to judgment." Wallace's own account reconciles the two but confirms the amount: he had signed an indemnity to Walsh, "so I had to pay back the money, and also pay all the costs of the action, about £200 more," then settled at costs plus £120, "amounting to £277," with £410 left nominally owing to him by Hampden. Wikipedia compresses this to "required that Wallace return the money to Hampden" (party wrong, amount unstated); the movement's own wiki says Hampden "sued Wallace" (party wrong). Recommend the page say: judgment against the stakeholder for Hampden's £500 deposit, borne by Wallace under an indemnity. Do not print £1,000.

GROUNDS OF THE RULING — all sources agree it was legal, not scientific, but they differ on which rule. Schadewald frames it as the Gaming Act 1845 having "made all wagers null and void." The judgment is narrower and the distinction matters: the court HELD the agreement was a wager and void, but held that s.18 did not bar recovery of a sum still in the stakeholder's hands where the depositor repudiated before payment over. The wager being void is not what won Hampden his money; his revocation before payment is.

BIRTH YEAR — Schadewald, citing Boase's Modern English Biography, writes "born in 1819 or 1820" and leaves it open. A dealer listing (Argosy Book Store, seen in search-result metadata only; the page itself returned HTTP 429 and was not read) and the movement's own tfes.org wiki both print a flat "1819–1891". Prefer Schadewald's hedge; the flat form has no visible source.

WHAT HAMPDEN WAS BEFORE 1869 — Schadewald: the thirty years after he entered Oxford "are lost to history," with only marriage and at least two children established. Bob Forrest states that at the time Parallax began lecturing "Hampden was busy studying Britain's coastal defences, with a view to improving them," giving no source. Unresolved; do not repeat Forrest's detail as fact.

MOVEMENT SELF-DESCRIPTION vs RECORD — tfes.org (The Flat Earth Wiki, movement-internal, and a wiki) opens: "John Hampden (1819-1891) was an English scientist of the Royal Academy." No credential of any kind is attested in Schadewald/Boase, in the 1875 newspaper interview, or in Wallace; Schadewald has him matriculating at St Mary Hall in 1839 and apparently leaving without a degree, and describes him as a gentleman of comfortable means. This is evidence of what the movement says about itself, not documentation. The same page states the court "deemed the bet to be invalid and Hampden's money was returned to him in full," which is closer to the law report than Wikipedia is.

IMPRISONMENTS — the counts differ by what is being counted, and the page should not print a bare number. Wallace's own chronology (My Life vol. 2): Old Bailey conviction on Walsh's prosecution 1871, bound over one year; a civil libel verdict of £600 to Wallace in 1871 (elsewhere £687 with costs), uncollectible because Hampden had assigned his assets to his solicitor son-in-law and declared bankruptcy; October 1872 and 13 January 1873 prosecutions respited on published apologies (the second, a full recantation, is quoted verbatim); then two months in Newgate; then Chelmsford Assizes 6 March 1875, one year plus two years' recognizances, released after about six months. Schadewald adds a week in gaol in July 1871 for want of sureties after Hampden wrote to Annie Wallace. Forrest says "no less than three jail sentences." Wikipedia gives "12 months' imprisonment … and keep the peace for two years," which is the 1875 sentence only.

THE CARPENTER PURCHASE IS SINGLE-SOURCED AND INTERESTED. The £100 for stock plus copyright of Theoretical Astronomy Examined and Exposed rests entirely on Schadewald's ref. 2.3: "Carpenter gives the amount in the introduction to The Delusion of the Day." That is Carpenter — a party to the transaction and the man whose stock was bought — reporting it himself. I could not locate a digitised text of The Delusion of the Day in the searches run (WebSearch on the title plus Hampden/copyright; Wikipedia's Carpenter article does not mention Hampden at all). Publish the £100 as "Carpenter's own account, relayed by Schadewald," not as an established figure. Also note the work bought has itself an unstable imprint: Wikipedia lists both an 1866 (London: Job Caudwell) and an 1869 printing.

PAGINATION OF WALLACE'S ACCOUNT — the LoC guide cites My Life v.2, pp. 381–393 for the Hampden chapter; the Internet Archive copy I read (myliferecordofev02walluoft) carries the same passage at printed pp. 372–375 in ch. XXXIX, "Hampden and the Flat Earth." Different printings. Cite the chapter, not a page, unless the specific copy is named.

DATE OF THE EXPERIMENT — Schadewald's chapter opens "On March 5, 1870" but his own narrative has the party assembling from 28 February, markers set 1 March, the first inconclusive observations 2 March and the decisive run on Saturday 5 March. Walsh's award is dated 18 March 1870 and was published in The Field on 26 March 1870. The repo's B03 currently pins nothing here, but if the page ever dates "the 1870 experiment" it should say 1–5 March 1870, award 18 March.

BEARS ON AN OPEN REPO ITEM (B03 / Manea Fen). The project state doc records Schadewald as saying 1839 for Rowbotham's first canal trials. Schadewald ch.3 in fact writes that Rowbotham's April 1870 party "reported the canal still as flat as it was when Rowbotham lived there in 1838" — i.e. Schadewald prints 1838 here, matching the repo's B03 rather than the state doc's summary of him. Someone should read ch.1 before treating "Schadewald says 1839" as settled.

BEARS ON THE PAGE'S JOHNSON ATTRIBUTION. The genealogy doc credits Charles K. Johnson with THE CONSPIRACY FRAME on the formula "Rowbotham and Carpenter said astronomers were wrong; Johnson said they were lying." Hampden, in 1870, said they were lying: his pamphlet opens on "the notorious rascality of the scientific world," and Schadewald explicitly marks this as the point where Hampden "broke new ground" against Rowbotham's and Carpenter's circumspection. The two claims are not flatly contradictory — Hampden's target was named individuals in a specific dispute, Johnson's was an institutional cover-up of a faked space programme — but the Johnson line as currently worded is too strong and should be narrowed, or it will be broken by anyone who reads chapter 2. I am NOT proposing Hampden as originator of anything; the fix is to the Johnson wording.

END DATE OF THE PERIODICAL — three-way, unresolved. (a) Schadewald ch. 4: "After a long struggle under three editors, it folded with the April 1897 issue." (b) The Internet Archive scan of the bound run (item titled 1893-1897) contains an "IN MEMORIAM" noticing the death of James Heywood on 17 October 1897 and of Henry George on 29 October 1897, alongside a reference to "The Universal Zetetic Society" — text that cannot have appeared in an April 1897 issue. The masthead of that page did not survive the OCR, so I could not identify its issue number or date. (c) Wikipedia's Universal Zetetic Society article says the magazine "remained active well into the early 20th century." I report all three and pick none.

WHO RAN THE PERIODICAL — the project's own source-genealogy doc currently reads "Lady Elizabeth Blount … Earth Review from Jan 1893" under her originator row, and Wikipedia credits Blount with founding the society and its publications. The primary mastheads and Schadewald both make Albert Smith the editor from No. 1 and Blount a contributor who debuted in issue 2 and later funded the society. This looks like a live error in our own doc and should be corrected there rather than silently reconciled here.

THE THIRD EDITOR — Schadewald says the Review ran "under three editors". I identified two by name: Smith ("Zetetes", Nos. 1–8) and John Williams ("Leo Castle"; Schadewald says "Excalibur" was also Williams). The identity of a third editor was not located in Schadewald ch. 4 or ch. 7, in the recovered OCR of the scan (which ends its recoverable mastheads at September–December 1896), or in the LoC guide.

BLAVATSKY'S EXACT ROLE — Schadewald says the Scientific American printing was "in a translation submitted by Helena Petrovna Blavatsky"; the Kook Science wiki says it was "translated by Madame Blavatsky"; Scientific American's own archive metadata bylines the item "By Madame Blavatsky & Shcepfer", which is a byline, not a statement of who did the translating. Submitted-versus-translated is not settled by any of these, and the piece is not located in Blavatsky's Collected Writings vol. I as searched. Do not publish "Blavatsky translated it" as settled.

WHICH TEXT THE EARTH REVIEW USED — Schadewald's parenthesis notes only that the lecture "had previously been reprinted in Scientific American" in Blavatsky's translation; it does not say the Review used that translation. The Review's own credit lines ("From the 'Scientific American,' April 27th, 1878") and a correspondent's note thanking a reader for sending copies of Scientific American — "You will see that we are making good use of the former" — make it strongly likely the Review reprinted the Scientific American English text verbatim, but I did not collate the two texts word-for-word, and the Review never names Blavatsky. State the chain as sourced, not as collated.

DATE OF THE WINSHIP CORRESPONDENCE ITEM — the reply "T. Winship. — Thanks for The Cape Magazine…" appears twice in the scan at page 96, once inside the July 1895 issue block and once inside the October 1895 block. The bound volume's page order is disturbed and the OCR duplicates pages, so I can place it in 1895 but not in a specific issue. A separate, cleanly placed item — "Thos. Winship. — Thanks for your letter and cuttings from Cape Argus. Hope you have received letter and pamphlets, forwarded." — sits in New Series No. 1, September 1894.

VOLUME NUMBERING OF THE MONTHLY SERIES — the scan shows "Vol. I. No. 1 (Monthly Series). APRIL, 1896" followed by "Vol. III. No 2 (Monthly Series). MAY, 1896". Whether the jump is a masthead error by the publisher or OCR damage was not determined; do not publish a volume number for this series.

NAME COLLISION, flagged so it is not reintroduced — "Albert Smith" is also the name of a well-known Victorian writer and Mont Blanc showman (Albert Richard Smith, 1816–1860), who has a Wikipedia article and no connection to any of this. Our man is Albert Smith of Blackburn and then Leicester, pseudonym "Zetetes", whose birth and death dates I could not establish in any source searched.

FOUNDING DATE — 1892 vs 1893, and BOTH sides need caveats. Schadewald ch. 4 says the UZS was 'founded late in 1892' and that the founding meeting was 'apparently' held Wednesday 21 September 1892 at Williams's home. HIS OWN NOTE [4.2] SAYS: 'The date is inferred. It is known that UZS was founded in September, and its financial year began on September 21. The location is also inferred.' So 21 Sept 1892 is Schadewald's inference from Rule 7, not a minuted date. Our project doc `claude/source-genealogy.md` item 10 presents it as a documented founding meeting and should be corrected to say 'inferred by Schadewald'. Against it: English Wikipedia ('Modern flat Earth beliefs') states 'After Rowbotham's death, Lady Elizabeth Blount established the Universal Zetetic Society in 1893' and cites Patrick Moore, 'Better and Flatter Earths', in *Can You Speak Venusian?* (1972) — a popular-astronomy humour essay, not archival work. Blount's own Wikipedia article makes the same 1893 claim and carries {{Sfn|Garwood|2007|pp=146-147}}, i.e. the standard scholarly monograph may also say 1893; I DID NOT READ GARWOOD DIRECTLY and cannot confirm what she says. Independent primary support for 1892, from the periodical itself: (a) *Earth Review* no. 1, January 1893 already describes 'The Universal Zetetic Society' as existing and directs subscriptions to 'the Secretary, Mr. John Williams, 32, Bankside'; (b) printed Rule 7, 'The financial year to commence on September 21st'; (c) Williams's own Secretary's Statement in v.1 n.5 (Jan 1894) — 'When, twelve months ago, some of us came together to consider the advisability of continuing our united public testimony' — against accounts closed 26 November 1893. 21 September 1892 was in fact a Wednesday (checked), which makes Schadewald internally consistent but does not validate the inference.

FOUNDER IDENTITY — Williams vs Blount. Schadewald and the primary masthead put Williams as founding Secretary–Treasurer with Blount as one of seven Committee members; Wikipedia (and possibly Garwood) say Blount established the society. Our own `source-genealogy.md` row for Blount reads 'Universal Zetetic Society (founding meeting 21 Sept 1892 ...)' as though she convened it — that framing is not supported by the primary officer list and should be revised.

BLOUNT'S PRESIDENCY — start date. Wikipedia says she became president 'After Samuel Rowbotham's death in 1884', which is impossible if the society dates from 1892 and is contradicted by the January 1894 masthead listing her as an ordinary Committee member under Secretary Williams. Schadewald ch. 7 has her as president only by 1904, and the 1906 *Zetetic Astronomy* rear cover names her President with C. de Lacy Evans as vice president. Note also that the 1890s UZS had NO president or vice-president at all — the structure was Secretary–Treasurer, Editor, and Committee.

MOVEMENT-INTERNAL GENEALOGY vs THE RECORD — label this one carefully. The inside rear cover of Blount and Smith's *Zetetic Astronomy* (1906) claims the UZS was 'Founded in New York in Sept., 1873, and in London in Dec., 1883 ... as The Zetetic Society, by "Parallax," and others' and is 'now firmly established, by E.A.M.B., (Lady Blount)'. John Williams is not named. This is the movement's own account of itself, not documentation, and it is the likeliest root of the 'Blount founded it after Rowbotham died' story. It is not pure invention: Schadewald ch. 7 independently records a Zetetic Society formed in December 1883 with de Lacy Evans as its vice president. The defect is conflation of that 1883 body with the 1892 UZS.

'LEO CASTLE' — one man or two? Schadewald ch. 4 states that 'Leo Castle' and 'Excalibur' were pseudonyms used by John Williams after he took over as editor. The Review's own correspondence masthead reads 'All letters must be prepaid and addressed to Leo Castle, c/o Mr. J. Williams, 32, Bankside, London, S.E.' — which on its face reads as two distinct people. This matters for authorship: the serial 'Universal Gravitation, a Pure Assumption' is signed Leo Castle. Unresolved.

WILLIAMS'S ADDRESS — the TFES wiki quotes 'John Williams, 96 Arkwright Street, Nottingham' with no date, which appears to conflict with Southwark. It does not: the primary run shows 32 Bankside through c.1896 and the Nottingham address in later issues, with POs 'payable at Nottingham'. Sequential, not contradictory — but the wiki gives no date and would mislead anyone citing it. (The TFES wiki is a movement wiki, not scholarship.) The Review itself notes 'several letters have been delivered opened by other Mr Williams' living on Bankside', so the surname was locally common.

JAMES NAYLOR — 'of Birmingham' in the January 1894 committee list and in Schadewald, but 'Mr. James Naylor, of Leeds' elsewhere in the same periodical. Minor internal inconsistency in the primary source.
BLOUNT'S JOURNAL *Earth* — 'published between 1901 and 1904' (Wikipedia, citing Garwood 2007 pp. 155–159) vs 'she edited from at least January 1900 to November 1904' (Schadewald ch. 7).
BLOUNT'S FATHER'S NAME — 'James Zecharias Williams' (Schadewald ch. 7) vs 'James Zacharias Williams' (Wikipedia). Trivial, but see the conflation warning in `reasoning`.

INSTITUTIONAL BRIDGE TO SHENTON — weaker than 'institutional'. Wikipedia, citing Moore 1972, calls Shenton's 1956 IFERS 'a successor to the Universal Zetetic Society'. Schadewald ch. 9 calls Johnson's society a 'spiritual inheritor' of the UZS and identifies the concrete link to the past as William Mills's marriage relation to Frederick Henry Cook plus an inherited library — not corporate continuity. The *Earth Review* folded in April 1897 and the society was reconstituted around Blount. The Rowbotham→Shenton chain is textual and personal descent plus asserted succession; it is not a documented unbroken institution, and the page should not say it is.

DATE OF THE HANDOVER, AND THEREFORE WHETHER AN INTERREGNUM EXISTED AT ALL. Schadewald: the mantle and library 'was passed on to Johnson in 1972'; the Irish Times, Independent and Guardian obituaries all give 1972. BUT Johnson himself dates it to 1971, twice and unambiguously: 'He departed for Heaven Above in 1971 ... I took the Mantle ... as he left, and wear it still' (Flat Earth News, Dec 1978) and 'till he passed up and I took the Mantle in 1971' (Flat Earth News, June 1979); his flyer likewise dates the absorption of the Shentons to '1971'. On Schadewald's dating the interregnum is roughly a year; on Johnson's own dating there was none. Report both.

WHETHER SHE RAN THE SOCIETY. Schadewald: 'there was a brief false start for the International Flat Earth Society as Shenton's widow, Lillian, tried to keep it going.' Johnson, by contrast, casts himself as leader from Samuel's death and her as a bystander to his succession: 'Lillian J. Shenton tarried for a while ... to see if the New Prophet ... could make the grade and to help' (Dec 1978). A third position: Patrick Moore, writing in England for 1972 publication and personally acquainted with Samuel, describes the society at that moment as having 'very few members, no organization, and no leader', and never mentions her.

WHOM SAMUEL DESIGNATED AS SUCCESSOR — this is what decides whether she is load-bearing. Wikipedia (bibliography Garwood 2007) and Schadewald both say Samuel picked Ellis Hillman, who then did little, leaving the succession to fall to Johnson via Lillian. All three 2001 British broadsheet obituaries say the opposite: 'Before his death ... Shenton decreed that Johnson should inherit his work' (Independent/Telegraph) and 'who specified before his death that Johnson should replace him at the society's head' (Guardian). If the obituaries are right, the edge runs Samuel-to-Johnson directly and Lillian is not on it. Weighting note, not a silent pick: the same obituaries date Samuel's death to 1972 (it was 2 March 1971) and the Guardian text has the Universal Zetetic Society 'founded in England in 1832 by Sir Birley Rowbotham' — both plainly wrong, so they are weak on detail.

WHETHER SHE TRANSFERRED THE BOOKS. Only Wikipedia, citing Garwood 2007 p. 320, makes her the transferor: Johnson 'inherited part of Shenton's library from Shenton's wife'. Schadewald uses the passive and names no transferor: 'The mantle of leadership along with a small but precious library of flat-earth books was passed on to Johnson in 1972.' Johnson's own accounts never mention receiving books from her — he mentions only letters ('I have a bundle of letters from Lillian'). So the single scholarly claim that makes her the pivot of this edge reaches us only as encyclopaedic relay, and I could not verify Garwood's own wording.

HER DEATH DATE. December 1974 per Johnson (Flat Earth News, Dec 1978). No other source located gives any death date for her at all — not Schadewald, not the Wikipedia articles on Samuel Shenton or Charles K. Johnson, not the Johnson obituaries. Uncorroborated and movement-internal; if published it must be labelled as Johnson's claim. It also creates a tension worth noting: Schadewald's membership card, paid up to 1977, still lists her as honorary secretary, so the title was posthumous decoration rather than an office she held.

SPELLING OF HER NAME. 'Lillian J. Shenton' in Johnson's newsletters (Dec 1978, June 1979) and in his IFERS flyer, and 'Lillian Shenton' in Wikipedia. But the IFERS-of-America membership card — the primary artefact — prints 'Lilian Shenton', with one medial L. Use 'Lillian J.' as the main form and footnote the card's variant rather than silently normalising a primary source.

Chapter number — RESOLVED as an edition artefact, report it rather than picking: the 2006 CD first edition credits Bennett with CHAPTER 12 ('In Chapter 12, Robert has written a detailed, technical and mathematical explanation'); the 2013 seventh edition credits him with CHAPTER 10. I confirmed the text is the same chapter, renumbered. The edge agent's 'ch. 12' and my 'Ch. 10' are both correct for their respective editions. Any published wording must name the edition.

The book contradicts itself about how much Bennett wrote. About the Authors (2013) says Sungenis 'authored all the chapters and appendices ... except for Chapter 10', but in the same volume Chapter 11 ('The ALFA Model') carries 'Dr. Robert Bennett / e-mail: robert.bennett@rcn.com' as its byline and Appendix 3 is headed 'By Dr. Robert Bennett'. Bennett's authored share is therefore at least Ch. 10 + Ch. 11 + App. 3, not Ch. 10 alone.

Publication year, unchanged from the existing project note: the CD first edition's PDF metadata is dated 14 June 2006 and carries ISBN 0-9779640-0-0; Answers in Genesis (Faulkner 2020) says 2007; the NPA wiki says Vol. I 2007. Existing house rule (2006, footnote 2007) survives this pass.

Proximate route to Dubay is NOT settled. Two candidates, and I am not choosing. (a) Direct from Galileo Was Wrong: the wording is in the June-2006 edition under Bennett's chapter credit, six years before Dubay's earliest datable version. (b) Via Malcolm Bowden: the Flat Earth Society wiki and (per the edge report) Dubay's own IFERS forum credit a Bowden video for this material, and Bowden's video description carries the same sentences in a slightly altered form ('Airey', 'If it was the telescope moving he would have had to change the angle') — and Dubay's trailing sentence in The Atlantean Conspiracy matches BOWDEN's form, not GWW's. I could not date Bowden's original video: the only copy I could reach is a 2020 third-party Vimeo re-upload, the YouTube original (87M2i61N1cU) returned no usable metadata, archive.org CDX rate-limited me, and I did not locate this wording in Bowden's True Science Agrees with the Bible (1998), whose text I could not reach. So the direction Bennett→Bowden is likely on dates but NOT established; Bowden→Bennett is not excluded by anything I found.

Mark J. Wyatt remains an unresolved possible intermediary (edge report): Dubay names Wyatt's 'Is Geocentricism Possible?' in the same passage, and the 2006 edition's copyright page credits illustrations to Wyatt 'used by permission', so Wyatt sits inside the GWW project. I did not locate Wyatt's article.

ALFA's first presentation: NPA wiki says 2011; Todd Wood's first-hand attendance report puts an ALFA talk at the November 2010 conference and Bennett's own ALFA Challenge blog is posting from December 2010. Prefer 2010 on the eyewitness plus the dated blog, but report both.

Plagiarism allegation vs. what the chapter actually shows. Palm (2014) alleges Bennett paraphrased Ashby and Kelly without attribution at specific pages of the 9th edition. In the 7th-edition scan I searched, Chapter 10 credits 'A.G. Kelly' by name in the two places I inspected (Sagnac stationary-lab; Hafele-Keating) and returns zero occurrences of 'Ashby'. So attribution is present in some places and alleged absent at particular pages I could not check (I did not have the 9th edition). I located no response by Bennett to the plagiarism charge in the searches I ran, though he did post a substantive reply on the same site on a different point.
Bennett's dates rest on one self-submitted profile (NPA wiki, 24 July 1940). Not corroborated in any source I reached. Do not publish a birth date as fact.

NAME COLLISION — flag before any automated enrichment: there is a different, unrelated Dr Robert Bennett in physics at the University of Glasgow with a ResearchGate profile. Nothing about him belongs in this dataset.

SPELLING OF THE NAME — four forms, all documented, none obviously wrong. The German national authority file (GND 113667779) prefers 'Schöpfer, Karl'; the German book imprints catalogued in K10plus read 'Carl Schöpffer' (double f); Scientific American printed 'Dr. SCHŒPFER' on the article and 'Shcepfer' [sic] in its author index; the 1900 New York title page reads 'Professor C. SCHOEPFFER'. Schadewald writes 'Dr. Schoepfer'. Do not silently normalise — pick a house form and record the variants.

WHICH PRE-MODERN SYSTEM HE BELONGS TO. Schadewald (Plane Truth ch. 4) calls him 'a follower of Ptolemy'. Frank Allaben, in the 1900 edition, says he 'maintained the truth of the Tychonian theory, founded on the supposition that the earth stands still in space, that the sun revolves around the earth, and that the planets … revolve about the sun'. Those are different systems. I read only parts of the lecture (the surviving clipping and sampled passages of the 1900 translation) and did not settle it from his own text; the passages I did read defend the rotation of the celestial sphere, which fits Schadewald. Report both.

DATE OF THE LECTURE PAMPHLET. Wikis (de.wikipedia, kookscience) give 1853 for Die Erde stehet/steht fest. K10plus holds only Berlin 1868 printings, explicitly '6. Aufl.' and 'Aufl. 4'; the 1900 New York edition cites a 7th edition, Berlin 1868. The 1853 first-edition date is not confirmed by any catalogue record I retrieved, but an 1854 open-letter rebuttal (Capaun-Karlowa) and an 1855 chapter-length 'Kritik der Dr. Schöpffer'schen Theorie' (Fleischhauer) put the work in circulation by 1854 at the latest.

DEATH DATE. GND gives '1876' with no month; de.wikipedia gives 1876; the kookscience wiki gives 'December 1876, age 64', which does not reconcile with the 13 March 1811 birth all three agree on. Use '1876'; do not publish a month.

URANOS DATE. K10plus: Leipzig, Henning, 1857, marked '2. Aufl.' Wikis: 1856. These are probably the second and first editions rather than a contradiction, but I did not locate a catalogue record for an 1856 printing.

WHICH LANGUAGE BLAVATSKY TRANSLATED FROM — unresolved, and it changes who the intermediate carrier is. Her English title and subtitle track the Russian edition (St Petersburg 1876: 'Zemlja nepodvižna' = 'the Earth is motionless'; 'Populjarnaja lekcija, dokazyvajuščaja, čto zemnoj šar ne vraščaetsja ni okolo osi, ni okolo solnca' = 'a popular lecture proving that the terrestrial globe rotates neither about its axis nor about the sun') far more closely than the German ('Die Erde steht fest' = 'the Earth stands fast'; 'Beweise, dass …' = 'proofs that …'; no 'popular'). Blavatsky was Russian. That is suggestive, NOT documented: I have no statement from her or from Scientific American about the source text, and the correspondence could be coincidence. Flag it as a hypothesis if it is used at all.
